div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

SOME very unscrupuloas person has defined a Chinese policeman as an "Asiatic collarer." WHY is a spendthrift like a restive horse ? Because he plunges into difficulties, and gets into axrear. Miss DE PINK (at a ball): "Be careful, Joshua, and do not step on my dress." Country Cousin: "Oh, I'm looking out for that. I noticed it had slipped down." FOND MOTHER: "So you are pleased with Mr. Grool, Amelia!' Fond Daughter: "I ant; he's a man after my own heart." "Are you sure of that?* "Quite sure; be asked me for it last evening." PaorEssoft or CHEMISTRY: "Gentlemen, I bola In my hand a phial of soda- What chemical shall I combine with it to produce a valuable article of commerce?" Goodsby, waking up: " Br-r-randy l" A TRAVELLER inquiring at a feudal castle whether he could see the antiquities of the place, received the simple answer from a servant, "I am sorry, sir, my lady and her daughter have gone to town.' "No," said a bride to her father, "there is no need of you going with me to the altar. I pre- fer to go without you. Tye been a great flirt, you know, and I don't want youth give me away." "WHAT nonsense!" exclaimed Bertha, "The idea of telling Mrs. Brown that you were only twenty three!" "Bat didn't I do right, dear I" replied Edith. "You know mamma has always taught us not to exaggerate. It is better to under rather than over state, you know." HERE is a gem by Sir Boyle Roche—one of the least known of his many masterpieces:—" Mr. Speaker, it is the duty of every true lover of his country to give his last guinea to save the remainder of 'his fortune." BRIGHTLY—" What would you do, doctor, if you bad a bad cold r Doctor (crushingly)—" I'd con- sult a reputable physician, sir!" Brightly (calmly) —" I don't suppose you could tell me where I could find one, doctor, could you r "Come and dine with me to-day, Grindstone," said Kiljordan, "the bill of fare will just suit you. Calves' brains is the principal dish." "I'll come, Kiljordan," said Grindstone, "in order that you may have one man at the table who can eat calves' brains without making a cannibal of himself." A WITTY old physician, on meeting a neighbour's ducks in the road, was saluted with the usual "Quack, quack, quack I" "See, here," he cried to the neighbour: " keep .these ducks at home, or I'll shoot 'ern. They're always indulging in personal remarks." DENNIS: "Mike, they tell me you 'ye quit work- ing in the powder factory. Is that true?" Mike: "Yes, indeed." Dennis: "What did you quit for? Was it too dangerous?" Mike: "Faith,' an it was. I believe that if I had worked there till this time, I'd a been dead a year ago." " BRIDGET," said a lady to her domestic, "where is the dust•pan ?" "With the broom, ma'am." "And where is the broom f" "With the dust-pan, ma'am." "Well, Bridget, tell me—wbere are they both!" "Sure they are both together, ma'am.' The mistress gave up in despair. AlartimEr., referring to M. Viennet, of the French Academy, observed: "We must not speak ill of his tragedies. At the siege of Leipsic he had one in his pocket. A cannon-ball struck against his breast; but the tragedy saved him. The missile had not strength enough to go beyond the third act." "I BELIEVE you're a fool, John," testily ex- claimed Mrs. Miggs, as her husband unwittingly presented her with the hot end of a potato-dish, which she promptly dropped and broke. "Yes," he added, resignedly, "that's what the clerk told me when I went to take out ray marriage licence."

" You'LL be glad to hear, John," said a farmer to his shepherd one day, "that the University of St. Andrews has made our minister a doctor." "I am oacways surprised at that," said the shepherd. "Mair than twenty years syne he cured my wife o' a colic. I think be should hae been made a doctor tang sync!" AN OLD RUSTIC (looking at his railroad ticket dubiously): "See here! I wanted a roan' ticket for Sempville, mister." "You have one, sir." "See 'ere, young man, ye may be smart enough to run a railroad, but ye can't run it into me that that 'ere aquae piece of paper's routf—allowin.. I be sixty years old the first day of next April." THE obliging visitor, to show that he is really fond of children, and that the dear little one is not annoying him in the least, treats the kid to a ride upon his knee. "Trot I trot! trot! How do you like that, my boy? Is that nice?"" Yes, sir," replied the child; "but not so nice as on the real donkey— the one with four legs." HOSTESS: (to Bobby, who is dining out with his mother): "Will you have another piece of pie, Bobby 7" Bobby: " Yes'rn," Hostess (smilingly): "And so you are one of the fortunate little boys whose mammas let them have a second piece of pie?" Bobby: " Yes'm; she does when we're out visitia', but at home I never get but one piece." RUNNING NO RISKS.—" Now, Johnnie, go and kiss your little sweetheart and make it up, ' said Johnnie's mother. "No I won't." "Go and tell her how much you love her, and how sorry you are." "No, I won't. Pa says he got into a breach of promise case by tellin' a girl that, and had to marry the old thing. I won't run any risks, I won't." A HACK driver comes near running down an old woman, but by great exertion succeeds in clearing her, and is congratulated on his skill by all observers "It was a close shaver cried the Jehu. "I was scared, because she would have been the thirteenth that I had run over this month, and thirteen is always an unlucky number for me." MIRANDA: "Well, Eliza, how do you like your husband ?" "He is a villian.' Miranda: -"All men axe; but what has he done?" Eliza: "You know he was a widower. Well, I've found out that all love letters to me were copied verbatim from the ones he wrote to his first wife when they were courting." Miranda: "Well, I wouldn't mind it. That's all past and gone. He never will send you any more." A YOUNG man at college wrote as follows to his father: "My dear father, I have only time—being greatly rushed with my studies—to send my love, and tell you that I wish you would send me 50 dols." The father replied: "My dear son, I have only time—being greatly rushed with my hay—to send love, and tell you that I have not sent you 50 dols."

THERE formerly lived in Kentucky a mischievous negro named Jake who was continually being brought up for stealing. One of Jake's arraignments was for the theft of a chicken. He was defended by his wealthy young master, Winston Jones, in a maiden speech, behaving just commenced the prac- tice of law. The forensic effort was a good one, but did not save the thief, and the judge said: "The Court sentences the prisoner to one week's imprisonment." Jake—" I thank you, Massa Judge; I thank you, sir; I thank you." Judge—" What are you thanking me for, Jake r Jake—" Why, I was s-fearin' that my character and Massa William's pleadin' would 'ave hung me I" STRANGER (at the door)—" I am trying to find a lady whose married name I have forgotten, but I know she lives in this neighbourhood, She is a woman easily described, and perhaps you know her —a singularly beautiful creature, with pink and white complexion, sea-shell ears, lovely eyes, and hair such as a goddess might envy." Servant— " Really, sir, I don't know ." Voice (from head of stairs)—"Jane, tell the gentleman I'll be down in a minute." "WHAT a resemblance there is between you and your husband, Mrs. Smith?" said a friend of the family. "Did anyone call attention to it before?" "Oh, yes!" broke in Fenderson, who always blunders. "They were walking down the street Vother day, and I heard a man remark, 'How much that woman looks like her son r No, no; that wasn't it," added Fenderson, seeing the cloud on Mrs. Smith's face; "what he said was, 'How much that old fellow looks like his mother 7" ON one occasion (says Lord Campbell) when Lord Eldon's merits were discussed among some lawyers, warm partisan of the Chancellor extolled him as "pillar of the Church." "No," retorted another, 44 he may he one of its huttreAses, but certainly not one of its pillars, ior he is never seen inside its walls.' LADY to chemist—" Have you any reliable corn solvent, something you can recommend?" "Cer- tainly, madam, here's an article. One customer of mine has been using nothing else for fourteen Tears." UNDESERVED adulation, expressed in poetic language, is now called "fancy soap," which is sup- posed to be an improvement upon the more vulgar term of "soft soap." "UNCLE JOHN, said a little girl to a Wall-street magnate, "what is a railroad puol 7" Uncle John: "A railroad pool, my dear, is where they water the railroad stock." A LAWYER was summoned as witness in a certain case. The judge, finding that the witness was lying badly, interrupted him, saying, "I beg you to forget your profession for a moment and tell us the truth."

div.head: " CAPIT.t'LL CHAT."
div.p: " CAPIT.t'LL CHAT."

The indefatigable 'and übiquitous Colonel North, it is stated, has a new project on foot. He has recently been pang a visit to the Channel Islands for the ourpos,d, it is understood, of considering the question of purchasing the many guano works in , the islands and of organising a syndicate for that purpose.

In politics Canon Liddon was a Liberal, but the only question in which he took a prominent part was the discussion of Lord Beaconsfield's Eastern policy. He accompanied Canon McColl in his tour through the Balkans, and the atrocities which they witnessed led Canon Liddon to attack the Jingoes when they returned.

The last sermon which Dr. Liddon preached was in St. Mary's, Oxford, on Whit-Sunday last. It touched on the great controversy which has arisen out of " Lux Mundi," but he did not take any side on the question. Dr. Liddon's fame as a preacher was as wide as the English-speaking world. On Sunday afternoons at St. Paul's, when he was in residence, all Christians of whatever denomination rushed to hear him. He always read his sermons, and was not very successful as an extemporary speaker. Canon Liddon was never married.

I hear that Mr. Gladstone was much touched when quite, recently a well-known society lady, who like himself has passed the threescore years and ten, wrote to him expressing her admiration for the articles in "Good Words." It elicited such a letter as Mr. Gladstone alone could write to one whom he and others had only suspected of being une grande dame.

The Duke of Connaught is going to join the roll of royal authors. According to "Vanity Fair," he has been employing his leisure at Balmoral in preparing the book which is to be issued as a sou- venir of his sojourn in India and of his voyage round the world. The Duchess has completed her list of illustrations.which are taken from her own sketches made on the spot.

Poor Dhuleep Singh! He has to go on his knees again. When he rebelled against the Queen's auth- ority, he returned to her Majesty the insignia of the Order of the Star of India, of which he was a Grand Commander. Now the Maharajah wants to get these precious articles back again, and he has had to petition the Queen for them. But I think her MajesZy may well draw the line at this point. In any case Dhuleep Singh has not yet had his request granted, and I should imagine the matter might well be relegated to the dim and distant future.

Cardinal Manning does not, I am told, entirely approve the conduct of his colleague in Canada in declining to sit at Lord Stanley's table because he was not placed next to Prince George of Wales. Cardinal Manning thoroughly understands the rules of precedence, and is aware that the position ac- corded to himself upon the Housing of the Work- ing Classes Commission was matter of courtesy rather than of right. Mr. Gladstone does not walk away from the Speaker's table because he is called in to dinner after Lord Hartington, or even Lord Carmarthen.

A discussion as to the largest parish church in England has been provisionally settled in favour of St. Nicholas', Yarmouth. The smallest is either the old church at Bembridge, in the Isle of Wight, or a church in one of the Dorsetshire parishes. St. Michael's, Coventry, which is 280 ft. long, including the tower, which has recently been opened to the church by the formation of an arch, includes in all 22,864 superficial feet. But St. Nicholas's, Great Yarmouth, claims to have 23,265 superficial feet,and therefore to be the largest of the strictly parish churches in England.

Private Thos. Atkins, of whose grievances a great deal has been heard of late, has still another. He is no longer to be allowed the privilege enjoyed by noble lords and his superior officers of remain- ing in debt. A new Army order directs that "when a soldier is in debt, either to the officer commanding his troop, battery, company, or division, or the public, the issue of cash to him should not exceed twopence a day. except in special cases, when the issue at a higher rate will only be allowed by the commanding officer." This regulation will, at all events, tend to keep the unfortunate soldier sober.

Mr. Raikes has issu.d a notice pointing out that it is an offence for any person to issue imitations of postal envelopes, stamps, telegraph forms, postal orders, and postmarks. /In future the Postoffice threatens to carry the la(v to its fullest extent, and seek for penalties not exceeding forty shillings from the instigators of this sort of thing. Another nuis- ance which ought to be put down is even more aggressive. It penetrates to the breakfast table ; and I know of nothing more humiliating than to open, one February morning, a letter in which an important cheque is expected, and find within it a draft drawn on the "Bank of Love." This should be not only criminal, but penal.

The report that the Liberal leaders are in anxious correspondence as to the policy of the Darty upon the eight hours proposal as adopted by the Trade Unions Congress is entirely without foundation. There is no probability that any leading Liberal would support the project in the form in which it was adopted by a small majority at Liverpool. That eight hours is better than nine or twelve, if eight hours could be universal, or even general, as the limit of a day's labour will, as a pious opinion, find a good many supporters in the next Parlia- ment; but it is quite certain that upon neither side in politics will the trade unions' resolution be endorsed by the leading statesmen.

One of the busiest persons at the Trade Union Con- gress was Mrs. Mole, of Liverpool. Mrs. Mole, like Mr. Hudson, is an instance of a capitalist becoming Socialist. She is the wife of a rich fruit merchant in Liverpool. She sat in a front seat in the gallery in the best position for hearing and seeing the Socialist delegates. No one followed the proceed- ings so closely as she did,and no reporter took more notes. She wrote all the time. Mrs. Mole is a lady of about forty. She dresses with excessive simp- licity. Her most conspicuous garment was a large loose jacket of white material. She wore a plain black felt hat. Mr. Keir Hardie was the guest of [Mrs. Mole during his stay in Liverpool.

Lord Sackville has come in for a good deal of rough criticism for his attempt to levy encroach- ment rent for the Child's Memorial at Stratford-on- Avon. his agent, Mr. G. 11. Brougham Gluier, evidently has a better opinion of him, vid,e this extract from a letter written to the Stratford Cor- poration The present peer is a very liberal man, and if a properly-worded letter asking as a favor that the right to charge a chief rent on the struc- ture should be waived, but at the same time admit- ting that such right belongs to Lord Sackville and cannot be disputed, I have no doubt you will get what you ask for." Apparently the properly-worded letter was not sent, or, if sent, it was not properly worded—like the letter Lord Sackville wrote about the Presidential election.

It is understood that the eight-hours day men upon the Parliamentary Committee of the Trade Unions Congress will as early as possible endeavour to obtain the issue of some general test to be put to the London candidates on this subject, and will instruct their supporters to press hard for pledges of Parliamentary support. It is by no means certain that the Tory candidates will be in all cases the least willing to go with Mr. John Burns in this matter. There are, it is believed, some on each side who will be prepared to pledge themselves to sup- port the eight hours movement. One of the most extreme of the Liberal candidates, Mr. W. Saunders, who is a friend and supporter of Mr. Hy. George, is apparently one of those most threatened with So- cialist rivalry. That a Socialist candidate will go to the poll in Walworth is asserted with unvarying emphasis.

Mr. Michael Davitt, who has permanently taken up his residence in London, is hard at work on the preparations for the forthcoming production of his new paper, "The Labour World.' Of course he is sanguine as to the success of the venture; but the starting of newspapers in London is a perilous business. No matter how good the contents of the journal, or the extent to which it has been adver- tised, the trouble and cost of distribution often upset the best laid plans. Qnite recently a weekly paper, on similar lines to Mr. Davitt's journal, was started under the most favourable auspices. The first num- ber contained contributions from several public men, and everything promised well ; but, unfortu- nately, the newsvendors did not come in their thousands to purchase the paper, as, of course, they ought to have done; and the result was that, after three or four issues, the journal came to a prema- ture end.

The two queens who take most interest in English matters, and who speak our language with marvellous accuracy and purity, are their majesties of Italy and Roumania. The former is supplied with every good English novel—or, perhaps, it would be safer to say with every novel by an author of repute—which appears; of the latter it may almost be said that she is 'plus anglais quo les anglais." Our royalties speak German.

-- It was mentioned some days ago that, roughly speaking,the rainfall of Manchester was double that of London, and that of the Lake District twice that of Manchester, whereupon a correspondent asked for particulars. I made the statement from recol- lection of a speech delivered in Manchester by one of the greatest living authorities some 25 years ago. But I have now referred the correspondent's ques- tion to that authority, and this is his reply "London., 24 to 25 inches Manchester, 36 to 45 to ' 50 inches ; Lake District, 50 to 75 inches; mouth of the Humber, 21 to 22 inches; West Coasts of Eng- land, Scotland, and Ireland, 30 to 50 inches: East Coasts, 20 to 30. A few miles north of Manchester the 36 becomes 59 inches. These figures are approx- imate averages. The minimums and maximums may be roughly obtained by dividing the average by three and adding one-third for the maximum and deducting one-third for the minimum. As, London 24 add 8, which equals 32, which will be a wet year, or deduct -8, reducing average to 16, which will be a dry year. Diagrams for rainfall should always be dotted on the line of average, the mini- mums below and the maximums above.

div.head: OLD TIME TEACHERS.
div.p: OLD TIME TEACHERS.

BY LUKE SHARP. How little the youth of the present day know about rusliments of education as they were acquired by us veterans in the olden time. It appeared to me when I was a boy that the teachers knew every- thing. A more accurate knowledge of the world and of humanity has led ime -since to believe that I was mistaken. I presumethut •-we were a pretty bad lot, taking it all in all, but still, as I think of the punishments, it seems to me that the teacher of that day rather overdid the matter of whippieg. The first teacher at Bruceville was a lady, and as near as I can remember she was very easy with us. The second was a man, and I have little recollection of him except that he was very hard on us. I remember once that he grabbed me by the hair of the head and jerked me over to the other end of the schoolroom and shoved me into the bottom of his desk, which was a tall, pulpit-like structure with a sort of cupboard underneath. In this cramped posi- tion I remained during the forenoon, and the teacher went off at noon, having locked me in there andlorgotten all about me. I will do myself the justice to say that the moment I found that I was left alone there, I braced my back against the back of the cupboard and promptly kicked out the door, bursting the lock and smashing the panel, and thus escaped. Public opinion was rather divided at the time as to whether I was justified in doing what I did or not. But there was no division of opinion about the thrashing I got for it from the teacher in the afternoon. I think a fuss would be mad* about such a thing as that now-a-days, but I kept still, both about the locking up and the whipping after- wards, for fear I should get another at home. The most brutal thrashing I ever received I do not know to this day what it was for. I was sitting in the schoolroom, in which the desks ran entirely round the room, and we sat on benches facing the school wall, while the large space in the centre was occupied by a big box-stove and the classes that were reciting. Of course I have missed many a thrashing which I ought to have received, but on this occasion I was quietly at- tending to my work, when the teacher, with wild, un- governable fury, came over to my side and began lam- basting me over the head and shoulders with a long hickory pointer, which he punished pupils with. It never entered my head to protest against this sort of treatment or to ask any impudent questions 4.s to what it was for. I merely covered my head with my arms and was beaten there until the pointer went into splinters. Then the teacher, apparently relieved, went back to his desk, and that was the end of it. This teacher is at present, I understand, a minister in a village within 100 miles of Detroit. I have often thought it was my duty to take a day off, sometime when busi- ness was slack, and go down and ask him what that thrashing was for. When we got our third teacher in Bruceville, who was also a man, we found him no less severe than the second one. In fact, I think he was even more so. He had a harder row to hoe, perhaps, than another teacher would have had, because we all knew him. He lived a couple of miles back from the villAge on his father's farm and he used to walk in and back again every day. One day he set four of us standing on a bench with dunce caps of paper on our heads. It must not be thought that this igno- minious position was the only punishment, because each of the four had been thrashed until the teacher's strength gave out. He merely added insult to injury by setting us up on the bench. While he was engaged in teaching a class, with his back towards us, the following awful plot was concocted: It was agreed that the leader of the con- spiracy, who was a boy a couple of years older than myself, should cough when the teacher was walking past us, and as soon as he coughed we should jump from our elevated position on top of the teacher. It was estimated that the impetus of this jump would be such that the teacher would be borne to the ground, and as we knew the rest of the pupils would not interfere we agreed to thrash him within an inch of his life, and then break for the tall timber. It was arranged—as well as we could arrange such a momentous matter in a whisper—that when we escaped to the woods we should take up the reputable life of pirates or highway robbers, or some such profit- able and indolent existence as that and never afterwards return to civilisation, unless it was at the head of a f,
rear-

full band who would burn and destroy the village. How- ever, it was agreed that these little details could be left until afterwards, when we mat in the forest which sur- rounded the village. The great thing was to attend to present matters and overcome and pummel the teacher. Duty first and pleasure afterwards. When the teacher finished with the class he was engaged with he was in the habit of walking around the school with his arms behind him and a switch in his right hand, and as he went he showered admonition and blows with equal in- discrimination. As he passed up the big boy gave a cough, and I made a wild leap on the teacher's back Unfortunately, or fortunately as the case may be, the other boys backed out at the critical moment. It was probably better that they backed out there and then than that they should have flunked while we were pirates and highway robbers. The most astonished man in the whole county was that teacher when I landed square on his shoulders. How easily the four of us could have borne him to the ground was shown by the fact that my own jump nearly accom- plished this desirable consummation. The teacher was forced down on his knees and had to spread his hands to prevent himself from lying prone on the floor. When I saw that the other boys did not take the jump, I thought it most prudent not to assault the teacher alone. I therefore did not strike at him as had been arranged. I picked myself up while he rose to the full dignity of out- raged manhood. -
_ 66 What do you mean by that ?" he shouted to me. I replied with the ready prevarication of a school- boy : " I fell from the 15ench, sir. I—I—am very sorry, sir."

" I'll teach you to fall from a bench," he cried, ind then looking at his switch and finding that he had worn it to pieces on us a little time previously, he ordered me to go to the woods, which were near by, and cut a switch to whip myself with. This was a refinement of cruelty that the teachers of that day loved to indulge in. I went out to the wood, and in the fence corner cut a long slender alder branch, which I trimmed neatly and brought it to him. I lingered until it was nearly noon time and then presented the switch. An alder switch is about one of the most innoxious things in nature. I often wonder why a teacher who was raised in the coun- try and among the woods anyhow did not know the utter uselessness of such an instrument of punishment. But this teacher took it in his hand and took me by the collar and dealt me a fearful blow, whereupon the alder switch, being full of pith, went at once to pieces with- out inflicting any injury. This was always considered a very great stroke of humour on my part, although I suffered for it from a genuine blue beech gad, early that afternoon. How- ever, that day was a very notable one in my career, be- cause the heroic leap upon the teacher's back, which the pupils knew the true inwardness of,whatever the teacher might have thought, gave me a sort of recognised rank as being the very worst boy in, the village, and on this reputation I plumed myself for many a day. Before bidding farewell to this teacher I may say that retribution overtook him in the shape of his own brother. He had a younger brother who went to his school, and the teacher was harder on him than any of the rest of us. I always looked on that brother as a sort of heroic fellow from the way he took his terrible thrashings. I never saw him whimper or cry, but he simply grit his teeth and stood it grimly. The teacher, however, over- looked the fact, although he was the elder, that while he was attending school the brother was working hard on a farm, and that the physical condition of the younger was superior to that of the elder. One day, after a par- ticularly atrocious whipping, the brother said nothing until they were going home together, whereupon the younger one, making some remarks about being outside of the precincts of the schoolroom,sailed into the teacher and thrashed him within an inch of his life. After tins episode the teacher resigned, and there were very few mourners in that school when heleft.—"Detroit Free Press."

\TER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 13, 1890 "LANCASHIRE ANECDOTES." I _ NO ROBBERY.
BY EDWIN WAUGH.

We take the following from a series of "Lanca- shire Anecdotes," published, price 2d., by Mr. John Heywood. BOTTLED VOTERS. _ The man at the flower stall, opposite my window, had got a friend with him to-day. The florist had nearly "sold up ;" and he sat upon the empty part of his stall, dangling his legs,and knocking his heels together, with an air of satisfaction it was pleasing to behold. His friend was seated close by, upon an up-turned hamper, under the shelter of the tarpau- lin which covered the stall.
"Well, Jim," said the florist, "who did thae vote for?"
"Nobody."
" He aw'; that ?"

" Aw geet bottle't." " Why; heaw did ta shap that?" "Well, thae knows, when th' nomination wur • o'er, o' Monday, there wur me, an' five moor, we wur sit i'th' Boar's Ted, drinkin' ; an' in coom Joe Buckley, fro Owdham, as breet as a squirrel. 'Neaw lads,' says he, heaw are yo geetin' on? To mun mind an' keep yo'rsels quiet; yo know what a day it'll be to-morn. There'll be nought but fuddlin' agate here, to-day. Ton be gettin into some mak o' lumber, if yo dunnot mind. Aw'd get eawt o'th gate if aw're yo. Aw'll tell yo what,—have a ride o'er to Owdham wi' me,—it'll keep yo eawt o' mis- chief. Aw'll find To summat to heyt an' drink; an' aw'll bring yo back again. Come on! Th' trap's at th' dur, here!' So we went ; an' th' owd lad gay us a good dinner, an' as mich drink as we'd a mind to teem into us. Well, when th' dinner wur o'er, he said, 'Neaw, lads, aw'm beawn a lookin' at a coal pit a bit aboon here; but yo needn't stir. Aw sha'not be aboon an hour or so. May yo'rsels a- whoam. But some on yo would happen like to look at th. pit. Its one o'th' finest i' England.' Well,— we wur ready for aught 'at coom first, just then,— so we agreed to go wi him; an' when we'd bin i'th' bottom o'th' pit an hour or two, they brought word 'at rope had brokken, an' we couldn't get up again till things wur put to read. Well, they fund us plenty o' drink, an we tunned it into us primely, till we o' geet as drunk as Chloe ; an', at last, we fell asleep, some i' one nook, some i' another. Well, —it wur for on i'th' next day afore we coom to. At last, Joe coom, an' he said, ' Neaw, lads, come on Yo'n no time to lose! They'n getten th' rope reet! Let's goo up.' Well,—what dost think ?—when we geet to' top again,—by th' mon,—th' election wur o'er! Eh, I wur some mad !

POACIEER.—Nawe. LANDLORD.—You're walking on my ground. POACHER.—WeII, yo leather-yed, I'm like to walk somebody's ground; I've nuan o' my own.

What mysterious fate Collier anticipated for him- self we do not know; but something terrible no doubt, for he strode down the road hastily without turning round to look after Lucy. She had heard his expressed wish, and blushed and smiled under her wide hat as she pursued her way to her new home.

CHAPTER XXII.- "th DEEP-LAID PLOT." THE papers which Collier, by his presence of mind, had gained, and put into the possession of Sir Walter Watson, were very important. They revealed a diabolical plot which would be more astonishing, by some deemed incredible, did not the annals of rattening, Irish outinge, and French crime: tell us that the facts of life far exceed in horror the imagination of the writer. Yet the men who had planned a swift and sudden death for the large and influential company who had intended travelling upon the railway had no real gtievances to be redressed, and certainly no "grudge" against the ladies and gentleman of the party. They only knew the manager of the works, the locomotive foreman and inspector, and the chair-

CHAPTER XXL AN ILN'TERynnv WITH A SATISFACTORY REMIT. •

STE WALTER WATSON WM furious when he was made acquainted with the results of the insubordi- nation in his pet workshops. He had viewed the strike in the nearest colliery with equanimity, and had even condescended to " chaff " the noble owner,
but a revolt in his own shops and works put things in quite a different light. Whatbusiness had the wortrnen towant moremoney

or time. Were they not mere machines, intended to do a certain amount of work per diem for so much wage? To do Sir Walter justice, he had always treated his men like mschines, and did not hesitate to use them as such, but at the same time he looked after them' and saw they were cared for, oiled and rubbed, but little polished, not nearly so well turned out indeed as the great" Watson" locomotive. Sir Walter, as we have said, was furious, and at break-fast a report of the state of things made him very " touohy. ' Even the sarcasms of his lady wife' failed to penetrate the outer layer of indig- nation which resisted all minor annoyances, and kept his mind unscathed by her shafts of ridicule. This thing had come upon him so suddenly that he had had no time to obtain hands to take the

places of the men, and consequently things went on badly on the line for a few days. The official trial trip of the new engine had to be postponed; the special train and the champagne luncheon; the speeches; and the spending of shareholders' money, had all to be postponed till a more convenient Seasoll. . .

Lady Watson followed her lord and maser into the study to assist him, as she said, in opening his correspondence, but, in reality, prompted by curiosity and to become cognisant of all that was going on. While thus occupied a servant entered and in- formed Sir Walter that a signalman desired to speak to him. _ _

"Show him in here," said Sir Water. "Yes, let the man come in, Johnston," assented the lady, seating herself in an arm chair in a judi- cial manner. She evidently believed that the busi- ness required her exclusive attention. "It's about this strike, I suppose;* said Sir Walter. "I thought the signalmen and pointsmen would be in it." "Let them go about their business," said Lady Watson, indignantly. "What have a pack of men to complain of, I should like to know?" "Not much, indeed," replied her husband. "I have built them cottages, drained their /and, given thorn wages and doctor's attendance gratis, and now they want more pay." "They will only drink it when they have got it," said the lady, contemptuously. "I have no patience with your British workmen as he is here." "You mustn't be led away by prejudice," began Sir Walter.

But just then the door opened, and George Collier entered the room, cap in hand, coolly but respect- fully, in no whit abashed by the presence of such grand people. "New, man, what do you want ? " was Lady Watson's encouraging address. George Collier touched his forehead with his finger, and rep:ied : "Beggin' yer ladyship's ,pardon, my business is with Sir Walter, my lady.' "Quite so, quite so," began the baronet, nervously, but Lady Watson cut him short. "o isolence, if you please, my man; mind your manners. There is no business which I may not hear. So go on at once, and don't be rude if you can help it." Collier glanced at Sir Walter, and then at his wife. _ _ _

"Am I to say what I have to say, Sir Walter, afore the lady?" "Of corn-se, of course," replied the chairman. "Only make haste, for I am very busy." Lady Watson contented herself with casting a contemptuous look at the man, and tnrning up her aristocratic nose at him, and saying: "Yes, be quick, stupid.' " I come here," began Collier, "to tell you, Sir Walter, that the men are all oat on strike at the works, and—" "We know that," said tho railway magnate. "Go 0n.,,

"And sir," continued Collier, "the ring-leader of the business has been tamperin' and endeavourin' to influence the signalmen, drivels, firemen, and shunters." " Well ? said Sir Walter. "Then, sir, the leader—Sandy Sam is his name— had papers, which prove that a most—saving your ladyship's pardon—a most damned plan of Satan's own devisia has been made up to wreck the special trial trip on Thursday." "Indeed," said Sir Walter, rousing himself. "How do you know this?" "Because that man Sam he came into my box last night in the cutting yonder. Ye may remem- ber me, Sir Walter; Collier's my name." "Yes; I remember you were instrumental in'saving my son a short time back." "Are you the man who ran an engine after Mr. Edward and brought him homer' inquired Lady Watson, with some civility and much interest in her tone and manner. "Yes, my lady," replied Collier, respectfully. "Then I am sure I beg your pardon," said Lady Watson. "I took you just now for one of those abominable men who are on strike. Here, take this, Collier; we are very much indebted to you, and Sir Walter shall promote you at once." "We have been thinking of it," said the chairman, "but nothing is arranged. Collier bowed deeply, pulled his hair, and stam- mered his thanks, as he pocketed, in a very crumpled condition the Bank of England note for ten pounds, which Lady Watson had in her gratitude and repentance handed to him. "Now what have you to say about this business, (bluer?" said Sir Walter. "Well, sir, I have brought these papers, which I think will surprise you and show you the evil designs of the men." "How did you become possessed of these ?' asked the chairman, after he had glanced at them. "They appear important, indeed" "Yes, sir. Sandy Sam, he came into my box and wanted to bully me into joinin' the league against the line. Of course, I wasn't goin' to, but I played 'foxy' and led him on to tell me things. I could see he was dangerous, and didn't know how to manage him until he said he wanted to learn the signals' so as to talk with his mates and spoil the traffic. He is a big fellow," continued Collier, after a pause, "and I didn't see my way to tackle him,but I found him easy at last." "You fought, then ?" said Lady Watson. "No, my lady, I offered to show him the private signals." "What!" exclaimed Sir 'Walter. "Told that scamp the signals. Here's a nice mess you have got us into." "No, sir," said Collier, quietly, yet with an eager- ness in his voice. "No, sir. I onlyoffered. I had just released the wires, and I made him a conductor. When the current was going hard it flashed through him, and knocked him senseless. I pretended ha could hear the words in the wire, and I nearly killed him. We've got him at the cottage, and here's his papers." "Bravo, Collier," said this baronet; "you have done well. These papers will give me power to checkmate the men, and they will soon return. I will not forget you. There is a meeting to-morrow, and I will bring your conduct forward. You shall have the next vacant station, or be superintendent here, which ever you like." "I'd rather remain in the neighbourhood, Six Walter, if all the same to you." "So you shall," said the chairman; "I will see about it. Meantime go home, and leave these things with me. I will go and see this Sandy Sam, and send him to the hospital, which is more than he deserves." "Good morning," said Lady Watson, very gra. ciously. "I will see that you are not forgotten, Collier." The signalman, making a respectful revereneq withdrew; and as he walked home he encounterei Lucy Layton, to whom he related his adventure, and the handsome way he had been treated. " Ah, you'll be wanting a wife now George," said his quondam flame, archly; "and I have some news for goo. I've got a nice cottage on the hill. Lady Deane's agent has let me have it cheap; and now I shall be able to---" She suddenly stopped, confused at her folly in so nearly committing herself as to her schemes. "To what ?" asked George Collier. "Nothing," she answered, evasively. "But I need no longer trouble you, George. The child and I will be able to look after each other. Gqpd-bye." "I wish I was its father." said the love-sick signalman, as Lucy left him. "I will be, too, or I'll be danged.---"

Yet to sacrifice these men, to pay off a fancied "grudge," and an imaginary injury, they were willing to consign 100 people to destruction, and if not absolute death, horrible mutilation. Let us see what they intended, and how, under Providence' the scheme "became known indepen- dently of the papers, which were vague, in the hands of Sir Walter Watson. _ _
_ We will disclose this scheme by-and-by, and meantime we will see what stops the astute Sir Walter took to find out whether the danger was imminent or not. _ _

The papers hinted at a revenge; but the nature I of this the engineer who had been deputed to examine the line could not make out. Apparently all was safe. The trains continued to run, in an irregular fashion, it is true ; the passengers were not many, and the goods traffic had been practi- cally suspended for fear of some c.atastitphe, and for want of hands. The railway strike movement was spreading, and threatened at one time to lead to serious con- sequences. The shops were silent, the furnaces cold. Loco- motives were only partially examined, and drivers, guards, and firemen difficult to procure in numbers sufficient to conduct the traffic with due regularity. How was this state of things to be remedied? To surrender would not do. Promises must be kept if made, but Sir Walter was not a man o promise unless he had previously made up his mind to perform anything. Sandy tiara was still lying senseless, and, though not dead, he had received such a shock as would in- capacitate him from work or mischief for some time. No intelligence could, therefore, be expected from him., and yet it was very necessary to discover the meaning of the hints which daily reached the chair- man concerning the instability of the line and the diro consequences that would ensue if a train, worked by strangers, passed over it. "The discovery came about in a curious way, and was made by Edward Watson by what apparently was "the merest accident." .

The lad's engineering tastes had se developed that his indulgent father had determined to have him practically and properly educated for the profession he desired, and, with a view to such a course, he permitted him to accompany the engineer on his surveys &c., and so Edward picked up some con- siderable knowledge of levelling, &c., gained a smattering, of facts, metals, minerals, and the weather eitects upon the former, which would prove useful acquirements in after life. One evening, when returning. along the towing- path of the canal, he was thinking how silent the neighbourhood was. No train was, as formerly, ',fettling over the priftty viaduct that spanned the picturesque dell, in summer so green with fern and leaf, now bare and damp in the. dying year's em- brace—misty and desolate. Edward stood still to gaze upon what he almost regarded as a rain. For nearly a week the traffic had been interfered with, and the angry men de. dared they would wreck any train that passed out ei ft— guided by strangers. They were quite ready and determined to do it. But bir Walter, as his son knew, was not to he baffled. Ile had secured the services of several drivers and firemen, labourers would act as guards, and young Edward himself had volunteered to drive the first train if his father would permit it. This the directors would not allow; but the lad was keenly alive to the necessity for caution, and had inspected the line very carefully with the engineer and "gangers." As he „proceeded along the towing path of the canal, he fancied he perceived a twinkling light in I the darkness of the dell. The railway passed, at a considerable elevation, above the ravine which it spanned upon a simple-looking, and apparently inse- cure viaduct of wood._ - -

The rails were laid upon the timbers, and sup- ported by beams fixed to the sides of the narrow gorge, at the bottom of which, a rivulet -trickled and turned aside to find its circuitous path to the larger stream that fell into the sea higher up the coast. It was in this ravine high up amongst the de- caying bracken and autumnal-tinted foliage, that Edward Watson perceived the light. ,At first the young man was inclined to pass on, for the.evening was damp and chilly. He had a long day's work, and before him, on the morn' he had to accompany the special, train to test the line with his father, the engineer, ;and several drivers and firemen who had been induced to come and assist in working the trains. The plan halleeen:kept secret, and no opposition was euspected from any of the malcontents who had remained quite quiet. - The light kept moving about in a most mysterious manner, like a Will of the Wisp, and after watching it for a time, Edward Watson saw it ascend on one of the supports of the bridge. "Someone is climbing up there. There can be no reason for that. We tested the timbers to-day, and all were right. Fancy old Marston troubling himself about it again." But as he reflected, tho young man perceived another light, then another, till finally four lamps were visible underneath the bridge immediately be- neath the metals. "There is something here we don't knew the meaning of," muttered Edward. "I will make a little closer inspection." He at once left the towing path and ascended the bill; then, turning into the gully, he made his way steadily and as noiselessly as possible up the bed of the rivulet. The lamps were quite distinct now, and occa- sionally a blow of a hammer was heard, echoing from the sides of the ravines. Edward Watson still kept on, and climbing with great caution, succeeded in concealing himself from sight, even had the darkness of the evening not enshrouded him. "The villains! I know them now," he muttered to himself. "There's Coles, Stanley, Rayburn, and Bistlett. Ha, my friends, so I have got you at last." He waited for some time, and saw the men deliber- ately cutting through the supports of the bridge and unscrewing the bolts. Were a train to pass over the metals that night, it would be " wrecked " to a certainty. This, then, was the manner in which the men on strike were about to be revenged upon those who had taken their places. Edward Watson recognised them all by the light of the laiithorns which each man carried; but to make sure the young man waited, and when the men descended from the bridge he followed them. They struck up the gully, and then descended again upon the railway, so that they might remain un- perceived. But they were recognised beyond a doubt. Then Edward hurried home and informed his father of the trap that had been laid by the ringleaders, and the diabolical act they intended to commit. "Leave them to me,' said Sir Walter. "I will checkmate them. I think we'll put an end to the strike now. Edward, you have done a good day' work." "Dear child ! " said Lady Watson, "his he might have been sacrificed." "And many more," said her husband. "Mine amongst them, and the new hands." "They are easily replaced," replied Lady Watson. " Common people like that are very plentiful. I suppose it is a dispensation." "You needn't find fault," said her husband. "Ii It hadn't been for a common person—" " We will not discuss such vulgar probabilities What is must be, I suppose. But about these wretches," asked her ladyship. "To-morrow will find us victors," said the chair- man. "Edward has given us a weapon to meet them with. I intend to invite them to my 'party,' and if they will not come, to carry them, and thea see how they will behave." The matter was discussed, and next morning the train was made ready at the "shops." The neat corners not taking charge, but coming to be in- structed in the signals, and the length of line affected by the strike—some twenty-five miles just then—and all the drivers in the branch Lad struck. A great crowd of malcontents and idlers were

div.head: FIENDISH CRIME IN FRANCE.
div.p: A FIENDISH CRIME IN FRANCE.

For downright cold-blooded deliberation the crime for which a man and woman have just been condemned at the Assize Court of the Department of the Deux Sevres rivals the murder of O'Connor by the Mannings. The victim's wife was a nurse, and the couple lived together at the little township of Broloux. One day last April the poor man's body was found some miles from his abode. There had been foul play, for his legs were tied together with rope, and heavy stones were attached to the body. The skull had been completely battered m, and it was evident that his assailant or assailants had intended to throw the body into a neighbouring stream. After a while suspicion fell on the wife, and eventually, under the searching gaze of a juge d'instruction, the wretched woman confessed that, aided by a man named Lamy, she had indeed made away with her husband. Lamy also confessed soon after being arrested. It had been arranged that they were to murder the husband on the 14th of March last, but on that date he did not re- turn home, and the wretches put off the execution of their project until the following night. On the 15th Lamy came armed with an axe and a razor, and gained admission to the house before the husband's arrival home. Immediately the latter did come he was struck violently from behind with the hatchet, andiell lifeless in the passage. The woman helped the murderer to wash the body and to carry it to the spot where it was found. The couple then went back to the house and regaled themselves with pancakes, which were made by the woman. It is no wonder that even a French jury could discover no extenuating circumstances, and that consequently the criminals were sentenced to be guillotined.

gatheied to see the train off. Amongst the foremost were the four men indicated by Edward Watson. and Sir Walter calling to them, induced them, though with a very bad grace on their part, to ap- proach the train. You know that we have supplied the places of the drivers and firemen, and I am glad to see that no outrage has been committed or damage has been done to the line. lam not wrong in supposing that you, as Englishmen, are above such unfair play." The majority of the men honestly renudiated any underhand proceedings. "Suppose now," continued Sir Walter, "that I asked yen to prove your words. I have acted honestly by you, and until the evil example was set you, you all did well. Suppose I ask for some of you to accompany me as security for the safety of the line?' "We'd go," said several voices. "There's been no underhand dirty work with us. We think we ought to get what we ask for. We fight fair." ,An elderly man stepped forward and said: "Sir Walter, you have always been considerate. We are not murderers. We are striking for a right, not for to injure you personally; and we deny that any one has injured you or yours." "Come with me then, Stanley," said Sir Walter. "Bring your wife and your daughter-in-law and her child, if you like. Anyone may get in and have a ride and a pleasant journey with some beer at the end of it. Come along!" "I'll go," said old Stanley— a kind of patriarch in the neighbourhood—" I'll go, sir, and bring Jane and the young ones." "Don't you be a fool, father," said the youtmer Stanley, who had been seen by Edward Watson the night before. "Don't you go." "Why not? We don't bear malice. There's iv} personal feelin' in it, least not me. No, I'll go, and Jane shall come too." "Jane shan't," replied the a striker." "I'm her mastEr, anyway. r.ou go if ye like, but take the consequences." "He must mean something," exclaimed young Watson, who had received a hint from his father. " They've been doing something underhand, and bringing you all under the law—depend upon it." "If he has he'll smart for it," cried several. "No skulkin'. Come along, lads. We'll take him with us; and you, Coles, you come too." " Net me," replied Coles, shaking his head. "I've an appointment.' "Ye must," exclaimed the men, determined to prove they had been "straight." "You're a leader, and up ye go. Come on, lads; we'll put them in." The two men were hurried into a carriage, and kept there. Several of the children climbed up, and the elder Stanley, with his reluctant son, his wife and children, were all shut up in the train, which two:at least of the party did not believe would ever reach its destination. "Checkmate," cried Sir Walter, as the train started. "Edward, my boy, the strike is over. The question is now settled. We will give them a fright, and you'll nee the men will return. Yonder is the ?WM,. Now for it!" (To hi continued.)

MY OWD LASS!
Aw wodn'd swap, for a King's creawn,
Mi kind °wit lass For nooan con cheer me when aw'm deawn

Like my owd lass. We've jogged together mony a year, Rare chums i' weather dull an' clear, We've laff't wi' glee, an' th heart-wrung tear We've dropt o' t' graveyard grass. For tho aw've mates o' every sooart, Some pious, an' some fond o' spooart, Aw've but one mate whose smile a cooart— That's my owd lass! Her hooamly ways, her blame an' praise, Aw know 'em weel, bi th' mass! An' th, mate for me—so wheer aw be - - Is my owd lass. A hen as tents her chickens weel Is my owd lass. As good as gowd, an' true as steel, Mi fond owd lass. floo's t' best an' dearest, to mi mind, Ov onny aw on Earth cud find; A mate for me bi Heaven designed, 'At's suited me fost-class. Id makes mi heart fair throb an' beawnd Wi pride, when t' childer frolic reawnd, An greet wi' mony a gleeful seawnd Ther mam—th' owd lass! Mi life's as breet an' joy's as sweet

As if aw'd lots o'-binss ; Wod good wur wealth beawt strength an' health, An' my owd lass! Aw cooarted, mi youthful pride, W' my owd lass; An' fain aw wor to mek a bride 0' my owd lass. A better bargain awst neer ged Than thad aw geet when aw wur wed; Wl' th' me:n'ry on't aw'm comforted When grief's black shaddo's pass. Sin t' sunny forenoon o' mi life, Hoo's clung to me 'mong th' tew an' strife, Far mon ne'er hed a better wife

Gri' this shall allus be ml prayer, That Heaven may in id beawnty spare Th' owd conqueror o' hooamly care, Till Time upsets ml glass. Mr. John Dillon, MX., speaking on Tuesday at the fMtnightly meeting of the National League in Dublin, stated that Mr. Tener, Lord Clanricarde's agent, was en- deavouring to get tenants from the North of Ireland for tt'e Woodford estate and had asserted that boycotting had ceased in that district. If Mr. Justice Harrison was right in what he said recently on that subject, then Mr. 'Eerier was not telling the truth ; and if, on the other "arid, Mr. Tener stated facts, Mr. Justice Harrison had no shadow of justification for his remarks. If northern !nen came to terms with Mr. Tener, they would find the efoodford evicted farms an expensive luxury. As for ?onotting, it had, in combination with the feeling of u°Pe which had been inspired in the Irish tenants, done !lions than either police patrols or coercion to put an end u° crime and to induce the people to rely upon moral Methods of agitation. Referring to the failure of the Potato crop in various parts of Ireland, he mentioned as reason why no appeal to charity should be made for e distressed districts, that on former occasions when ramley had been subscribed for the poor tenants, much _ 4fX it had found its way into the pockets of the landlords 4).! rent. The Government had professed themselves r friends of Ireland, and upon them lay the responsibi- itr of coping with the distress now threatened.

Mr. Thomas Birtwistle, secretary to the United Textile Factory Workers' Association and representative of h' ncas ire, in the course of an interview on Monday said his withdrawal from the Parliamentary Committee Of the Trade Congress had the full concurrence of the delegates representing the cottom trade, and would Probably be followed by other resignations—certainly by the resignation of Mr. Mawdsley, the spinners' representative. Before announcing his resignation, Mr. Birtwistle consulted the textile representatives, Who were unanimously of opinion that he could not honourably continue in office. In this view Mr. Broad- hurst and many other leaders concurred. Mr. Mawdsley decided to take the opinion of the council of :tee Spinners' Association, which meets next month, fore taking any final step, and it is generally thought that others will withdraw after consulting their constituents. THE SOUTHAMPTON STRIKE.
MILITARY CALLED OUT.

The strike at Southampton on Tuesday assumed a very serious phase. The large trading companies of the port locked out their employes, numbering about a thousand men. In consequence of the violence of the crowd which assembled in front of the dock gates, the military were summoned, and 250 men of the Yorkshire Regiment, with twelve officers, were sent by the authorities. Several alleged blacklegs were ill-treated. In the afternoon the London Dockers' delegate and the local secretary were charged with having assaulted a watchman, and were ' bound over to keep the peace. Exciting scenes were witnessed in the streets at night, the troops trying to dis- perse the crowd by playing on them with the fire hose. I Ultimately the Mayor read the Riot Act and the military charged the people with fixed bayonets. The strike tilt Southampton caused some excitement and checked business again to a considerable extent on Wednesday. There were further encounters between the crowd and the soldiers, but these were not so serious in character as the disturbances on the previous night. The Mayor's house was menaced, but no damage was done, and the friends of the dockers, though incensed at his Worship's attitude in the dispute, were dispersed with little trouble. Owing to the real of the pickets in pre- venting new hands from entering the docks, even by sea, the Admiralty ordered a patrol of Southampton Water. The masters met yesterday, and urged the men to return to work, saying they weuld give the grievances of the dockers every consideration. The labourers insist on sd. per hour for day work, ed. an hour for night work. and 245. for a week's wages. Mutual efforts at conciliation were put forth yesterday, and it is believed that the strike will soon end, though the masters assert that they cannot pledge themselves to recognise the union only. The representatives of the Southampton dockers held a meeting which lasted from four o'clock till half-past ' seven on Thursday evening, and by a majority of eleven to five it was decided that the men should return to work on the concession granted by the employers a fort- night ago. There was a stormy scene before the vote was taken, but Mr. Tom M'Carthy point- ed out that the men began the struggle with- 1 out first obtaining the authority of the London executive, and under conditions which practically pre- eluded the possibility of success. Afterwards repre- sentatives of the Seamen's and Firemen's Committee were called in and the result communicated to them. Mr. Walsh, the London delegate, being, it was under- stood, in full accord with Mr. M'Carthy. In an inter- view subsequently with a reporter Mr. M'Carthy said the Southampton men chose to begin a fight without first obtaining the authority of the central body, and even after the latter had warned them against it. Local bodies must not take the initiative into their own hands.

div.head: SHOCKING COLLIERY FATALITY.
div.p: SHOCKING COLLIERY FATALITY.

On Monday forenoon, an inquest was held before Mr. 8. Brighouse, coroner, at the Boar's Head Inn, Lea Green, touching the death of Thomas Hitchen, 15 years of age, of 680, Mill-lane, Thatto Heath, son of Thomas Hitchen, under manager of the Sutton Heath and Lea Green Collieries, who was killed in the Lea Green Colliery, on Thursday morning. Mr. H. Hall, Government Inspector of Mines, was pre- sent, and Alr.Pennington, certificated manager, appeared on behalf of the firm. The first witness called was Thos. Hitchen deceased's father, who said his son had been employed in the mine for about eight months. About i half-past seven on the morning in question, he was in his cabin, when he heard a " journey "of coal wagons pass his door. He was then told that something had hap- pened, and on going out into the level he found his son sitting on the first wagon of the "journey." He had his head hanging down, and it appeared to have been crushed against the end wagon of a previous "journey," which was standing in the shunt, near the bottom of the pit shaft. The boy was dead. He thought deceased had attempted to unhook the pony while riding on the wagon, and that he had mis;alculated the distance from the other " journey" of waggons with which they had collided while he was bent down. In reply to Mr. flail, witness said pony-drivers were supposed to get off the waggon before unhooking the pony. He had never before seen anyone attempting to unhook the pony whilst riding on a waggon.—Thomas Balmer, 14 years of age, a door-tenter, said he was rid- ing on the end waggon of the " journey " and deceased rode on the front. When nearing the shunt deceased I leaned over the side of the waggon and the collision took place. The pony was galloping. There were two oil lamps and two torches in the shunt and there was plenty of light to see the " journey " in front, if deceased had looked.—James Farrar, another pony-driver, also gave evidence as to the collision.—Mr. Hall, the Govern- ment Inspector, said that nine out of every ten accidents of the kind were brought about by lads driving too quickly, and in his opinion that was the cause of the present accident.—The Coroner briefly summed up the evidence,and the jury returned a verdict of "Accidental Death."

div.head: LABOUR AGITATION IN AMERICA.
div.p: THE LABOUR AGITATION IN AMERICA.
ATTEMPTS TO WRECK EXPRESS TRAINS. KNIGHTS OF LABOUR ARRESTED.

An attempt was made on Monday night near Pough- keepsie to wreck the St. Louis and Chicago express, leaving New York Central Railway at ten o'clock in the evening. A flagman discovered ties on the track, and on attempting to move them was fired at from some bushes. He then ran to the southward and set the danger signal, thus preventire, the wreck of the train. Some fears are entertained lest the mob may attempt to set at liberty the four men who have been arrested on suspicion of having wrecked the Montreal express last week, on the New York Central Railway. A New York telegram says :—An attempt was made on Monday night to wreck the St. Louis and Chicago express on the New York Central and Hudson River Railway, near New Hamburg, sixty-four miles from New York. The train consisted of ten coaches, including six sleeping cars, which contained 150 passengers. The train left New York at six o'clock in the evening. Some men who were rowing on the river opposite Hamburg, saw suspicious persons working o 1 the line. They alarmed some of the employes of the company, and the line was examined, and it was found that several ties had been taken up and the metals loosed near a deep culvert, into which the scoundrels had evidently intended to throw the train. The St. Louis and Chicago express was due ten minutes after. The discovery was made only just in time to signal the train and prevent a terrible disaster. Detectives and police are scouring the country round about, with the hope of tracing the would-be wreckers. Three more arrests have been made in connection with I the wreck of the Montreal express last week near Bin— mingham. A later despatch says the wreckers fired at a flagman while attempting to remove an obstruction at a culvert to repair the line, but he was unhurt. Advice's from Albany state that the Knights of Labour are intensely excited over the recent arrest of three of their number for alleged complicity in the train wreck- ing at Sloatsburg. They declare their intention to try and procure a habeas corpus to discover the right of the company to tear men from their homes and secrete them without trial.

A Philadelphia correspondent states that four men have been arrested at Albany for placing obstructions on the New York Central Railroad, and wrecking a passenger train on Friday. All are Knights of Labour on strike. One is reported to have confessed, involving others in the crime.

div.head: DEATH OF CANON LIDDON.
div.p: DEATH OF CANON LIDDON.

The death of Canon Liddon, canon resident of St. Paul's Cathedral, occurred on Tuesday forenoon at West- on-super-Mare,where he was staying with a sister, Mrs. King, and her daughters. Death is attributed to syncope, occasioned in all probability by suppressed gent. Dr. Henry Parry Liddon was the son of a naval officer who had settled in Devonshire, where the distinguished preacher was born in 1829. He became a student of 'Christ Church, Oxford, where he graduated 8.A., in 1850, taking a second class in classics. In 1851 lae ob- tained the Johnson Theological Scholarship, and was ordained deacon in 1852 and priest in 1853, proceeding to the degree of M.A. in the last-named year. From 1854 to 1859 he occupied the post of vice-principal of Cuddesdon Theological College, and he was also examin- ing chaplain to the late Bishop Hamilton, of Salisbury. By this prelate, with whom he was on terms of intimate friendship, he was in 1864 preferred to a prebendal stall in Salisbury cathedral. In 1863-65, 1870-72, and 1877- 79 he was a select preacher at Oxford, and attracted large congregations by his discourses. In 1868 he was Bampton lecturer, and from that year until 1875 a member of the Hebdomadal Council at Oxford. In 1870 his merits and abilities were recognised by a cluster of honours and dignities conferred upon him. He was appointed a canon residentiary of St. Paul's Cathedral, and Ireland Professor of Exegesis at Oxford, and at the same time created a D.D. and an honorary D.C.L. As one of the leaders of the High Church party. Dr. Liddon has worked earnestly for the reunion of Christendom. He deeply sympathised with Dr. Dollinger and the "Ord Catholic " movement in Germany, and took part in the Reunion Conference held in Bonn, in 1875. He resigned the Ireland Professorship in 1882, and during the later years of his life it is un- derstood that he had in contemplation a life of the late Dr. Pusey. His published works include " The Divinity of Jesus Christ" (Bampton Lectures, 1886), " Walter Ker Hamilton, Bishop of Salisbury: a sketch, 1869, "Some Elements of Religion" (Lent Lectures, 1870-2), "Sermons Preached before the University of Oxford, 1873," " Report of the Reunion Conference held at Bonn," translated from the German of Professor Reusch, with a preface by H. P. Liddon, D.D., 1876. Dr. Lid- don has also edited Bishop Andrewes' "Manual for the Sick," and in conjunction with Dr. Bright, "English Church Defence Tracts," 1872. But it was chiefly as a preacher that Dr. Liddon was known to the majority of , his countrymen. When he preached on Sunday after- noons the great basilica of St. Paul's was filled with a sea of upturned faces, which seemed to hang on his im- passioned utterances.

Two examples of the Chinese alligator have just reached the Zoological Gardens. They are the first that have been ever exhibited here alive. The alligator is so distinctively an American animals-that the proof, so recently as 1879, of the existence of a species in China was extremely interesting. Nevertheless, the Chinese classics contained numerous references to the creature, and even pictures, which could be easily recognised as being meant for a crocodile of some sort. It is to be hoped that the specimens at the Zoo will bear out the notion of the extreme longevity of the reptile. Its name is apparently used in certain parts of China in the same sense as Methusaleh in this country. Marco Polo wrote about thia animal, and recommended its gall as an excellent remedy for the bite of a mad dog and for various other complaints, so that it seems to have been the mediceval equivalent,of some of our much-advertised remedies of the present, day. Curiously enough, the beast is even now made use of in Chinese medicine.

div.head: LIQUOR AND LAUDANUM.
div.p: LIQUOR AND LAUDANUM.
TERRIBLE ASSAULT ON A WIFE.

A more terrible picture of the miseries wrought In poor men's households by the use of intexicants has rarely been drawn than that which came forth in the evidence given in the Preston Police Court lathe case of a man named Moss, who was sentenced to three months' im- prisonment with hard labour for an aggravated assault upon his wife. Moss, it appeared from the eviclence of his victim and her daughter, came home the worse- for drink, cursing and swearing vengeance against his wife. The woman at the sound of his voice had takerenefuge in a cupboard beneath the stairs; but the brut& overcame her efforts to hold the door, dragged her forth by% the hair of her head, and dashed her to the ground, breaking her arm. He then possessed himself 4 a shovel and beat her about the head with it till she was insensible. For such brutality the sentence, together with the separation order, was certainly not excessive; but the cross- examination of the woman suggested only too plainly the causes of her husband's fury, and it might be of his drunken habits. Mrs. Moss, in brief, confessed that she was an habitual laudanum drinker, and that for twenty years she had been the slave of this degrading vice. An ounce and a half a day was, she said, the quantity she consumed. "She cannot live without it," said her daughter, adding that after her mother had taken it "she could work like a black." This indeed was the man's excuse; and the daughter admitted that her father was accustomed to give his money to her,about a pound , a week, because her mother pawned his clothes and ap- plied the money in getting drink.

div.head: WOMEN'S HAPPIEST HOUR."
div.p: WOMEN'S HAPPIEST HOUR."

Under the influence of that universal inquisitiveness I which is a prevailing characteristic of modern periodical literature, an American journal has started the question "Which is Women's Happiest Hour ? " As the journal in question is specially designed for women, its readers ought to be qualified to throw light on this interesting question; yet the replies are curiously divergent. "When love is a shy new comer, and hopeleads it by the hand," seems too vague and general. It is too much like the "toasts and sentiments" of other days. On the other hand, the notion that a woman "is most happy when, having brought a man to the point of proposing, she makes him wait a minute or two for an answer," is obviously too suggestive of the hardened flirt. This correspondent is very properly rebuked by one of her own sex, who would prefer "the feelings of the woman who gives herself freely and gladly to the one she loves." One correspondent "doul not think she has had her happiest hour yet f another, with the lack of logic which old-fashioned men delight to charge the other sex with, recalls two "happiest hours." One was when she visited Stratford-on-Avcn, another when she arrived at Bayreuth to hear "Parsifal" for the second time. It will be perceived that temperament has some- thing to do with these answers. One despondent person declares her belief that "the happiest hour of a woman's life is her last, because then she knows that her toils and troubles are over." Against this we are enabled to set the cheerful good sense of the mother who advises those who want to know happiness to realise Emerson's motto, " Help somebody," and who affirms that the happiest of all hours in her own life have been those spent in wit- nessing the development of her only child.

TERRIBLE Missicass By DAHONIETANS.—NPWS has been received in Paris of a terrible massacre by the Dahomeyans. After destroying thirty villages belong- ing to the Egbas tribe, they took 3,000 prisoners, and killed the children who were too young to carry off. King-Behauzin then marched into the interior and took 2,000 additional prisoners, killing 1,000 of the women. Mn. MILITARY INSUBORDINATION AT CORK.

On Tuesday, at Cork, the troops were on brigade drill in the park. Having returned to barracks several notices of courts-martial were read out before the men, five of them being appeals against sentences of the com- manding officer. On the cases being announced three men out of the five deliberately and in the most insubor- dinate manner flung dc,wn their helmets, and stood forward to receive punishment. The sentences being pronounced, three of the men threw down their helmets,, and refused to take them up until forced to do so at the point of the bayonet. They hen put them ogOhe wrong way, and made faces at their officers. Whenlhey were marched off under arrest, they went in a most defiant manner.

div.head: IRISH CENTENARIANS.
div.p: IRISH CENTENARIANS.

People are slow to believe in centenarians now-a-days, and demand strict evidence on the point of age. Regis- tration returns were not in past times kept with suffi- cient care to supply clear proof; and in the absence of public records from remote periods, it is not yet possible to verify absolutely the eggs of very old people. Still, the Registrar-General for Ireland has been able to satisfy himself,that his returns of centenarians are fairly reliable. His tables show that last year 195 persons-79 males and 116 females—died at the age of 100 years or upwards. He made special inquiries into these cases. It was found, he says, in almost every instance that, so far as the Re- gistrars could ascertain, the ages was correctly stated, and in many cases historical references were given as collateral proof that the entries were reliable. The good old age of 95 was attained io Ireland by 662 persons- -306 males and 356 females.

div.head: BRITISH ASSOCIATION.
div.p: THE BRITISH ASSOCIATION.

The sectional meetings of the British Association were resumed at Leeds on Tuesday, when a large number of interesting papers were read and discussed. In the Geo- logical Section the principal topic of interest was in refer- ence to the discoveries of coal in Kent and Sussex. Mr. Whittaker made some practical suggestions as to future borings, based mainly on the result of borings already made. In the Geographical Section Miss Dowle, the granddaughter of the late Mr. R. Chambers, described her adventures during an expedition which she made through Ruthenia, in South Poland, attended only by a peasant. Mr. T. Crook read a paper in the same section on the state of the Ordnance Survey, in the course of which he entered a strong protest against the mode in which the work of the department was carried out. He read aletterfrom Sir Charles Wilson,who said that no one could be more alive to the necessity for a revision than the directors of the survey, but the department had not a free hand in the matter. It was agreed that a resolu- tion should be drawn up for the consideration'of the Corn- mittee of Recommendations. In the Economic Section Mr. G. H. L. Pickard read a paper on "Factory and Workshops Acts, past and present," in the discussion on which several gentlemen having a local and practical knowledge of the conditions of factory life took part. Mr. W. H. Preece, the post-office electrician, in the sec- tion devoted to mechanical science, contributed a 'paper on the form of submarine ,cables for long distance tele- phones. The proceedings of the British Association practically closed on Wednesday, when only four sections sat, the remaining four having finished their business on Tues- day. In the Mathematical Section Professor Barrett read a paper giving the principal details of the report of a committee appointed to investigate molecular phe- nomena attending the magnetisation of iron ; in the Geological Section Mr. Lobley read a paper on" The origin of gold " ; and in the Economic Section Mr. E. L. K. Gounor discoursed on "Drawbacks of mcdern economic progress." Mr. William Thomson, Manchester, brought before the Chemical Section the subject of the unburnt gases emitted from gas stoves. The General Committee met in the afternoon, when grants amounting to £1,335 were made to various committees for scientific purposes. It was announced that for the Leeds meeting 1,775 tickets were taken, and that the total amount received was £1,776,
