A MYSTERIOUS DEATH.

STRANGE CONDUCT OF BOYS. A remarkable story comes from Preston. A boy named Bunting went out with several comrades to play a few days ago, and never returned. His playmates, after some pressure, said that while he was swinging on the Jib of a crane he fell into the canal and was drowned, phough they tried repeatedly to rescue him. For , many days the canal has been dragged, but in I vain. On Thursday the body was discovered, not In the water, but buried beneath a heap of sand ;at the rear of a block of new houses in the town. Two of Bunting's playfellows made, during Wednesday after- noon, an extraordinary confession to a detective. They •said efforts were made to rescue the lad, but when he was dragged to the bank he was dead. They carried the body through the streets in the direction of Bunting's home, but, fearing that they would be blamed for his death, they dug a grave with slates, at the rear of the ' new houses, and buried him.

div.head: MIL BRITNNER'S SON DROWNED IN
div.p: MIL BRITNNER'S SON DROWNED IN

ITALY. News reached Northwich on Tuesday morning that Mr. Sydney Brunner, second son of Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., had been drowned on the previous night on Lake Como, near Bellagio. Further parti- culars were received on Thursday. From a hurried note received by the family, it appears that Mr. Brunner, M.P., with his two sons and Mr. Robert Mond, had taken a boat on the lake on Monday afternoon in order to bathe. There was a very strong wind at the time, and the water was very rough. While the two young men were in the water the boat became unmanageable:through the violence of the storm, and wa&blown far away from the unfor- tunate bathers, so that those in the boat were unable

to render them any assistance beyond throwing overboard every available article which could aid in supporting them. By the time assistance reached the spot, Mr. Sydney Brunner had sunk, and Mr. J. F. L. Brunner, his brother, was rescued in an ex- hausted condition. The deceased was in his 24th year, and notwithstanding a serious illness at Christmas, he left Winnington Old Hall, Northwich, on Thursday previous to the accident in the best of health and spirits. According to a telegram received at Northwich, the body was recovered on Thursday morning.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting of this Authority was , held at the Workhouse, Dutton, on Tuesday. Col. Ashton presided, and there were also present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Aaron, W. Whitlow, Heywood, Brandreth, Parr, Baguley, and Jackson; H. Linaker (clerk), IL G. Livaker (assistant clerk), and Farrington (nuisance inspector).

div.head: RE APPOINTMENT OF NUISANCE INSPECTOR.
div.p: RE APPOINTMENT OF NUISANCE INSPECTOR.

Mr. Aaron, in accordance with noticeof motion, moved that Mr. Farrington be re-appointed nuisance inspector at £l4O a year, and canal boat inspector at £lO a year. --The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner seconded.—Mr. W. Whitlow: I think he works as hard for his money as most of the officials do.—The motion was agreed to unanimously.

THE ALLEGED POLLUTION OF KECETVICK BROOK. A letter was read from the Local Government Board In reference to the application of the Rural Sanitary Authority for consent to institute proceedings under the Rivers Pollution Prevention Act, 1876, against Messrs. W. R. Earp and Co., of the tannery, Preston-o'-th'-Hill, In respect of the alleged pollution of the Keckwick Brook by refuse from the tannery. The Local Government Board stated that they had determined to hold a local inquiry to be held on the subject by one of their inspec- tors. The inquiry would take place ELS soon as the engagements of the inspectors would permit and due notice would be given. They also wished to know as early as practicable of the precise place at which the inquiry could be most conveniently held.—Mr. Aaron said he understood the brook was now a good deal clearer than it used to be.—Mr. Whitlow: It is worse than I ever saw it.----Mr. Aaron thought they should press the Local Government Board to hold the inquiry as soon as pos- sible.—Mr. Brandreth : I suppose you will have to bring up those who first made the change ?—The Clerk said they would give notice to Mr. Evans when the in- quiry was to be held, and he would have to come for- ward to make his complaint.—lt was agreed on the motion of Mr. Aaron. seconded by Mr. Brandreth, that the inquiry should be held at the Red Lion Inn, Preston Brook.

ARE WATER ANALYSES RELIABLE? A discussion took place with regard to the alleged pollu- tion of a well at Halton Gate. It was stated that the water from this well had been analysed ,apd the analyst had re- ported that it was a second-class water, but fit for domes- tic use.—Mr. Whitlow said he had himself seen impuri- ties from a pigsty running down the sides of the well. lie very much questioned the analysis,and suggested that another analysis should be had.—Mr. Farrington corrob- orated the statement of Mr. Whitlow as to the pollution of the well,and said he had been surprised by the result of the analysis. It was decided to instruct Mr. Farrington to send another sample for analysis. This was the principal business.

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Colonel Ashton presided, and there were also present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Rev. Dr. Gastaldi ; Messrs. Baguley, Brandreth, W. Whitlow' Jackson, Grice, Heywood, Fisher, Aaron, Philips, Parr; H. Linaker (clerk), and 11. G. Linaker (assistant clerk).

DOCTORS' CHARGES. Mr. Brandreth called the attention of the Board to what he considered were heavy damages made by two War- rington doctors who had been called in to certify as to the condition of a lunatic. He found that at Chester the medical fee was only 10s. 6d., and he did not see why they should pay so much more.—Mr. Fisher thought that 10s. Bd. would be a very small professional fee for coming all the way to that Workhouse.—The Clerk said that at Chester the Workhouse was only about a ten minutes walk away.—After some further conversa- tion it was decided to leave the matter over, Mr. Bran- dreth remarking that it might be brought up again if need be. THE CALLS .-AN IMPECUNIOUS rowssinP. Mr. Brandreth reported that all the calls had been paid with the exception of that of Hatton which was due on the Bth August. Letters had been received from the assistant overseer of that township in which he expressed regret that they had not been able to meet the call of £45. In a second letter he said he could not get the rates in.—Mr. Parr : It is not for want of looking after I can tell you.—Mr. Aaron said it was high time that that sort of thing was stopped and he moved that the overseers be summoned. He did not believe in making fish of one and flesh of another. He held it was not the overseers but the assistant overseers who were to blame.—Mr. Parr said that in the case of Hatton it was not the assist- ant overseer who was to blame, and Mr. Aaron was talk- ing of what he knew nothing about. He thought the assistant oversecr of Hatton went for the rates about twice a week, but he could not get blood out of a post, and if farmers had not the money they could not pay the rates.—The Chairman said there was no seconder to Mr. Aaron's proposal, and consequently it fell through. THE ESTIMATE. Mr. Brandreth in submitting the estimate for the en- suing half-year said the rateable value of the Union had Increased during the year by £1,459, the smallness of the increase being to some extent accounted for by reason of the Ship Canal Company having applied for certain as- sessments being struck out during the construction of the Ship Canal. The Canal Company, however, made up the deficiency in the poor rate. A rate of sd. in the £ produced £4,555 and it was recommended that a call of sd. be made on the overseers. This was an increase of id. in the £ as compared with last year, but last year they were very much behindhand with their funds, and there was a talk of having a second rate of 3d in the £. They could therefore scarcely compare this year vrithlast year. He moved the adoption of the report—Mr. Hey- wood seconded.—Mr. Parr: The Ship Canal is making the rates heavier then.—Mr. Aaron said they in Weston had an extra rate of £7B from the Ship Canal last ye ar. —The motion was then agreed to. A CORRECTION.

The Clerk explained that in a report of the proceedings of the Board at the previous he had been made to speak in favour of prosecuting the overseers of townships which had not then paid their calls, while as a matter of fact some members of the Board suggested that course and he (the Clerk) advised the Board not to prosecute as they had never had to paosecute hitherto. Several mem- bers corroborated the Clerk as to this version of what had been said at the previous meeting. This was all the business of public interest.

The London bootmakers continue to come out, and by next Monday, unless the masters accept their state- ment of wages, practically the whole of them will be on trike. The winter orders are now in however, and it is shought thattrade cannot be suspended long.
CHARGE OF THEFT AGAINST A RAILWAY GUARD.

At the Southwark Police Court, London, on Monday, Henry Bell, a guard in the employ of the London, Brigh- ton, and South Coast Railway Company. was charged with stealing a £lO note from a Gladstone bag. The Rev. H. Finder deposed that on the 28th of August he was a passenger from London Bridge railway station to Anerley. Fle had a quantity of luggage, amongst which was a Gladstone bag. All the luggage was put in the guard's van. On arriving home he discovered that the lock of the Gladstone bag had been tampered with, and that a £lO note had been abstracted. Knowing the number of the note, he at once gave notice to the police and the note was stopped. Mrs. Grindlett, the wife of a shopkeeper living atCroydon, stated that on the 28th of August the accused purchased two pictures, and in pay- ment gave her a £lO note, which she cashed and gave him the change. Mr. Pierpoint, station superintendent at London Bridge, stated that on the accused a key was found which opened the bag from which the £lO note was stolen. Mr. Fenwick remanded the accused for a week.

div.head: ST. HELENS REVISION COURT.
div.p: ST. HELENS REVISION COURT.

Mr. J. T. Foard, revising barrister, commenced the revision of the voting lists for the county borough of St. Helens, in the assembly room of the Town Hall, on Wednesday night. Mr. J. P. Mearns, solicitor, and Mr. J. Bain, registration agent, ap- peared on behalf of the Liberal party, and the Con- servatives were represented by Mr. J. 0. Swift, solicitor, and Mr. W. Lamb, registration agent.

ASSISTANT OVERSEERS AND THEIR DUTIES. Mr. Mearns, addressing the revising barrister before the commencement of the ordinary business, said ti ere was one matter he desired to mention affecting Mr. Parkinson, the assistant overseer for Eccleston. 'J he agent of the party whom he (Mr. Mearns) represen:ed told him that for reasons connected with his business ha wanted a list, of persons who had not paid their borough rates. He wrote to Mr. Parkinson several times, and waited upon him at his office and house, but he had not been furnished with that list, nor had Mr. Parkinson given any reason why he had declined to do so. Perhaps his honour would ask Mr. Parkinson for an explanation.—The Revising Barrister asked Mr. Parkinson why he had not supplied the list asked for.— Mr. Parkinson replied that the list of those who had not paid their rates had been published in the usual manner, and that was all that he was required to do.— Mr. Mearns contended that by section 50 of 6 Victoria, c, 18, assistant overseers were liable to a tine for wilfully refusing or neglecting to make out any list.—Mr. Swift rose to speak, whereupon Mr. Mearns said—This does not concern Mr. Swift.—Mr. Swift : Yes, it does; it is wasting my time.—Mr. Mearns said it was not wasting time.—Mr. Swift said the list referred to in the section quoted by Mr. Mearns meant the list of.voters.— rho Revising Barrister said he did not think Mr. Parkinson was bound to furnish the list asked for. It was a per sonal matter for Mr. Parkinson and the agent, and there was no compulsion. - -
NOT A LODGER,

William Middlehurst, son of Mr. Win. Middlehurst, of St. Ann's-gardens, Prescot-rd., claimed a lodger's vote in respect to apartments in his father's house.—Mr.Parkin- , son (assistant overseer) stated that the house was as- sessed at £6O, and the claimant said he paid 7s. 6d. per week.—fhe Revising Barrister : What rooms do you oc,- cupy P—Claimant : I occupy the back bedroom on the landing.—The Barrister: But of what other rooms are you the user P—Claimant : I occupy them all.—The Re- vising Barrister: That will not give you a tenancy.— In reply to Mr. Mearns, the applicant said he had the exclusive use of the bedroom.—The Revising Barrister : But that does not make a tenancy.—The claim was dis- allowed.

div.head: DOMESTIC SEPARATION AND ITS CONSEQUENCKS.,
div.p: A DOMESTIC SEPARATION AND ITS CONSEQUENCKS.,

- _ Henry Telford claimed an occupier's vote for 282, Boundary-road, and was objected to by the Conserva- tives. He stated that he had occupied the premises for about three years, but resided with his mother and father at 103, Boundary-road.—ln reply to Mr. Swift, he said his sister lived at 262, Boundary-road.—Mr. Swift: Is it a place of 'business in which you have set up your sister? —Claimant: Yes, that is so, but I pay the rent.—The Revising Barrister said the claimant was a man who did not occupy the house. He claimed a vote as the occupier of a particular house, but he said he lived elsewhere. There was no constructive occupation of the house by him, because it was occupied by his sister. His sister might be entitled to a vote as resident occupier, but he did not see how the claimant could have it any more than he himself (the Revising Barrister) or any one else. He might go and stay there occasionally, but that did not make him the occupier.—ln reply to Mr. Mearns, the claimant said the house was open for him to stay there at any time he liked. There was a room fur- nished for him and for his use.—The Revising Barrrister (to Mr. Mearns) : You are rather suggesting all the essen- tials necessary for him.—The claimant, in reply to the Revising Barrister, said he had furniture of his own there. His sister carried on business there, but it was his business.—Mr. Swift: Who takes the profits ?—Claim- ant did not reply, and the Revising Barrister said the vote would be allowed.—Mr. Swift : I think it is more than your honour is entitled to do according to law.— The claimant was then recalled.—Mr. Swift: What furni- ture have you there ?—Claimant: I could not give you details, but I have some.—Mr. Swift What are they ? —Claimant : Well, say a chair and a table. (Laughter.)—Mr. Swift : What for? Claimant : I occupy them when Igo there.—Mr. Swift : What, the chair and the table? (Laughter.) Claimant : I occupy the chair wheal go there, but I don't sit on the table. (Loud laughter.)—Mr. Swift: Do you mean to say that you have actually bought a chair and a table for your use when you visit there? Claimant: I bought them and sent them there, and I use them when I go there.—Mr. Swift: What sort of business is carried on there ? Claim- ant: It is a butcher's shop.—Mr. Swift: Who takes the profits? Well, they are my profits, but I give them to hen—Mr. Swift : Her husband is away from her? Claimant: Yes.—Mr. Swift: And yau have set her up in business? Claimant: Yes.—Mr. Swift: For her to maintain herself and children while separated from her husband? Claimant: Yes.—The Revising Barrister said it was difficult to justify the vote. The facts did not seem clear, but he would allow it.

div.head: POLICE °mom CALLED.
div.p: A POLICE °mom CALLED.

Michael Keenan claimed a vote in respect of his occu- pation of a house, No. 16, Gailen-st. It appeared that his father lived on the same premises, and up to the commencement of the present year the father's name ppeared on the rent book.—The claimant stated that he had paid the rent for the past six years, but the revising barrister said that fact did not prove that he was en- titled to a vote if the house had been in his father's name.—The claimant continued to urge his claim, not- withstanding the declaration of the revising barrister that the vote could not be allowed.—The Bevising Barrister called for a constable to remove the man from the court, and, on the appearance of an officer, Keenan was quietly led outside.

THURSDAY. The revision was resumed before Mr. Foard, at the Town Hal Lon Thursday forenoon, and agiin in the even- ing. At the former sitting a discussion took place with reference to the filling up of declarations by illiterate men. Mr. Swift contended that it was necessary for the person administering the oath and receiving the de- claration to certify on the declaration that it was read over to the deponent and that the deponent seemed to clearly understand it. Mr. Mearns urged that this was not necessasy, as all that was required of the person administering the oath was to ascertain that the depon- ent was actually in his presence.—After several points had been referred to his Honour held that Mr. Mearns was right in his contention.—Messrs. William Roberts, George Roberts, and Daniel Roberts, claimed votes for their copper works on the canal side. It appeared that the claimants resided at 15, Croxteth- Toad, Liverpool, and the Liberals objected on the ground that this place was outside the seven miles' radius.—Mr. Win. Roberts stated that he had come 56 miles to support the claim, but the objection was sustained.—Andrew Brown, was on the register for 16, Rigby-st., and was objected to by the Conservatives. A boy, residing in the neighbourhood, appeared on Brown's behalf, and pro- duced rent books. Mr. Swift said the rent books dis- proved the lad's statements as to the occupancy, and he thought if votes were to be allowed on such evidence, it was opening a very wide door to corruption.—Mr. Mearns submitted that the rent books were correct, and agreed with the lad's statements. His Honour subsequently allowed the vote, and Mr. Means remarked that one tale was good until another was told. He thought it was clear enougli if Mr. Swift would only admit It.—Mr. Swift: If you try to deceive the court in the way your agents are doing I shan't admit anything.—Mr. Mearns It is you who are deceiving the court if you have the rent-books and misrepresent what is in them.—The Revising Barrister: Now that will do. The next case,. please.—The Conservatives had objected to the vote of John Watson Scholes, of North-road, on the ground that had removed from the house before the 16th July last. Scholes proved that he did not leave until the 28th July, and said he now resided at Cheadle, Manchester. Ile had come from Manchester in consequence of the abjec- tion and he wanted his expenses. His Honour craered the Conservatives to pay him 155.—The Gourt.adicurned at 91.5 in the evening until 10 o'clock on Friday morn- ing.

On Wednesday night a thought -reader at Chicago per- formed one of the feats of the late Mr. Irving Bishop, driving blindfolded through crowded stree.ts and finding a name on a hotel register selected by a ,rukt committee. Soon afterwards he fell into a cataleptic it similar to that which resulted in the death of Mr. Bishop, and it was at first thought he was dead, but the physicians suc- ceeded in restoring him. On Thursday forenoon, a serious gaa explosion% attris buted to leakage from a gts engine, occurred at the electro-plate works of Mr. Worsnop,in Cheapside, The explosion, which was very lend, almost brought down the building and set It on fire. John Edgar Wor- snop, aged eighteen, was burled in the clAris, and Yen not been found. A young woman named Itartky Wa. killed, and a labolarer seriously injured,

• WE are glad to see that the Corpor" A Stitch In Titne. ation of Warrington are taking that stitch in time which will save nine by adopting the Infectious Diseases Prevention Or which became law so recently as the 4th August of the present year. As the adoption of the Act is not compulsory, it will be well if other Authorities take the trouble to consider its provisions, and resolve to bring them into operation at the earliest opPOl- - It is far from satisfactory to realise that all the precautions that one community may take for the prevention of disease may be rendered nugatory through the indifference or negligence of an adjoining town or parish; and we cannot helP thinking that it would be better, on the whole, if Parliament made the adoption of stringent sanitarY regulations compulsory rather than permissive' Recent revelations of the microscope place it he" yond doubt that infectious diseases have their origin in spores, or disease germs, which are devel- oped in the persons attacked; and that, under 4.1 favourable conditions, an epidemic will spread just as fire will spread—if no steps are taken to keep it under. As it happens, the ravages of ill fire are visible to the meanest apprehension, and ample precautions are everywhere taken t° prevent outbreaks. Disease is tenfold more destructive, but because its origin is not alwaYe apparent we too often neglect it until it is not only beyond control, but has made havoc in a score a homes. We are learning better; but are slow t° apply the results of our knowledge; and the CO munity requires drilling by such legislative measures as the one under consideration. It is not unlikely that the Act will be regarded by some ef those who most need it as a nuisance rather than as a benefit; and it may thus happen that the work of the Medical Officer of Health and his assistants will be rendered all the harder. There are Town , Councillors and Aldermen, who, although owners ' of dwelling-houses, care little about them, excePt as to making sure of the rent. They are tempted to resist regulations as to sanitation because they may mean putting their hands in their pockets and making their property really fit for the habitation of human beings. They have their day, but their day will cease to be when the workers come to thoroughly understand how much of their wealth which is their health, depends upon living , houses which are well situated, well ventilated, and free from sewer and other foul gases. Turning to the principal provisions of the new , Act, which is one of 24 clauses, we observe that clause four provides for the inspection of (lair° where there is reason to believe that infections disease in any district is attributable to the supply; and power is given the local authorith under certain specified condititons, to prohibit the supply of milk from a particular dairy for a definit° period. This is beginning in the right way--at the fountain head. Clause five deals with the cleansing and disinfecting of houses and other P. . mises. The responsibility is thrown upon the owner or occupier, who may be called upon t° meet the expenses of the disinfection, if they ner lect to do the work themselves. There is, h 0 ever, a sub-section which is intended to protect the poorest of the poor, by providing, in certain case' ' for houses being " clec.nsed and disinfected by the officers, and at the cost of the local authoritY• Similar regard is shown in clause 15, which runs as follows :

"The local authority shall from time to time PO- vide, free of charge, temporary shelter, or house ac- commodation, with any necessary attendants, for the members of any family in which any infectioug disease has appeared, who have been compelled leave their dwellings for the purpose of enabling such dwellings to be disinfected by the local mall(/' rity." It will be remembered that there was a similar clause in the Warrington Improvement Bill, with the difference that it was proposed to take Pawet to charge people the cost of nurses, Sz-,c. ; but provision for charging was struck out when it wa pointed out, at the Town's Meeting, that it wagh*l be unjust to compel a man, struck down with ae infectious disease, to leave his oWn home, go jO "temporary shelter, or house of accommodation, in the interests of the public, and bear the expel's° himself. Parliament, it will be seen, has taken the same view of the matter; for the Act provides that the accommodation and nursing shall be "free cif charge." Perhaps the most important and far- reaching portion of the Act is that which ig covered by clause 7. It provides for a penalty exceeding £lO on any person who shall cease t° occupy a house, and shall fail to disinfect the house or room in which there has been infectious disease within six weeks previously, disinfec-: tion to be carried out "to the satisfaction 01 a registered medical practitioner, as testified h 37 a certificate signed by him." This will throW extra work upon doctors as well as householders ; but it is work which they will be quite willing te do. A like penalty of £lO may be imposed ia case of ceasing to occupy and neglecting to inforta the owner of the house of the infectious diseasc, or in case of giving a knowingly false answer to any person negotiating for the hiro of the hou.s; It is highly probable that there will.be not a teo.. Ibreaches of the first portion of this clause throul I ignorance of the Act; but, as ignorance of the flan. is not regarded by the law as a valid excuse, ot te. ders must be prepared to pay some penalty, if net.: full penalty. Other clauses relate to prolubi 1.5. the retention of dead bodies after infectious di ease; and to dealing with the bodies of Pers"it Where is dying of infectious diseases in hospitals. is thought that removal would involve risk, it declared unlawful to remove a body from a hospital,

It becomes an offence, too, to hire or use a public conveyance "other than a hearse for the conveyance of the body of a person who has died of any infectious disease" without Previously notifying the owner or driver; and owners and drivers become offenders if they do not, immediately after use, provide far the disinfectic,n of their conveyances. The other clauses give bfflctials power of entry into dwellings, and provide for he payment of expenses as in case of the Acta !elating to public health. Taking it altogether, the Infectious Diseases Prevention Act is one of the )310st valuable measures that has been placed upon ,the statute book during the past session. It has been long attel well considered, and, as it is admir- blY calculated to prevent the spread of disease, It is to be hoped that, ere long, it will be in force throligherat the country.

Chemical THE Chemical and Copper Workers and of Widnes and St. Helens have C°l)Per Workers, been somewhat late in getting themselves thoroughly organised; but the demonstration which was held at Southport, on 89.tiirday, shows that they are now strong in "Tubers, and that they are disposed by zeal and '2"ergy to make up for lost time. It is a great deal s° be able to say that already wages have been advanced and hours of labour shortened, through the action of the union. Mr. P. KERLEY, referring a Widnes firm, stated that wages had advanced sulhiBliums varying from two shillings to twenty ln gs per week. It is customary witk those Ishe are opposed to unions, and reason upon what they would call purely economic lines, to argue that when trade is good and profits large wages 'pill advance as a matter of course. But this by no Isealis necessarily follows; and, to take the case before us, we would ask if it is at all likely that .7agea would have largely advanced in the chemical trade, along with a reduction of hours,if measures to achieve these ends had not been taken by a strong tili°ll? Individual application might have gained something; but it is too much to assume that it Would have been as successful as a conjoint de- Itiand• An employer may say, even when trade is Lt°°d, that he can spare a particular applicant ; but 4is cannot thus deal with the bulk of his workmen, 11111e85 he is prepared to cut off his nose in order to ksi/Ilite his face, and men do not as a rule go into 7inesB with that object. The claims of work- ;,'Lea, may, however, even in the best of times, rf Pushed too far; but employers may well be .st as to that to take care of themselves. Still, is a matter which the chemical workers 'secl to consider. "Hasten slowly" is a good Otto; and there is some danger that their Zeceas thus far may lead them to overstep 'ue line. Their main object is, and should be, trade object; and they run the risk of getting °IT the track when they determine to try to donain- ste the situation municipally. If they will move 14 this direction, they cannot move with too much csirelmlapection ; for it must be remembered that theY court opposition, and if the opposition Prove too strong for them, it will endanger, if it , °ea not wreck, their union for trade purposes. , They will do well to have in mind the fable of the who pat his hand into the jar of nuts, and, by trying to grasp too many, lost all. Let them work hard in seeking to get all labourers in the union sshe are at present out of the union. They cannot RO wrong in that direction, so long as they do not Ned to coercion or intimidation.

t°llhr little party, of four—two ladies and two of hbe o other.sex"—found it very convenient to get Ive ;and, in the course of our goings to and fro, get,visited Colwyn Bay, Old Colwyn, Conway, fai43°B-Y-Coed, Ton t-y-pant, Peninaonmawr,Llan- tila-„Pean, Aber, Llanberis, Carnarvon, and Beau- ``?, besides obtaining-, in sailing down the lo "glimpses which should make us less for- of sundry•other charming spots.

th4jad how pleasant to get back to Llandudno in , ehe evening to listen to the strains of M. Riviere's banal The orchestra performs on the sixh— ni t%O forenoon; but in the erening there is a ~c/ttnY concert in tile Egyptian Hall, also on the ' . This is the treat of treats, and that it is 14-015reciated is shown by an attendance each even- reaches into the thousands. The great pla„“tetion is still the baud, and visitors from other ttees in order to hear it make use of the late tie-4 for Rhyl, Carnarron, and intermediate sta- -14; but there is alwaysin addition, some voealist Q.o,.rtey and sometimes there are two, The Pier datoLltly, in arranging these concerts, have un- 3, made" a palpable hit:" sor,e„ is famous for its glorious glens; but the ing is lost which 4rt cannot restow when 4jd ate turned into show places at so much per wood „"There is a pleasure in the pathless the tB' and that pleasure reaches its climax when °ist hears the roar of a waterfall, and, the-Tglin:' through fern and briar, breaks in upon Ana l'On of delight" enshrined in its "cool grot ''''ssY cell."

- 4 to be faced at the start by a notice board This Way to the Fairy Glen " ; to be called Desterat a Wicket to "Pay here—fourpence"; to be with " photos " of the place you are going ; Etild to find an easy artificial path all the
way,—well, it may do f.ar dainty shoes and ginger- bread misses; but it 'isn't seeing Dame Nature's Holy of Holies in the holiest frame of mind.

Anyone v- dm wants to have a day amongst the glens car., ocarroly do better than do as we did, take 11, rain to Beftws, walk on to the Fairy Glen, f°': ward to the falls of the Conway, then on to the two bridges (close together) across the Machno ono ot 13hom said to be a Roman bridge nearly two thook4sand years old—and finally to Pandy Mill and fall, which have been more frequently painted by artists professional and amateur, than any other bit in iVales. The way back is down by the Con- way at its junction with the Lledr, or up the Lledr valley, and return by train from Pont-y- Pant.

I Leaf, flower, fern and furze, linger long in a glowing prime in these sheltered vales. The hill sides which get plenty of sun are even now ablaze with the blossom of the heather and the gorse ;and what a grand sight it is to see their intermingled colours of yellow and purple, with a ground of deep green! It is nature's own floral carpet. How is it that it is not copied? Is it that there is need of the o'er-arching blue of heaven to get the finest effect.

Whilst we were at Llanberis, Snowdon was seen under a blue sky, and the summit looked so near, although so far, that the ladies tholight it could be reached easily. And it was reached, but not easily; for the summit recedes as tourists ad- vance, and for a good hour or so vanishes al- together. But our party had faith in the fixity of mountains—if not the faith which removes them— and after a little over three hours' climbing they were enabled to stand on the highest point and realise for a brief space what it is to be" up in the world."

It was a fine day, and we had 'a fine view—a view very much above the average, though there are odd days in the year when the range is wider than that offered us on Monday. But it was some- thing to see hill upon hill, and "Alps on Alps arise," besides close on a score of lakes and tarns gleaming in the sunlight like burnished silver. It was something, too, to have our appetites sharp- ened by hard walking in a cool breeze, for— Oh, there is sweetness in the mountain air, And life that slothful ease can never share. But the sum of somethings was the "jolly good tea" which we got on the top of the mountain. It was a grand addition to the grand scenery.
But enough of these notes for tho present; the Queen of Roumania is at Llandudno; and, as she may call any minute, we must be ready to receive her Majesty.

div.head: ASSAULT ON A __WORle-S- :FOREMAN AT _WIDNES,
div.p: ASSAULT ON A __WORle-S- :FOREMAN AT _WIDNES,

At Widnes Police Thursday, Joseph Finney, I 12, Latham-st., was summoned for using threats to Thomas Harrison, a foreman at the works of Messrs.; Sullivan and Co.—Mr. J. W. Knowles, instructed by the ; firm,prosecuted.—On the second inst. Finney and Dutton, two employes of the firm, caused a disturbance in the works about their work, and Harrison, learning they had been drinking, told them they wanted some more beer. The men left their work, and in the evening meeting Harrison in the street Dutton knocked hint to the ground and Finney used very threatening language.—Finney pleaded guiity, and said he did not mean any harm.— Mr. Deaconsaid such conduct mild not be tolerated, and 'ordered the defendant to be bound over to keep the peace for six months, himself in £2O and two sureties of £l.O each, or in default a month's imprisonment. POACHING AT CLIFTON. At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Major Haslehurst and Mr. G. L. Wigg, George Hargreaves, and Edward Andrews,young men were summoned forhaving on the 28th August at Clifton trespassed upon land in the occupation of Wm. Baker,farmer, in search of game. —Wm. Wild, shepherd, said about 7 o'clock on the night In question he heard a shot, and shortly afterwards saw the defendants, each with a gun near the end of the slaughter-house. He watched and saw defendants on the land about 20 yards from the footpath and one of them fired a shot. Poaching was carried on every night by somebody, and on the previous night, he found a partidge that had been shot.—By Hargreaves : He saw them examining the end of the smithy for shot marks.— Hargreaves said he and Andrews had a new gun on trial and they went to the commonto try them but there were too many children about, they sauntered on to the old smithy where they made a chalk mark at which they fired. They never had one foot on the field.—ldajor Hazlehurst said trespassing was continually taking place on the land about that neighbourhood, and to a certain extent what Mr. Baker thought fit to do was a proper thing. At the same time there was no evidence that they were in pursuit of game, and the Bench would accept their statements, still they had no right to shoot on the highway and had committed a breach of the law. There was an element of doubt in the case and the de- fendants would be discharged. UMBRELLAS lIE-COVERE.D at the shortest notice.—J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st.. Warrington.—Advt. MR. T. SNAPS G.C. AND MISSION WORK. Mr. Thomas Snape, C.C. for the Widn es Division, pre- sided on Thursday night at a meeting in Grove-street, Methodist Chapel, Liverpool, to bid farewell to two col- oured students who were brought over to England from Sierra Leone, and who had studied at the Methodist Institute, Manchester. They will return on Saturday to their native land, where they will engage in mission work. In opening the proceedings, Mr. Snape referred to the great interest which was now centred in that Part of the globe to which their two friends were about to return. The vast continent was two and a half times as large as Europe, and of the 10,000 square miles of territory which it contained, our country (holding more than any other civilised country in the world) had made I itself responsible for the future of a large portion of the continent. He spoke of the many illustrious mission- aries who, in consequence of the deadly climate, had been lost, and pointed out how England must not mere- ly increase her possessions and material wealth in Africa but must endeavour to be of service to the natives of the country. To do this it was necessary to extend mission- ary operations, and by what better means could they do this, he would like b know, than by engaging the ser- vices of the natives themselves ? The peril the climate held out to Europeans ceased to be a petil with them, and that was the reason these two natives, after under- going a thorough training, were now returning to their native country in the great and noble enterprise of spreading abroad the gospel of Christ amongst their people. div.head: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.
The monthly meeting of members was held on Wednesday. Mr. Taylor presided, and there were present the Rev. Dr. Oastaldi. Messrs. H. Coleburn, W. Mellor, and W. F. Salk eld (sec.)

. STATISTICS. The chairman reported that the interments for the five months ending August 25th were 179, last year 182, increase 17. The fees received during the same period amounted to £169 7s. 9d. ; last year £139 17s. ; increase £29 10s. 9d.

div.head: FINANCB.
div.p: FINANCB.

The Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £lB 6s. 6d.; and interest falling due amounting to £4B 10s. 2d. The Committee sug- gested that a call for £l2O be made upon the overseers. —£6o on Sinking Fund account and £6O on general ex- penses account.—Mr. Coleburn moved the adoption of the minutes.—Dr. Gastaldi seconded and remarked that the business of the Board was most economically manag- ed, and the call was only what one might expect.
- THE CEMETERY ACCOMMODATION-INTERESTING DISCUSSION.

The Secretary presented the following report :—As re- quested by the Board at the last meeting, I have en- deavoured to fcrm some idea of the time the present cemetery will be sufficient for the interments which will be required therein. Making allowance for the in- crease of population, and for the very large influx of persons Likely to come in the town by reason of the Ship Canal. and increased dock accommodation for shipping, as well as works which may reasonably be expected to be made in future years, I beg to submit the following report, after having the benefit of the advice and assis- tance, of the officials employed in the grounds. We have carefully examined every section of the plan of the cemetery, every grave is distinctly marked therein that is buried in, as well as those that remain vacant. And the conclusion arrived at is that it is quite ample for the next twelve years,—if the land occupied at present with shrubs, trees, and flowers were utilised, then we say five years longer,-17 years. As regards the land belonging to the Burial Board, and now in the occupation of Mr. Joseph Savage, as yearly tenant (say about 4± statute ames), the period of time that it will suf- fice for interments would very much de- pend upon how it was laid out for that purpose. No buildings need be erected on it, nor broad ornamental walks made, as in the present portion, but if reasonable and moderate paths were made to divide each section, and for the use of the public at funerals and other; times, I consider there is land sufficient (judi- ciously laid out) for interments for seventy years after the present one is filled up. It should be stated that there is a large number of graves and vaults that are freehold and are only part filled, the total number sold is 2,013 grants of right to them, and interments will take place in these for many years to come. I therefore humbly submit as my opinion, after muclh thought on the subject, and with some experience, thatthe Burial Board possess land sufficient for Use purpose of the Cemetery for the next 80 or 90 years.—The Secretary said ke had written to Mr. Evans, agent to Sir Richard Brooke, asking the lowest price for fiveor six acres of the field adjoining the land belonging to the Cemetery and now occu- pied by Mr. John Morris. Mr. Evans had in re- ply asked for a plan of what the Board proposed. He (the secretary) had lit on the best authority that the whole of the land surrounding the ceme- tery would be opened out for building purposes, and if the Board intended to louy land the sooner it was done and the better.—Dr. Gastaldi said it would be pre- posterousto buy more land for the purpose of burying the dead when they had made provision for nearly a :century, and he thought the question should be left alone.—Mr. Mellor suggested that the matter should be ' postponed until next meeting to see what the price of the land would be. There had been a great deal spoken about recreation 'grounds, and if the Board tould ' see their way clear to purchase a few acres of land and throw it open with the present land not in use., it would make a. very excellent recreation ground, as it was in a central position. The purchase would entirely depend upon the price naked.; he-should never large the, Board to pay an extravagant price.—Dr. Gastalcli But don't you think it is the duty of the Commissioners to provide a play ground for the people, and [not the Burial Board—Mr. : Oh yes, but no doubt the Commissioners would be pleased to rent the laud at a moderate rate that would recoup the Burial Board for their outlay.—Mr Coleburn considered the Board had amply done its dutyin providing a burial plans for the next 80 or $2 years,.and thexatepayers ought not to bel further saddled with expenses that ought to fail upon 1 a future generation.—Mr. Mellor said the land would become more valuable, and it•would be a capital invest- ment.—Dx. Gastaldi asked how much rent was paid for • the ai statute acres Oho Boarddi..l not at present use. Did the rent pay for the money they had laid out—The Secretary said they received £9 a year.—Dr. Gastaldi' said to pay a proper interest, the Board should receive' £32.—Mr. Coleburn -said the Board had been indiscreet from the first. If they thought of purchasing more land they should 'have been very quiet and not have made the matter public. The landowners would naturally put an increased price on the land.—Mx_ Mellor: If they do we don't need to buy it.—Eventually the subject was ad- journed until tile next meeting, when there would ,pro- bably be a better attendance of members. sr.7GESTr,D IMPROVEMENTS.

Mr. Barker, sur ..eyew to t-h-e-Bei-a-t:ci--oi.Co.namissioners appeared before the Board andpointed out that the fence of the field belongingto the Board and adjoining the cemetery want in a line with the proposed Victoria-rd., and he wished permission to set it straight. Er showed that while the Board would lose a little land at one end they would gain it at the other. On the proposition 4p= the chairman, seconded by Dr. Gastaldi, the desired per- ;mission was granted.—Mr. Barker also produced plans, showing how it was proposed to round off the corner of / the cemetery to sake a better approach to Victoria-road, and also to the cemetery. There would be about 251 square yards of land required from the cemetery, but the: shrubbery or the graves would net be interfered with. The Commissioners proposed to build a substantial brick wall and place the post boa in an ornamental setting in the centre.—The members agreed that the alteration would be a good improvement all round, and on the propesition of Mr. Mellor, seconded by Dr. Gastaldi, the Commissioners were granted permission to perform the work.—A discussion ensued as to whether it would be necessary to obtain the sanction of the vestry.—The Chairman said the Law Clerk (Mr. Lake), considered such a course unnecessary.
