div.head: VILE DEN AT RUNCORN. SAVAGE ASAULT ON A NAVVY.
div.p: A VILE DEN AT RUNCORN. SAVAGE ASAULT ON A NAVVY.

Bartley Dugan, a dock labourer, was brought up 4t Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, charged with assaulting George Davies, a navvy.—The prisoner pleaded " guilty but it was defending myself."—The prosecutor said he lived at Ellesmere Port, and on Sunday he came to Runcorn for a bit of a walk. About-8 o'clock at night he went into a house in back Cooper-st., with a woman named Harriett Baxter. He was drunk, but he knew what he was doing. There were two men in the house (prisoner being one.) Some beer was fetched in; lie could not tell whether he or the woman paid for it; but 'he wanted a drink. Zfe insisted upon having a drink and while the other man held him down in the chair by tiie neck, the prisoner struck him twice on the head with a thick stick, lie bled very much and his wounds had to be dressed by a doctor. Ile met the woman in Taylors' public house at the top of King-st. Bythe prisoner : He never threatened to knife him.— John Molyneux, 22, St. gehn-st., said he heard scream- ing in the yard and he went there and he heard the prosecutor say "give me my 2s. and I will go " but the men would not give him the money and the prisoner knocked him senseless with a stick.—Jane Richardson, 51, Cooper-st., corroborated, she saw the prisoner strike the navvy on the head four times.—The prisoner said he was in Enoch Ditchfields.owhen the prosecutor entered. The prosecutor threatened to knife him and Enoch struck mim then prisoner struck him twice with the stick.— Harriett Baxter who was tender the influence of drink said the prosecutor gave her 2s. to fetch some beer and she gave him the change. The prisoner had nothing to do with it. Enoch Ditchfield struck the first blow and then gave the stick to the prisoner to lay on him. Some- body picked up the change off the table.—Major Hazle- hurst said it was a very bad assault and'sentenced the prisoner to two months hard labour.

RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS. A special meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Thursday morning_ Present: Messrs. S. Taylor, J. Meadowcroft, W. Asher, H. White, W. Mellor, E. W. Humphreys, W. It. Wass, R. Abel, P. Smith, E. Imison. W. Hankinson, H. J. Grice, and J. Dobson, with F. A. Lake (law clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), and M. Barker (surveyor). Mr. W. Lightburi took the chair. The newly elected members signed the roll and necessary declaration.

div.head: ELECTION OF CHAIII/LiN.
div.p: ELECTION OF CHAIII/LiN.

Mr. Lightburn said the first business was the election of a chairman for the present year. This arose through the fact that while Mr. Taylor was chairman his peiiod. of office tertninated, and his re-election would be neces- sary.—Mr. Once proposed that Mr. Taylor be elected chairman for the ensuing year. They had every con- fidence in Mr. Taylor's ability and it would give great satisfaction both to the members and to the ratepayers to see Mr. Taylor in the chair again.—Mr. Meadowcroft seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously.
ELECTION EXPENSES. Mr. Lightburn, as returning officer at the recent elec- tion, submitted an account of the expenses, amounting

to £l7 9s. 6d.—Mr. Meadowcroft : How does that com- pare with previous years P—The Secretary Last year £l2 7s.—Mr. Hankinson : What are the items of ex- penditure?-Mr. Lightburn: Officers' fees am ou tit to £7ls.; G.Cooper, for dinner £5145.; Mackie and Co.,adyertising Is. ; G. Bellamy, advertising £1 ; billposting 4s. ; Woodland, printing £1; C. Dutton, ss. ; a stallholder, 2s. 6d. ; cab to and from polling station with voting papers, &c. 3s. ; total, £l7 9s. 6d.—Mr. Meadowcreft : How many officials were there P—Mr. Lightburn: Seven. —Mr. Meadowcroft : £5 14s. seems to me a consider- 'able amount for dinner.—Mr. Taylor: Dinner and lunch. --Mr. Fisher: I suppose there is nothing unusualabout it ?—Mr. unison : Except the figure. (Laughter.)—Mr. Mellor said when Mr. Lightburn and himself were re- elected the members paid for the dinner out of their own pockets. He did not know whether they departed from the ordinary coursa of things ; if they did, he was very sorry, because it affected his poc- ket. Mr. Taylor said there seemed to be smiles round the Board when the figures were given The amount might appear large to some people but he assured them that the candidates had had no portion of it in any shape or form. The officers and those connected with the election participated in that lunch and dinner and it was hard lines if the officers of the Board should ' go to the polling booth at 9 o'clock in the morning, and stop until 5 o'clock at night, and then depend upon any candidate either successful or unsuccessful as to whether they should have anything to eat or not. If the Board wished he should be pleased as chairman to pay the whole of it, but it was a hutnilating position for the officers to wait, with their hats under their arms, for some candidate to ask them to have something to eat after his day's labour. Surely a town of the importance of Runcorn can afford once a year to treat their officers respectfully and with some little consideration. The candidates and others not official, had not had anything at the ratepayers' expense.—Mr. Lightburn said Si) charge was made to the ratepayers for anything other than food. Champagne was paid for outside the Board.—Mr. Taylor: There were no cigars, nor anything stronger than water taken at the ratepayers' expense Mr. Lightburn said a bad precedent had been set in previous years, by some of the chairmen paying the entire expense, ana he thought Mr. Taylor was quite right in taking the stand he had done. The charge was one no reasonable man could ob- ject to.—Mr. Irmson said he did not understand anybcdy objected to it. Last year it was suggested that the accounts should be passed through the Finance Committee and any expression of this kind would be avoided.—Mr. Meadowcroft said Mr. Taylor's speech had no relevancy to his inquiry. He did not suggest that any portion of the account had been received by the:candidates in any shape or form whatever. He simply asked for an ex- planation of the amount, because it was considerably in excess of the amount paid in previous years—Mr. Taylor moved that the accounts be passed.—Mr. Hankin; son seconded. Carried unanimously. It was understood that in future the account would pass through the Finance Committee.
THE STANDING COMMITTEES.
On the motion of Mr. Grice it was resolved that the Standing Committees of of the Board consist of the whole 4•7 the members.
WATERLOO BRIDGE COMMITTEE. On the proposition of Mr. Taylor the Waterloo Bridge Committee was re-appointed without change.
fIST CommITTEE.
On the proposition-Wit;:gn-lit:l;-,-i-he Baths Committee was constituted as follows i—Messrs.lmison,Hankinson, Timmins, Humphreys, Wass, Mellor, and Grice.

div.head: NEW ACTS.
div.p: NEW ACTS.

The Clerk said he had received copies of the Public Health Act Amendment Act and the Infectious Diseases Prevention Act, of 1890. There were soma good provi- sions and considerable additional powers were conferred upon local authorities. The former, act gave the Board power to do considerable work in private streets and private drains, and also to recover the costs from the property owners. The Public Health Act was referred to the Highway Committee and the Infectious Diseases Act to the Health Committee.

div.head: GAS AND WATER.
div.p: GAS AND WATER.

The minutes of the Gas and Water Committee con- tained the report of the engineer; who stated that the mean rainfall for the month had been 3.242 inches. The water in stock was 9,979,877 gallons. The illuminating power of the gas during the month had averaged 1909. candles. The Committee recommended that the tender of Bayliss, Jones, and Co., of £ll7 10s., for the gates and fencing at Pex Hill, be accepted. Instructions wero given to charge all gas and water fittings and work done for the Committee of the Board at cost price.—The minutes were approved, on the motion of Mr. Brown.— On the minutes of the Hig,hway Committee being brought forward for confirmation, Mr. Sadler said at the last meeting a dangerous hole was reported at St. Patrick's new schools, and it was recommended that notice be served upon Mr. Mulholland to fence it off.—A Member said no danger existed, but the Committee had found an excavation having a frontage to the street of 22 yards. and a depth of 5 to 6 feet, and partially filled with water. It appeared to him (Mr. Sadler) that Dr. O'Keeffe must have been a somnambulist, or his vision must have been terribly defective if he could not see such an excavation. It was intolerable that minutes should have to be with- drawn on such flimsy pretences.—Dr. O'Keeffe said he had not the slightest knowledge that this attack would be made upon him by the Chairman of the Highway Committee. It was disgraceful. If he had defective vision, it was not his fault, and as for somnambulism, it was evident from Mr. Sadler's use of such a term, that his education had not been neglected in his early days. (A laugh.) As he had pointed out, there was only a single house in the neighbourhood of the excavation, and that was a public-house, which he was not accustomed to frequent. The excavation was not on the highway at all. He maintained that his formerstatements were per- fectly correct.—The Chairman said these personalities must be suppressed in future. If the members of the could not conduct their business without the introduc- tion of personalities, he, as Chairman of the Board, would resign. He would not sit there and hear persona- lities bandied about, so the Board could take it as they liked. ItRALTE OP TILE TOWN."-ALLBGED NUISANCE. The minutes of the Health Committee contained the report of the medical officer, who reported that during August there were 99 births and 58 deaths, being at the respective rates of 38'23 and 2245 per 1,000. There were 31 deaths amongst children under one year and 10 amongst children between one and five years. ' Zymotic diseases e,ansed 14 deaths. Notifications of infectious diseases as follows were received :—Measles 1, enteric or typhoid fever 18, scarlatina 27, whooping cough 30, erysipelas 6, diptheria 1, cholera (English)2. There were 21 patients in the Infectious Diseases Hospital. Five had been discharged and two had died..—The Nuisance In- spector reported that there had been ten deaths from diarrhcea, two from typhoid fever, and two from whoop- ing cough.—lt was recommended that Miss Warburton be appointed matron of the Accident Hospital at a salary of £3O per annum.—Mr. Carey moved and Mr. Wright seconded the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Midwood complained that since the introduction of the new process there had been very serious nuisances caused by the bad gases evolved. The tenants of 10 houses in John-st. had given notice that they could not stop any longer in conse- quence of the gases coming from Messrs. Hutchinson's works. He should like the Committee to make an in- spection and see if something could not be done to stop these gases.—Mr. Carey said s they had given Mr. Low, the waste heaps inspector, special instructions to investi- gate and report upon these alleged escapes of gases in order to imform the Committee whether the escapes arise from the new process or from some other source of which there were several. The first authority respon- sible for these escapes by the new process, would be the Inspector under the Alkali Act and he had no doubt his attention had been called to the subject.—Mr. Brown said he did not think the waste heaps were being as carefully laid as they were.—The minutes were passed.
THE MEDICAL OFFICER. ' On the proposition of Mr. Carey seconded by Mr. Hargreaves, Dr. Cooper, was re-appointed medical Officer of Health for the ensuing twelve months.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.
Onthe recommendation of the Finance Committee ac- counts amounting to £15,065 is. 3d. were passed for payment.
'THE THARSIS DRAIN.

Messss. Oppenheim and Malkia wrote stating that the Tharsis Copper Company objected to pay the account as rendered for the making of the Tharsis drain (Bowers Brook). The General Purposes Committee recommended that the solicitors be instructed to insist upon payment. —On the motion of Mr Carey the minutes was adopted. ADOPTION OF THE TECHNICAL EDUCATION ACT. The proposal of the General Purposes Committee to adopt the Technical Education Act, which was adjourned from last month, came up for discussion,—Mr. Carey at the outset pointed out that the Science acd Art Schools which had been carried on for about 15 years had met with a formidable difficulty and that was the announced intention:on the part of several of the subscribers that they would contribute no longer. This year there had been passed by Parliament, The Technical Educa- tion Act, which empowered local authorities to provide precisely the education tke Science and Art School had been endeavouring with varying success to give; or the Authority could assist that instruction from time to time. The amount the Au/.iority could raise in orre,year had not to exceed one penny in the Z. Certain sums of money had be -set tweet for the eurpose of this technical education. AS-ithinthe last sessicn the sum -of £BO,OOO had been handed over to the Couuty Council of 'Lencashire locate purposes of technical edecation and the Treasury have set asiele £.8,0M for the seine purpose. ft was therefore -metremely desirable that the Local Board should take such steps in assistbre, technical education, that they corrld apply for their :due share of these sums. He stated that little more than £lOO would be required to keep the Science-and Art Schools in exis- tence and he proposed the adoption of the Act.—Dr. -O'Keeffe seconded, and alluding to the need and value of technical education in a town like Widnes, said it would be deplorable if through the apathy of the Local !Board, this advantage should be lose—The Chairman supported the proposition and said the Science and Art 'Schools had very good premises, and he w-as very glad to say that the place -was altogether too small for the re- quirements of the pupils.—Mr. Brown asked if there , were no means of assisting the schools idthout adopting the Act.—The Chairman said by adopting the Act they would have more :efficient-echools, and they would have , a chance of getting from-the County Council as much as the people of Widnes had eubscribed to the school, and that they would -be in a pesition to-extend the schools, materially.—Mr. 'Brown.: Mere is always a tendency to , extravagance when there is the public purse to pull at— The Chairman said the Authority would be vested in the Local Board, and so far as they cocld see the require- ments would not be a farthing in the Z.—Dr. O'Keeffe said a large room at Simms Cross Schools might be utilised until the finances would permit of larger premises being übtained.--Mr. -Carey ,sciid if they bad a room for the , teaching of art, he did not think' it would be necessary to enlarge the premises for the teaching of science.—The 'motion was carried unanimously. THE PROPOSED CHARTER OF ffNCORPORATION. The question of incorporation was next discussed, and the speeches chiefly were a repetition of the arguments used at the last meeting.—The Clerk had received from Me. F. Gaskell, the following resolution passed by the owners and occupiers' assoenition -:—That this meeting is of opinion that incorporation will involve additional expenditure: that the question being of great import- ance should be therougrhly and caref Lilly discussed and a poll of the ratepayers taken before it is decided and that before the poll is taken full information should be placed in the hands of the ratepayers."—Dr. O'Keeffe said there, had been enough information given already to reach: from Widnes to Liverpool. He did not see why a cor- poration should spend mere-than a 'Local Board. They would not pay the Mayor a falary, and they would not need any additional officials. The town business could be menaged as eoonemically by a corporation as it was , by the Local Board, and they would make themselves more respected. They would have a better and purer , election, and a householder would be equal to any other ! ratepayer. The resolution of the owners and occupiers' , ' association was intended to temporise and postpone the matter from time to time in order to prevent them from • kaving the honour of becoming a corporate body. Wid- nes was the largest Local Board districtin the Kingdom, had the largest rateable value and the population was increasing annually, and he thought that the hour had come for incorporation.— Mr. Taylor ' said incorporation meant the introduction of party pcAitics and he maintained that the . rates would be increased. In the first place they would have to build the Town flait.—Dr. O'Keeffe: We ought to have done that before.—Mr. Taylor: And that means 2d. is the Z on the rates for 35 years.—De. O'Keeffe: If the manufacturers had continued to live in Widnes, the Town Hall would have been built in its entirety.— Mr. Carey Question.—Dr. O'Keeffe And we should have had a revenue from it. Dr. O'Keeffe moved that ' the Board recommend the ratepayers of Widnes that a charter of incorporation should be obtained for the township at as early a day as possible.—Mr. Wright seconded the motion, and said there must be something in incorporation or there were a good many boroughs in the country going wrong.—Mr. Brown said there had been nothing laid before them showing that they would have any advantage by being incorporated. When he considered the price of gas and water and the ratei, in Widnes,he found they were managed as cheaply and effi- • ciently as any corporation, although only a Local Board.

There was one thing they would lose if incorporated and that was the regular examination of their books by a Government auditor. He did not think the benefits they would get as a corporation would compensate them for their present advantages.—Mr. Hargreaves said there was one great advantage and that was vote by ballot, and they would be less subject to red tape.—Mr. Carey said there were good arguments on both sides, but so far as he was able to ascertain the facts, in incorporation there was a danger of increased expen- diture. There was another objection and that was the introduction of party politics into their elections. An advantage would be that they could manage their own affairs and not become a district council under the County Council. As to the auditing of the accounts they could surely get a chartered accountant who could do that efficiently, but he would not keep them straight as to the legality of the expenditure. lie did not think the information given on the subject exhaustive, and he proposed an amendment that a Committee of five members, all residents in the township, should investi- gate the subject and report to the Board .—Mr. Brown seconded.—Dr. O'Keeffe then gave the statistics he gave at the last meeting, and contended that 99 out of every hundred in Widnes were in favour of incorporation . Eventually the following gentlemen were formed a Committee to deal with the subject :—Messrs. Gossage, Carey, and Dr. O'Keeffe. Wrizilt, Sadler Midwood, Liddell, Brown, Heyes,

IZYTRAORDINARY FATALITY TO A SCHOOL GIRL. A DOCTOR CENSURED. Mr. Worsley, the coroner, held an inquest at Runcorn Police Court, on the body of Martha Jane Martin, six years of age, dalghter of Thomas Martin, of Stone-st. Mr. R. Moore was foreman of the jury. On Monday, when returning home from school, the girl fell down, and the slate pencil she was carrying came in contact with her left eye. She died on Wednesday from the injuries.—The father de- posed ne went to Dr. McDougall, and the doctor told him to take the child to his surgery. He did so, and the doctor put a piece of plaister on the wound under the , eye, lie afterwards went to Dr. Mangan, who told him , the girl had not been properly treated, and that the plaister should not have been placed on the wound.—A juryman inquired if there was anything wrong in the doctor's refusal to go to the child.—The Coroner said he did not think there was any blame attached to the doctor's action.—The inquest was adjourned in ! order that a post-mortem examination might be made.— The inguiry was resumed yesterday afternoon. Dr. Carruthers said he had made a post-mortem examination of the body. Externally there was bruising of the left upper eyelid and eyebrow, and there was a superficial longtitudinal wound about half an inch long on the eye- lid. The wound was not punctured and did not penetrate the eyelid. On opening the head, he found the membranes of the brain congested and there was small , extravasation of blood over the left orbit. There was a ' small round fracture of the bone forming the roof of the left orbit on the near side. The fracture was about a quarter of an inch in diameter and the edges of the broken bone projected inwards. He considered the cause of death was convulsions caused by irritation of the membranes of the brain from the fractured bone. This was a most extraordinary case from the fact that externally there was nothing to show that there was any internal injury whatever, and nothing to suggest a fracture of the skull. Nothing could have been done in the way of an operation to save the child's .life.—ln answer to M. Duckett, Dr. Carruthers said the only evi- dence of injury was a slight scratch and a bruise and the proper treatment was to put a pad of lint on and a bit of plaister over it, which Dr. Mc- Dougall did. The proper treatment was pursued.— Mr. Coventry-said he was not satisfied one iota. Could Dr. McDougall have ascertained by a minute inspection of the wound whether anything serious was likely to follow P—Dr. Carruthers said Dr. McDougall could not possibly have found out when the child was alive what lie (Dr. Carruthers) could not see when the child was dead, when a more minute inspection could be made.— The jury retired, and after an absence of about a quar- ter of an hour, the foreman (Mr. R. Moore) said the jury believed Dr. Carruther's statement as to the cause of death, but in their opinion the remarks alleged to have been used; by one member of the medical profession I • against another deserves great censure. A verdict of "Accidental death" was recorded.

THE FLOWER QUEEN AT RUNCORN. Bethesda Congregational Sunday School has re- cently been repaired and decorated,'and the entrance improved at considerable cost, and in order to obtain the required sum, it was decided to give two performances of the operetta" The Flower Queen, or the coronation of the rose." Although per- formed in the town on three previous occasions, the operetta evidently holds a prominent place in the affec- tions of the Runcorn people, the public Hall on Tuesday and Wednesday evenings being crgwded with an enthus- iastic audience. No expense had been spared to make the performances as perfect as possible. The stage was transformed into a scene of sylvan beauty, and when occupied by a " bevy of sweet girls" as the chorus of flowers, excited unbounded admiration amongst the spectators. The argument of the piece, is, stated briefly. "The flowers meet in a secluded dell in the forest, to choose their queen. A person discontented with the world seeks, in the same place, retirement from its cares and disappointments. The flowers tell of love and duty; and the Recluse, learning to fill well the station allotted by Providence is to be happy, resolvesto return again to usefulness arid contentment among his fellow creatures." The Rose (Queen Elect) was personified by Madame Laura Haworth, and she gave a most bright and artistic rendering of the part. Her voice had lost none of its charms and several of the solos were re-demanded. The duet (Nightingale and Rose) in which Mr. FL W. Handley played a flute obligato was a pretty piece of vocalisa- tion, and was deservedly encored. On Wednesday even- I ing, in response to encores, she sang "Sing sweet bird," I and "Coming through the Rye." As the Recluse Mr. Fred Owens was an unqualified success. His fine bari- tone voice was heard to great advantage in the various solos set down to his part, and ha was honoured by several re-calls. Vocalists of local repute took the following solo parts ma manner that disarmed adverse criticism : —Lily, Miss Handley ; Crocus, Miss M. Ileatheringtm ; Dahlia, Miss fleatheringtoa ; Heliotrope, Miss Newall ; Mignonette, Miss Temperle3- ; Japonica and Touch-me- Not, Miss E. Ainsworth ; Sun Flower, Miss Wright ; Violet. Miss Polly Crosby; Tulip, Miss Birkett ; Holly- hock, Mies N. Handler; Dandelion, Miss E. D. Wright. They were well supported by a numerous and well- trained chorus. The chorus of heatherbells and chorus of bluebells were formed of young children,appropriately attired, end their singing and dancing was much ad- mired. The performance concluded with " The Wan- , deriw,' Gipsies," the vocalists being dressed in charac- ter. Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys was the conductor, Mr. W. Handley, stage director, Mrs. W. B. Kay, pianisi.,, Mr. H. W. Handley, organist, and tilere was an efficient orchestral band. The lime light effects were manipu- lated by Mr. J. Rhodes.

div.head: RECREATION aiorticro – AND 'COMMON._ LANDS_ COMMITTEE.
div.p: RECREATION aiorticro - AND 'COMMON._ LANDS_ COMMITTEE.

Mr. Imison said considering the favourable reception the question of a recreation ground received at the hands of the ratepayers at the recent election, the Board would agree with the necessity of appointing a committee to continue the work partially began by tbe last committee. He proposed that the committee consist of Messrs. Ilankinson, Wiswall, Dobson, Mellor, Pritchard, Grice, Imison, Abel, and White. He would be glad to add the name of Mr. Meadoweroft if he would act, as the com- pany he represented was largely interested in the Common Lands, and his co-operation would be of great benefit.—Mr. Meadowcroft said he was already surDci- ently engaged and must decline to serve. Mr. Pritchard was possessed of much infortnation on the subject.—Mr. Lightburn : There is a lot of matter in existence which will assist the Committee very much.—Mr. Grim secon- ded the motion which was carried.

div.head: DIODE OP ELECTION.
div.p: THE DIODE OP ELECTION.

Mr. Humphreis:-,-,;;;;a-u;t ;;;;tnitiee be appointed to consider the possibility of effecting an improvement in the present mode of conducting the annual election of Commissioners. He said that even without applying for any extra powers at all, he was certain there might be an improvement effected in the present system, which would tend to reduce the evils which were pretty well admitted at the last election. One useful mode would be to provide a booth open only to persons who wished to vote, so that there need not be that necessity to go into a hole and corner to find a quiet place to mark his paper without being badgered by the unfortunate candi- dates and their agents. He should like at the same time to enter into a larger question, which was shadowed forth in some of the speeches and addresses.—Mr. Light- burn said they had been expecting month after month that district councils would supersede the Commissioners altogether, and then they would vote by ballot and entirely upset the present mode of voting. However, there could be no harm in ap- pointing a committee, and he seconded the motion. —Mr. Humphreys said there was absolutely no chance of district councils coming into existence fora consider- able number of years.—Mr. Ta}lor said if a Committee could bring about a change in the present mode by petitioning the Local Government Board or the members of Parliament or push forward districtcouncils, he should be pleased to support the formation of the Commission. Everybody saw the necessity for a change. The motion was carried and Messrs. Imison, Mellor, Grice, Fisher, and Humphreys were constituted the Committee.

div.head: FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.
div.p: FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.
This Committee was formed as follows :—Rev. Canon Wood ; Messrs. T. Riley, H. J. Gri:ie, W. Handley, W. Hankinson, E. Wynne • Humphreys, J. Pritchards, .1. Simpson and Dr. MacLennan.

div.head: PItESCOT.
div.p: PItESCOT.

WESLEYAN CHAPEL.—On Sunday two sermons were preached by the Rev. J. T. W. Stafford, newly-appointed minister, at the above place of worship. There were collections in aid of the new vestries scheme. There was a very good attendance. SALVATION ARMY.—Staff-Captain and Mrs. HogF,,ard led a special demonstration of the Prescot Corps, on Saturday, Sep. 6th. The demonstration commenced with a public ham tea served up in real Salvation Army style. Captain and Mrs. Stephens, of 'Matto Heath, with their soldiers, and also Capt. Beenham and Lieut. Parkin and soldiers from Liverpool with their Brass Band were present. CONGREGATIONAL SUNDAY SCHOOL.—On Saturday the teachers and friends in connection with the above school, had a picnic to Hoylaka and West Kirby. The party, numbering about 40, left Prescot by the 1.16 train, and arrived at West Kirby about three o'clock, and proceeded by the Mersey tunnel to their destination. The trip was much enjoyed by all. The weather was all that could be desired considering the quantity of rain that has so lately fallen. The arrangements for providing tea, were left in the hands of the pastor, the Rev. A. N. Gilmore, and the secretary, Mr. G. Brown, both of whom ably carried out their duty. TILE BRESCOT CATHOLIC BENEFIT SOCIETY.—On Monday evening, the annual dinner in connection with the above society (whose head quarters are at the Yew Tree Schools), was held at the Plough lan, Prescot, kept by Mrs. Haydon. About 60 members sat down to a dinner at three o'clock in the afternoon which was a credit to the hostess. After dinner which all enjoyed, and at which the Rev. Father Brindle was present, Mr. Arden, of Whis- ton, was unanimously voted to the chair. Having thanked the members for the honour they had conferred on him he said he was happy to see so many members present as it plainly showed they had not many on the sick list. He congratulated them on the great success of their branch. In 1884 they had only about 20 members worth about £l5, but at the end of 1889 they had about £53 in cash and between 50 and 60 members. At the present time they had 60 good members and cash in the bank and in the treasurer's hands amounting to over £7O. Father Brindle, in reply to a vote of thanks, spoke upon the advisability of providing for a rainy day. The Chair- man then proposed the health of "His Holiness the Pope and clergy." Other toasts were "The Queen and Royal , Family," and "Prosperity to the Society." Songs were sung during the evening by Mr. M. Brodeuch, the chair- man, Mr. John Scholes, Mr. Paul Conroy, Mr. J. Gavan, Mr. J. Caveney, Bro. Kennedy, Bro. Clines, Bro. Gormon and Bro. O'Brien who gave an Irish song which all en- joyed but no one understood.

PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of this Board • was held on Thursday afternoon, when there were present Major Wareing (chairman), the Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester, the Rev. Dean Finegan, Messrs. J. Burchall, W. Middlehurst, J. 'Archon, .1. Ellison, J. Ransom W. Tyrar, J. Golds- worth, C. B. Johnson, Mr. F. Stapleton-Bretherton,J.P, (ex-officio), and Mr. S. H. Hartley (clerk). Wointlionsc Ismerss.—Mr. Hale, master of the work- house, reported that there were 507 inmates this week, 499 in the preceding week, as against 506 in the corres- ponding week last year. During the week there had been 82 vagrants relieved, against 57 it the corresponaing week last year. THE LATE STACK FIRE AT WHISTON.—At a meeting of the Visiting Committee held, it was recommended that no reduction be made in the charges for the fire brigade's attendance at Mr. Ashcroft's recent fire at Whiston, and that if the amount (211.15.) is:not paid forthwith legal proceedings be taken for its recovery.—Mr. Middlehurst said that the charges for the use of the workhouse fire brigade had been settled long before the fire in question, and they could not see any reason to alter that charge.— Mr. Sylvester said his attention was called to one of the regulations that made it incumbent upon every fireman to give notice of any fire taking place, and he was in- formed that one of the firemen of the brigade watched the fire in question for about half an hourbefore he gave an alarm.—The Chairman said that first of all the regu- lations applied to their own premises. The steam fire

, engine belonging to the guardians was not a public fire engine, and they would not send it out unless they had instructions to do so from the person whose premises were on fire.—The minutes were adopted. ANNUAL POOR LAW CONFERENCE.—The Clerk intimated that the 16th annual conference of the North-Western Poor Law Union was fixed to be held at Southport ors the 3rd and 4th October. It was decided to send a deputation to the conference. A COUPLAINT.--A letter was received from a ratepayer at Bold complaining of the non-attendance of the assist- ant overseer at his office on several occasions and it was decided to make inquiries into the matter. CONTRIBUTION ORDERS.—It was decided that contribu- tion orders be issued upon the township of Eccleston and Windle to pay the sums of £252 ss, 11d. and £92 2s. id. respectively as their proportions of the county rate. AGED PAUPERS.—The Clerk reported that he had pre- pared a return for the Local Government Board, show- ing the number of persons,6o years of age and upwards, in receipt of relief in the Union. It showed there were 144 males and 52 females receiving indoor relief, and 212 males and 671 females receiving outdoor relief. AN APPOINTMENT.—Mrs. Sharpe, of the Aston Union, was apptinted night nurse at the workhouse. This was all the business.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

THE WESLEYAN CIRCIIIT.—The newly-appointed min- ister to the Frodsham circuit preached on Sunday morn- ing and evening in the Trinity Chapel, Frodsham, when very good congregations assembled. Tnisirr CHAPEL Cm:int.—The members of the choir and friends, numbering, some thirty-five, had their annual choir trip on Saturday. A thoroughly enjoyable outing was the result, the party returning home by the 1035 p.m. train
HA YDOCK.
TELEPHONIC COMMUNICATION.—The work of establish- ing telephonic communication between the Haydock police office, and the Ashton police office, is being pro- ceeded with.

THE NEW KING AND PRINCESS PITS.—The sinking of these new pits, which was commenced in god earnest a few weeks ago, is now at a standstill, owing to Mr. M. Stevenson, the contractor, having thrown up the work. Negotiations are in progress for the letting of a fresh con- tract, and it is hoped that the work will shortly be pro- ceeded with.

SERIOUS SURSIDENCE.-A serious subsidence of land has taken place in Kenyon's-lane, Haydock. Several cottages have given way to some extent,and the tenants, becoming alarmed, have vacated them. The water mains have been broken, and have had to be taken up and relaid. The subsidence is due to the colliery workings which extend beneath Ken:y-on's-lane. A Suspicions CincindsrANcp.—About five o'clock on Wednesday morning, as a collier named Jackson was proceeding to his work along the canal towing path, at Blackbrook, he found on the bank a man's hat, basket, and can. He could not find an owner for them, and the fact of them being found close to the water's edge points suspiciously to a case of suicide. The police, however, have received no intimation of anybody being missing, and thus the find reins ins shrouded in mystery.
PENICETH. CHAPEL ANNIVERSARY AT PANKETH.
Anniversary sermons were on Sunday preached at Penketh Wesleyan Chapel, by the Rev. T. Ross. There were good congregations.

A VILLAGE WEDDING. On Tuesday afternoon, the interest of the inhabi- tants of Penketh was concentrated in an event which seemed to command almost absorbing atten- tion. This was the marriage of Miss Garnett, daughter of Mr. R. Garnett,J.P., of Hall Nook,to Mr. Chas. Robinson Doeg, of The !lollies, Norfolk-road, Carlisle, all the accessories of the ceremony being of a quaintly picturesque character. At two o'clock a varied procession of friends and rela- tives, terminating with the bride and her father, with the bridesmaids, consisting of her sisters, the Misses Fanny and Hilda Garnett, left Hall , Nook on foot, and reached the chapel shortly after, when the marriage service was solem- nized by the Rev. J. Gunnell, superintendent of the district, assisted by the Rev. Alfred Freeman and the Rev. Thomas Ross. The bride was attired in phosphorus blue amazon cloth, with gold. Cairene embroidery, and her maids in dresses of velvet of a lovely art green shade. After the ceremony, as Mr. Wigfield played Mendelssohn's " Wedding March," the procession re-formed, headed this time by bride and groom, who were warmly tied lovingly greeted on all hands by attached village friends and neighbours of the bride, who giatefully remembered her kindly work and intercourse in the village where she had been born. Amongst them several were loud in their expressions of regret at her departure. Flower 3 were strewn in her path by her tiny niece, Miss. Helen Mary Parker, and other children. The scene from the chapel dour to the residence of the bride's. father was one long to be remembered on account of its unique aspect. On either side the road was. lined with joyous villagers, who greeted most heartily the newly-married couple. One old lady,. whom we noticed supported by a friend on one• side and her trusty stick on the other, was evi- dently much.affected, and we learned that she was a pensioner of the bride's, in her 95th year. The children from the village day school in united chorus sang "God bless the bride and bridegroom." Subsequently an "At Home" was held at the residence of the bride's father, the guests including Mr. and Mrs. David Garnett, Mr. and Mrs. Brad- shaw, Dr. and Mrs. Hurter, Mr. and Mrs. likieg (Carlisle), Mr. and Mrs. Charles Parker, Miss Parker, Mr. and Mrs. and Miss Wigfield, Mr. and Mrs. Fildes, Mr. Sam Fades, Mr. Potts, Miss Longbottom, Miss Bessie Dutton (Moore), Mrs. John Fairclough, Rev. John and Mrs. Gunnell, the Rev. Alfred and Mrs. Freeman, the Rev. Thomas and Mrs. Ross, Mr. and Mrs. William Garnett, Mrs. Coop, Mr. and Mrs. Tom Gandy, Mr. and Mrs. Brett, &c. The wedding pre- sents, numbering about a hundred and fifty, were the admiration of all. In the evening the bride and bridegroom left for a tour in Scotland, and will sub- sequently take up their residence at Carlisle.
PROPOSED PUBLIC PARK, &c., FOR PENEETII.

_ On Monday evening, a meeting of the employs of the Penketh Tanning Company, and Messrs. R. Garnett and Sons, was held at the works of the Penketh Tanning Corepany, to discuss the advisabil- ity of forming a Limited Liability Company, for the purpose of acquiring land to be laid out as a park for recreative and building purposes. There was a, large attendance. Mr. C. E. Parker, managing' director of the Penketh Tanning Co., addressing the meeting, intimated that at the last meeting of the shareholders and directors of the company, a con- versation took place relative to the practicability and wisdom of the members of the company assist- - ing the employees in inaugurating such a scheme as. he was about to sketch. It w propf-d that Limited Liability Company be farmed for recreati7.? (;e ac 'and building purposes, to include a public hall, swimming bath, bowling green, cricket and lawn tennis grounds, cottage gardens, and building land. The shareholders of the Penketh Tanning Company, Limited, were willing to subscribe a considerable portion of the money required as soon as they have the assurance that the workmen really desire the above-mentioned things, and that they were willing to assist in attaining them, by backing their desires to the extent of taking shares in the ccmpany. Mr. Parker proceeded to say that while the scheme sprung from the Penketh Tanning Company and was primarily intended for the benefit of their work-people, they are ready to welcome the co-operation of the principals and the employes of Messrs. R. Garnett and Sons, who had already indicated their approval of the scheme, and also that they consider that the inter- ests of the workpeople would not be endangered, but rather firrthered, by throwing the advantages of the company open to the general public of Penketh, and therefore, if that meeting of workpeople ap- proved the schemel and took a goodly number of shares, a public meeting would be hereafter held for the purpose of explaining the scheme and offering shares to outsiders. Mr. R. E. Garnett spoke on behalf of Messrs. R. Garnett and Sons, and said the scheme was a big one and would require the hearty support and co-operation of every individual; he hoped it would be an entire success, and the men would keep up their enthusiasm and each do his very beat. Mr. James Dodds, as one of the share- holders of the Penketh Tanning Company, said that as far as be (And, be was sure. he spoke for the, other shareholders as well) was concerned the move- ment would have his entire sympathy and support. He thought that such an institution would prove a great blessing to the men and their families, and to the whole neighbourhood. The following also spoke upon the subject :—Messrs. R. Greenhalgh, T. ' Tetlow, A. IVhite, T. Seed, W. Longshaw, E. Cross, and D. Garnett. A considerable number of names were afterwards given in for shares in the com- pany.

Mr. Brewis, derk to the St. Helens borough magis- trates, and who recently resigned the Town-clerkship, has taken the residence of Mr. John Pennington, at the corner of Hardshaw-street, opposite the Town Hall, in which to' carry on his practice. The position is a most convenient one.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
A JUVENILE NEWSBOY,

John Mullin was summoned (under the Better Protec- tion of Children Act, 1889) for allowing his son, aged seven years, to sell newspapers. P.C. Cunliffe said that on the 28th ult. he saw the lad hawking newspapers in the neighbourhood of Horsemarket-st. The Bench fined the father ss.

ONE WAY OF "CHEERING UP." On Wednesday, at the Warrington Police Court, Julia Noakley was charged with drunkenness and disorderly conduct in Bridge-st., on the evening before. Prisoner told the magistrates that she had been teetotal for two years, and now a very little drink took effect on her. She heard that her son, who is in the army, was sick in hospital, and thought a "gill of ale would cheer her up." Mr. Fairclough : It has not cheered you up ; it has cheer- ed you down. A fine of ss.,including costs, was imposed. A VIOLENT WOMAN.

Yesterday, at the Warrington Police Court, a woman named Martha Pritchard was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Dakba's-court, on the previous afternoon, with having assaulted Isabella Harding, and with having broken windows at the house of the latter. It wag stated that she hit Mrs. Harding on the eye with her shoe. Alderman Harrison said the conduct of the prisoner was like that of an heathen, rather than a civil- ised person. She would be fined 103. and costs for the drunkenness, ordered to pay the damage, and also to find two sureties for her good behaviour.

div.head: i "BLACK SPOT."
div.p: i "BLACK SPOT."

At the Warrington Police Court, on Wednesday, two women of bad character, named Catherine Smith and Mary Connolley, were brought up on charges of drunken- ness. P.S. Jones stated that he had occasion to go through the house occupied by the prisoners, and he found nothing but a little straw in one of the corners. Inspector Spinks said that there was no furniture in the place, which was used for an improper purpose. The Chief Constable said that if the owner or agent of the property knew who occupied it, they would rather close the place than let it to such people. Prisoners were sent to jail for a month, with hard labour.

div.head: BOY DRTJNICARD.
div.p: A BOY DRTJNICARD.

The Warring,t3n magistrates had a shocking case be- fore them on Monday. A lad named William Cunning- ham, who has just turned 15 years of age, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Scotland-road, on the Ist September. P.C. Monaghan said that he saw the defendant " staggering drunk outside the Theatre, from which he had been ejected. He had been quarrell- ing with another lad, whom he wanted to stab. Mr. Ashton, the manager of the Theatre Royal, said that Cunningham behaved in an extraordinary manner in the Theatre, and had in consequence to be put out. It was stated that the prisoner had been summoned for be- ing drunk as late as July last. The Bench seemed puz- zled to know what to do with the case, but ultimately the lad was ordered to be detained in custody until six o'clock.

- - - How DISEASE IS SPREAD. At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday. Charles 33uxton, a married man, living in Robinson's-yard, off Croesley-st., was charged with keeping lodgers in an unregistered house. Inspector Spinks said that on Sun- day morning at 2.30 o'clock he visited the defendant's house. He found the defendant and two little children -sleeping on a floor downstairs, and his wife and two lodgers were drinking together. He also discovered in a little room above a man, woman, and two children sleep- ing on some old dirty clothing. Inspector Norman said that there were ten persons in the house,which was only adapted for two. The house was very dirty. The Bench considered the case a very serious one, and comment was made on the unhealthy state of the place. They fined Buxton 40s. and costs, or in default a month's imprisonment with hard labour.

div.head: COI7PLE OF BAD CEARACTERS.
div.p: A COI7PLE OF BAD CEARACTERS.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, Bodelia Knockton and Elizabeth Ellen Fleming were summoned for doing wilful damage to some property belonging to the executors of the late Mr. Porter, en the Ist September. A witness was called to show that ten panes of glass had been smashed, and also the window frame and door of a cottage had been broken, the amount of damage being estimated at 10s. The Chairman stated that that was Knockton's forty-second appearam.:e, and Fleming was almost as bad, having been 25 times before the magis- trates. Each of the prisoners would be committed for a monthc Fleming was then charged with creating a breach of the peace, by -fighting, in Buttermarket-at., on the 2nd September. P.C. Bell proved the case, and the prisoner was ordered to be bound over to keep the peace, the alternative being 14 days' imprisonment.

div.head: -WIFE DESEETION.
div.p: -WIFE DESEETION.

John Vielterl, a labourer, was charged at the Warring- ton Police Court, on Wednesday, with having deserted Us Wife and children, who had been left chargeable to the common fund of the Union. Mr. Shearer said that the prisoner's Nvire and three children were admitted to the Workhouse on the 28th May. A warrant WaS issued for the apprehension of the prisoner, who was not found until this week. His family were in the Workhouse for six weeks, the coat to the ratepayers being £5 Cs. The magistrates sent him to prison for a month, with hard labour.—At the Police Court, on Thursday, a man named ThonutAGarritty was charged for the fourth time with neglecting to maintain his child. Ile had served im- prisonment for six weeks, then three months, and again three months, for this offence. It was stated that during the last five years he had scarcely done anything towards maintaining his family. He was now again sent to prison for three months, svith hard labour.

ItUNC°RIv.Ma. H. H. BAINBRIDGE'S Taunr.—The football season opened at Runcorn on Saturday, a match having been arranged rrelinainary to commencing the usual list ar fixtures. The players were :—Runoorn S. Houghton:, back; Davies, Crompton, and Gayter, three- quarter backs; H. aughes and Evans, half backs; Broady,Hughes, Davies, Hughes, Riley, Lee, Dolan, Hampson, and Rigby-,, forwards. The Manchester dis- trict team started, and Gayter saved,though the District men got under the Runcorn posts. Houghton and Crompton got away,,and the District men were pressed back. A nice bit of passing by Hughes andßiley got the ball in close proximity to the Manchester line. Evans ' cornlng from the pack gave to Hughes, who threw to Crompton, the latter soon getting over the line, and from, the place he kicked a beautiful goal. After some desul- tory play 0. Hughes got a free kick, Crompton making a bold bid for goal, a minor resulting. Crompton received the ball from the drop out, and closing up, coolly dropped a magnificent goal from near midfield, the feat being hailed with much enthusiasm. Nothing daunted, the visitors played strongly, Mullineax and Buck making efforts to get off. The Runcorn forwards pressed on into the Manchester half. Here a smart bit of passing by H. Hughes to his brother, W. Hughes, took place. The last named ran and threw to Crompton, who in turn passed to Gayter, who crossed the District line near touch, Houghton making a good attempt at goal. This breught half-time, the score reading—Runcorn, 2 goals, I try ; District Team, nil. After the interval W. Hughes re- started, the play being most interesting. An excellent dribble by Dolan was taken up by Riley, who scored a well merited try, Crompton missing at goal. Davies got the ball from Crompton, in succession from Hughes, and in going behind the posts was tackled by Wardley and Ruck, losing possession, but Dolan was up, and easily completed the try, Crompton scoring the goal. Im- mediately afterwards Crompton picked up, and easily got under the posts, and again completed the try. Final score :—Runcorn 4 goals, 2 tries, 2 minors to nothing. Sr.ELENS V'• MANCHESTER BANGERS.—The St. Helens , . . _

(Rugby) Club opened their new ground off Knutsford- road, on Saturday afternoon, between 2,000 and 3,000 spectators lining the enclosure. The opposing team was the Manchester Rangers' and the following were the players : St. Helens—J. Lomax, full back; T. Sudlow, Foulkes, and J. T. Unsworth, three-quarters; W. Cross and F. Little, half backs; A. 13orthwick, Baines, Glad- win, Basnett, R. Twist, John Brownbill, Joseph Brown- bill, P. Guest, and Rankin, forwards. Manchester Rangers—J. Gadd, full back; Danhill, Cunliffe and A. Hammett, three-quarters ; W. Parlane and P. Meehan half backs; H. flasleham, J. Scowby, G. Pollard, E. Mee, Arley, S. Grange, A. Storer, W. Storer and R. Hammett, forwards. Mr. Naylor, of Wigan, referee. Lieutenant Colonel Wilcock, chamnanof the Saints' Com- mittee, kicked off for the homesters, and the ball was soon traversing the field, play being fast and exciting. After some scrimmages with the visitors quarters Cross picked up and cleverly dropped a goal, the first major point of the season. Encouraged by their success, , the homesters exerted every effort and the oval was passed from Little and Foulkes to Sudlow, who ran down touch, dodging and handling off his opponents and grounded near touch. On appeal a scrimmage was ordered, and Cross passed to Unsworth,who appeared to get over the line. Another scrimmage, however, was formed and the ball sent into touch. The throwing sent the oval into Joseph Brownbill's hands, wno dropped over. His brother took the place but failed to convert the point. At half time the score was as follows: St. Helens 1 goal (dropped), I try and 2 minors, to Rangers 1 minor. After the restart operations were located in the Rangers territory, and a poor return by Gadd was pick- ed up by Sudlow, who rounded his men in fine style and I grounded near the posts. The visitors appealed for being in touch, but the referee granted the try and Borthwick converted It into a goal. Pariane, Meehan, and Ham- mett made strong attempts to score for the visitors and after several line-outs and scrummages in the home territory Hammett picked up and dashed over. Herbert Hasleham took the place kick and failed. The game ended, St. Helens, 2 goals, 1 try, and four minors, to Manchester Rangers, 1 try, 1 minor. ASSOCIATION.

MR. DAVITT ON THE LABOUR PROBLEM.

In an interview with a representative of the "Pall Mall Gazette," Mr. Davitt is reported to have said: The labour problem is now the most vital issue that con- fronts the statesmanship of the civilised world. It is going to occupy the serious attention of European Governments for the next ten years, and the danger is not so much the opposition that may be expected from kings and capitalists as from temporising and compro- mising action on the part of 'politicians who call them- selves the champions of the working classes. I look for the true labour leaders from among working men, and my paper will strongly advocate suchorganisation and such a course of policy on the part of the industrial classes as will enable men from their own ranks to repre- sent them on all public bodies, from the village board of guardians to the Imperial Parliament in Westminster. I am for payment of members together with the thrcAwing of the cost of elections—with safeguards against frivo• bus contests--upon local rates. But we must press for- ward, also, for universal adult suffrage, a seconci ballot, triennial Parliaments, and the " ending" not the" mend- ing "—of the House of Landlords.

div.head: ONE WOMAN'S NERVES.
div.p: ONE WOMAN'S NERVES.

Looking backward to a certain lonely and unhappy time, a lady says : " I dragged on in this miserable condition for years, until I got tired of doctoring and taking stuff that did me no good. One physician attended [no for eighteen months, giving me but little relief. " I slept only in a broken fashion, and arose in the morning very little the better for having gone to bed. There was often severe pain in my head and over my eyes, and an almost constant sense of sickness. The skin gradually got dry and yellow, the region of the stomach and bowels felt cold and dead, and the natural energy and warmth appeared to be ebbing out of rac like the water oat of a river at low tide. " In June, 1889, whilst living at Moredown, Bourne- mouth, I had a worse attack than any I had before. I was taken with a feeling of cramp, as if pins and needles were running into me all over my body. I could not move and had to lie helpless in bed. The doctor was sent for, and attended me every day, but did not seem to know what to make of my case. In fact, ha was puzzled, and finally said, ' I don't really know what your complaint is.'

"I trembled and shook and felt as if I should fall to pieces. I was first hot and then cold, and so dreadfully nervous I could not bear anyone in the room with me, and yet I did not wish them far away in case I should call out for help. Every time one of these spasms came on I said to myself. I am sure I shall never get up , again.' ' "I took nothing but liquid food, and yet could not re- tain even that on my stomach. By this time I was nothing but skin and bone. My legs went clammy, as if had no blood left in me. My memory completely failed. I never expected to recover, and that was the opinion of my friends. After they had called to see me they would go away saying, 'She will never get better.' My head ached so dreadfully I thought I should lose my senses.

"I had given up all hope, when one day my friend Mrs. West, of Bournemouth, called and asked what I was taking. I said, 'Oh, I'm tired of taking things: it's no use; I shall die." Then she told me she was once ill much as I was, and was cured by Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. 'Well,' I said, 'l'll try it if you will send for it.' She did so, and I seemed to feel better on taking the first dose, and after three days I was able to walk across the room, and by the end of the week I went downstairs. Now lam well as ever. All my nervousness has left me, and I can eat and digest my food without feeling any distress.

"I want to say finally, that I knew about Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, and should have tried it years before if certain acquaintances hadn't said, • Oh, don't take it, for it will do you no good.' They said that because it was advertised, not because they knew for themselves. It was bad advice for me, and cost me years of torture. From what I have said—which Is but part of my story—the people may infer what I think of this remedy. I thank God that I did resort to it at last before it was too late." (Signed) Mrs. Jane Foster, Darracott Road, Pokesdown, Bournemouth, Hants, March, 1890.

It is only necessary to add that the malady from which Mrs. Foster suffered was indigestion, dyspepsia, and nervous prostration. Brought on originally by grief and shock at her husband's sudden and violent death, her system did not rally until Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup removed the torpor of the digestive organs, and thus enriched the blood and fed the nerves. It always has this effect in like cases. We can only regret that she foolishly procrastinated in the matter of using it. Her statement of facts may be relied upon, as the case has been thoroughly and impartially investigated.

CRICK_IST.

After threatening to end in the tamest manner, the last and most important match of the- Scarborough Festival came to a very exciting termination on Satur- day, the Australians winning by a narrow margin of eight runs. Overnight the English side had been left with five wickets to fail and 48 runs to ge to win, and in the absence of rain it-was felt that the-chanc,es were slightly against them. Alittle of the rain which earlier in the week had fallen so plentifully in Scarborough might have made all the difference, but wit/rev-bright dry morning the vrickets was perhaps rather:nexn-e difficult than at any time during the match.

At first it seemed as though the Englishmen would be beaten without a struggle, Peel, Gunn, .Lohruann, and Briggs being so readily-got rid of,that nine wickets were down for 66, or an addition of only 15 runs,- to the over- night score of 51. Then however, when the pone seemed hopeless, no fewer than 33 runs being wanted with a wicket to fall, Messrs,. Mods and M'Greger played up magnificently, scoring at every opportunity and show- ing the utmost coolness and judgment. or the first few overs it was taken for granted that the Australians would win, but amid) gradually increasin,o,.. excitement the score was hit up to )0;or only nine.runs,slaort of vic- tory. Before anything more could be •dene, however, WGregor was out leg, before wicket, .the Australians winning a desperately fought-out match, by eight runs.

The side they beat was certainly one of the strongest they have met during their tour, and they clearly owed their victory to Turner, who scored 34 rand 2,1, the two highest scores in the game, and took 13 for 57 runs. In the last innings the great bowler took .seven wickets for 46 runs. Briggs fonthe English side, ,it will be remem- bered, obtained 15 wickets for 57 runs, aad thus, though he had not such an array of first-class batsmen against him, fairly divided the bowling honours with Turner. Despite the unsettled weather the Scarborough Festival was a great success*. and we are officially informed that the Scarborough club. will clear £5OO by: the nine days' cricket.

It has been definitely arranged between the manage- ment of the Manhatten Athletic Club, New York, and the Salford Harriers that a team, of amateur runners be sent out to America on September 16th. The English- men will be W. H. Marton, ten to twenty miles champion; E. W. Parry, cross country national champion; G. H. Morris, 1,000 yards champion; T. L Nicholas, 220 and 440 yards champion ; and N. B. Morgan, 100 yards champion. It is currently stated that a sum of £lOO will be needed to cover the expenses of the two months' trip. They will visit all the chief centres. Berths have been secured on the White Star line steamer Majestic.

EXTENSIVE PROSECUTION OF SOUTH YORKSHIRE MINERS.

• On Wednesday, at Barnsley, 423 miners, employed by the Monetton Main Colliery Company, near Barnsley, were summoned for absenting themselves from work. Two hundred and seventy-one were sued for 15s. each, and the remainder for 7s. 6d. each, the total claim being £260. The men refused to work on Saturday and Mon- day last, owing to notices being given to other employes. Work, however, was resumed on Tuesday. The owners complain bitterly of the losses caused by men neglecting work, and restricting the output during the present pros- perous state of trade.

div.head: HOLDING LIFE CHEAP.
div.p: HOLDING LIFE CHEAP.

A remarkable instance of indifference to pain and death,and of the promptitude to throw away life on what seems the most insufficient provocation, is recorded in the Indian papers as having occurred in the native State of Rajputana. A tax levied to pay certain villiage ex- penses baying been demanded, the religious devotees instigated by the head of the monastry, refused to pay it. In this refusal they were supported by devotees from neighbouring villages, their number in the aggregate amounting to about one hundred and fifty, who threatened that they would bury themselves alive if not exempt from payment. Their threat was no mere empty one, for on the Thakoor declining to yield to their de- mand, they forthwith began to carry it out bv burying two of their number. Upon the officials interfering with their resolve they drew swords, daggers and knives, and defied interference. Assistance ultimately coming to the authorities, a number of the recalcitrants were ar- rested, and on being tried were sentenced to various terms of imprisonment, three years being apportioned to the abbot. This was not the only occasion when he had been the cause of much trouble to the powers that be. He had been arrested some time previeusly, where- upon nearly a hundred of his followers rushed into the compound of the British Political Agent, and demanded the abbot's release, threatening to kill themselves if their demand was not granted. Four graves were dug, and in each a man sat himself down, ready to be entombed if their leader was kept in custody. The contemplated wholesale self-immolation was, however, averted through the tender-heeztedness of the political agent, who thoup ht It best under the circumstances to comply with the • demand of the abbot's infatuated followers.

div.head: LABOUR ORGANISATION ON THE SHIP CANAL.
div.p: LABOUR ORGANISATION ON THE SHIP CANAL.

The active workers of the Navvies, Bricklayers' Labourers, and General Labourer' Union are making a vigorous effort to enrol into the union the navvies en- gaged upon the Manchester Ship Canal Works, with the object of further consolidating the organisation and forming a bond of unity between the workmen of Lon- don and the provinces. The object of the union is gener- ally to improve the condition of the members, and specifically to maintain better wages and secure shorter hours, and to do away with "sub-contractors and other sweater." ,About 300 of the Ship Canal men have al- ready joined the organisation, and branches have been formed at Salford, Eccles, Cadishead, and Warrington. ' The last-named branch was formed on Sunday, when a , meeting was held at Arpley, in the open air. It was at- tended by about 500 persons, 19 out of every 20 of whom were Ship Canal navvies and labourers. Mr. A. Wit- hams, of Eccles, acted as chairman, and the principal speaker was Mr. John Ward, the president of the union, who addressed the meeting as a worker speaking to workers, and afterwards made a personal canvass for members amongst those present. Some twelve months ago, Mr. Ward said, when the labour movement took a new shape in London, it was thought by the excavators and navvies in that district that the best thing they could do as a body of working-men was to form a union of their own. After a year's work they had now about 9,000 members. Having organised London, they had gone, into Essex, where some 700 men of the union went out on strike. They successfully conducted that dispute, and gained for those 700 men a rise of wages of a.,halfpenny per hour, to range over nearly i ; three years. That meant that with an expenditure of , only £47, which amount the union spent in fighting the question,they had put into the pockets,or would do dur- ing the next three years, of those men, close on £5,000. ' The union now wanted to extend its operations in the provinces, and with that object was seeking to get the men employed on the ship canal to join. For the kind of work done on the shin canal the navvies were not receiv- ing the wages they should do. This state of affairs could only be altered by combination. It was computed that there were about 180,000 navvies knocking about the country, and ,up to a few years ago they had not the slightest semblance of a union to protect their interests, and to demand better wages in the future than they had had in the past. Those who did hard work, as they did, should receive higher wages. Some 80,000 of their class could not claim, a home at the end of each week. How was it that, while other working men were looked upon with respect, and were treated as fellows in the labour world, they were looked upon as mere lumps of corrup- tion, in the way of everyone? They were not respected because up to now they had not respected themselves. They were crushed down; their wages were low; and their work was hard. Of course, some of them took to beer as a means of excitement after their heavy toil. That was the reason that drove many thousands of them to drink. If their condition in life was made easier, their minds would tend to higher things and they would require more intellectual pleasure. This was what was meant by unionism, and a man who stood aside when his particular trade was being organised was an outlaw te labour. It was as the president of the union, and as the representative of 9,000 London workingmen, that he was appealing to them that morning to combine with others to get a better condition of life in the future. In answer to a, question, the speaker said that the minimum wage of the union was 6d. per hour, but that did not prevent 'anyone joining. They wanted men to join in order that I they might obtain the minimum wage.—A number of those present joined the union at the close of the meeting.

div.head: .ANCIEN2 ORDER OF FORESTERS.
div.p: THE .ANCIEN2 ORDER OF FORESTERS.
A HUGE DEFICIENCY.

' The serious deficiency of £2,770,251, which (says a correspondent of the "Standard ") the recent valuation has shown to exist in the funds of the courts and dis- tvicts of :the Ancient Order of Foresters, and against which there is a set-off of only £137,769, has caused the High Court of the Order to set about a thorough and drastic reform of the financial position of the largest friendly-seciety in the world. For four years the High Court has, been nibbling at financial reform, afraid, from theadvice of false friends within and the fear of corn- petition.without, to take measures necessary to put the Order in a 'solvent posillion. The deficiency of nearly three millions sterling which now exists in the funds of this mast society has grown up gradually, as the result of the imperfect...knowledge possessed by the pioneers of the friendly society movement. This Order, the same as others,commenced with the inequitable equal contribution system,,by which the man of forty paidthe same contribu- tion as the man of twenty. The contribution paid for those •benefits by the man of twenty was probably fairly- adequate, but it was grotesquely inadequate for the man who had reached double the age, and whom exper- ience has shown to draw very much larger sick benefits from thedunds of his court. As ,a consequence many' of the older courts only met their fiabilities year by year by using the,contributions of new members. The evil and the slough of financial insolvencrin which the equal con- tribution system was landing the 'order were eventually recognised,by actuaries, and the clear-minded among the members :; ,but it reguired many years of persistent hard work to induce lodges to adopt the sensible graduated scale of contributions, by which each member, whatever the age at which he joined, paid for what he received. Another cause of decay has been theinadequate contribu- tions paid for benefits received. At the recent High Court meeting, a London delegate frankly admitted that for more thantwenty.years he had paid an insufficient contribution for the benefits he had received. The oppo- sition to any increase in the contributions, or a propor- • donate decrease in benefits, has always come from the alder members, -who have profited in the past, and wish to profit in the future, at the expense of their fellow- members. The only argument—if, indeed, it can be , termed argument .atall—which has been used against the ref= party at the High .Court meetings has been the -sentimental one of consideration for 01.11 members who wererthe pioneers of the movement, and who had been taught to expect these excessive benefits. It speaks well for the sturdy common-sense of the workingmen legisla- itors who compose the High Court meetings that they lave made short work;of this sentimental clap-trap ' and have determined, as far as in them lies, to pay con- tributions which will honourably meet every liability immured. Until this year the legislation adopted was always of a permissive character. So long as help could be obtained from the central fund, insolvent lodges would do nothing to help themselves: Of forty-three lodges with a degree of solvency of less than fifteen shill- ings in the pound, which applied to the Hull Executive Council for relief, only two did 'anything to improve their financial situation. Well might the High Court postpone the granting relief to these oourts until such time as new general laws have been adopted Which would compel thein to adopt reforms wittin before grant- ing relief from without. By the operation of the new law adopted this year, the courts with a relative degree of solvency of less than fifteen shillings will receive the Contribution from the High Court relief fund equal to one-half of the deficiency on the court assenting to an alteration of the scale of contributions paid and benefits received which will make up the other half. The contri- bution of the High Court, instead of being paid in a lump sum, as relief has hitherto been granted, will be spread over a number of years; and before the second contribution is paid the court will have to satisfy the Executive Council that they have complied with the con- ditions imposed when relief was granted. By the general working out of this system of relief it is hoped to gradually build up the Ancient Order of Foresters, which numbers 670,000 members, on the basis of financial Stability.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBEB 13, 1890.
