WARRINGTON GRAMMAR SCHOOL.

Mr. 11. W. Curjel, 8.A., has just been appointed to an assistant mastership at Shrewsbury School. After a successful career of five years at the War- rington Grammar School, Mr. Curjel won in 1886 an open mathematical scholarship at Exeter College, Oxford, a first class in mathematical moderations in 1888, and a first class in the final mathematical schools in 1890. CRTTCHLET, High Clogs Tailor. Bold-st.Warrington.—Adrt. CHOIR TRIP TO LLANDUDNO.

On Monday, the junior 171-e-a-er-s- of St. Paul's choir had their annual trip to Llandudno. The party, who were accompanied by the Vicar (the Rev. S. Wilkinson), Mr. and Mrs. J. Lythgoe, and Mr. John Parkinson, left Warrington by an early train, arriv- ing at their destination about 10.30. After luncheon, the young people spent a delightful day. Tea was partaken of at 5.30, and a start home made at 6.30. The weather was fine. BAD FISH IN THE MAUKET.

At the Bor-o-u-ge-FoliCe.C-O-u;:t.-on-konday. Mr. R. Norman, nuisance inspector, made an application to the Bench for the destruction of a quantity of fish, weighing about 601b5., which he had seized in the market on Saturday night. He had obtained a certificate from Dr. Brooks, acting in the absence of the medical officer of health, certifying that the fish was unsound and unfit for human food. The applicaUon was granted. CRITCHLEY'S Tailoring meets the times.—Advt.
THE WORKINGMEN'S OPEN AIR TOTAL ABSTINENCE
MISSION.

On Sunday, on the enclosed ground off Bewsey- st., the usual meetings were held. In the afternoon Mr. J. Price, president, presided, and Messrs. R. Storey, C. H. Mills, and J. Drury gave addresses. At another meeting in the evening, Mr. J. Price in the chair, the following gentlemen gave addresses— Messrs. J. Drury, J. Kilduff, and J. Yarwood (of Oldham). Several persons took the pled'ge.

ACADEMY-ST. MISSION. On Sunday anniversary services were held at the Academy-st. Mission. Sermons were preached in the morning and evening by Mr. W. G. Taylor, of Liverpool, there being a large congregation on each occasion. In the afternoon a service of song, en- titled "Driven from Home," was rendered by the choir, and was received with much satisfaction. The proceeds of the three services amounted to £l3 7s. id., which is to be added to the fund for building a new and more commodious place of worship. CRITCHLEY, Practical Tailor, Bold-it. ,Warrington.—Advt. THE LATE Mn. J. STIR% : BENEFIT CONCERT. A concert for the benefit of the widow of the late Mr. James Stirk was given in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-st., on Monday evening. The vocalists were Messrs. J. Dillon. J. Bate, and Lawton, and Miss Cavanagh. Mr. Dillon sang "The Desert" and "Sands of Time," and each time was encored. Mr. Lawton contributed " Hybrias the Cretan" and "Queen of My Heart," and Miss Cavanagh gave in- terpretations of the songs "Never Again" and "Ferryman John." Mr. Bate rendered "Passing Away" and "We may be happy yet." For the latter he secured an encore, and responded with "The Scout." An instrumental band, under the leader- ship of Mr. J. Caldwell, performed at intervals. Messrs. J. Caldwell and F. Bate were the accom-, panists. CHILDREN'S TEAT AT CROFT. This annual treat took Mace on Saturday after- noon, the weather being fine. The children began to assemble at the Board school at one o'clock, and shortly after two, the children and young people of the parish formed a procession, and, headed by the school banner and the band of the 11 Company (Leigh) of the 4th L.R.V.' they proceeded up Heath lane as far as the Plough Inn, and then returned, and went through the village to the Smithy, and back to the school. They afterwards went to a field, lent by Mr. E. W. Sankey, of Heath Farm, where games were engaged in until four o'clock, after- wards the chiFren partook of tea in a tent at the General Elliot Hotel (lent by Mr. Owen, jun.). The teachers, friends, committee, and bandmen had tea together in the schoolroom, and afterwards went to the field, where football, racing, &c., took place, and the band played for dancing until dusk, under the conductorship of Mr. Charles Wood. ANOTHER STREET ACCIDENT. Shortly after eleven o'clock on Wednesday fore- noon a married woman, named Mrs. Braden, of 59, Nicholson-st. was proceeding down Horse- market-st., `Warrington, when she met with a some- what serious accident by being knocked down by a butcher's cart belonging to Mr. Gill. The driver of the cart, when opposite Skelton's shop, had to run close to the kerbstone to pass a trap on his left, and the woman, who was walking in the gutter, and who is very deaf, did not hear his shouts. Before the vehicle could be brought to a standstill she was knocked down by the shaft and trod upon by the horse's feet. Mr. G. W. Heywood, a member of a London branch of the St. John's Am- bulance Corps, who was luckily on the scene, at once had the woman's wounds temporarily dressed. He, along with Police-constable Bell, conveyed her to the Infirmary in a cab. Although the woman re- ceived several severe cuts about the head, and had her ankle hurt, the injuries Were not of such a serious nature as to detain her in the Infirmary, and after her wounds were dressed by Be. Bowden, she was taken to her home. CRITCLILEY'S Tailoring meets the limes.— Advt. BOLD-ST. WESLEYA.N CHAPEL. Anniversary services in connection with the Bold- at. Wesleyan Chapel were preached on Sunday, morning and evening, by the Rev. Alfred Freeman. one of the newly-appointed ministers to the War- rington Wesleyan circuit. Collections were taken on behalf of the trust funds. In the morning the rev. gentleman selected as his text 2 Timothy i. 12, whilst in the evening he founded his discourse upon Luke vii. 1-7. Referring to the centurion's relation to his servants, the preacher observed that there were masters whose care for their servants was determined by the statute books of the realm. They cared as much as they were compelled to care ; their main business was to get as much for as little as could be accomplished. On the other hand there were masters—and very many of them, thank God! —who took a very different view of their obliga- tions. He urged any of his hearers who might be employers to cultivate that spirit as much as pos- sible. It would go far- towards settling vexed questions between capital and labour. At the even- ing service the choir sang the anthem "0 send out Thy light." C nvermigv. Practical Tailor. Bold-st.. Wan ington.—Advt. SUNDAY EVENING CONCERT AT THE 'PUBLIC HALL. The first of a series of sacred concerts to be held during the coming winter was given in the Public Hall on Sunday evening. There was a fair attend- ance, and an excellently arranged programme was successfully rendered. The concert was opened with an organ solo," March Triomphale," by Mr. W. S. Woods, a performance which, it is scarcely neces- sory to say, was highly appreciated. The vocalists were Mr. Dean, Madame Kellie, Madame Vernon Heywood, and Mr. Walter Reynolds, the accompani- ments being played by Mr. W. Johnson, A.C.O. Each of the lady vocalists made a very favourable im- pression, Madame Kellie singing " Angels ever bright," and "I know that my Redeemer liveth," and Madame Vernon Heywood" 0 rest in the Lord," , and "Woe unto them." Mr. Dean and Mr. Reynolds were also successful in their appearances, the former rendering the recitative, " Ye people," and the air, "If with all your hearts"; and th,e latter gave the songs. "Nazareth," and " Behold I stand at the door." The quartette "Ave reruns" having been given, the concert was brought to a conclusion hy the audience joining in the singing of" The Old Hundredth." BATHS, all kinds.—J. S. Garlands, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge Street, Warrington. Branch—Earlestown.—Advt. FORMATION OF A LIBERAL CLUB AT BIIIITONWOOD.

- - - On Monday evening a meeting of the Liberals of Burtonwood was held at the Bridge Inn there, a goodly number being present. Mr. Thomas Hough- ton presided, supported by Mr. Thomas O'Brien The object of the meeting was the formation of some kind of representative body to assist the Liberal Association of the Newton Division in the ' work of revision and registration, and to promote the self-culture of the members. After some dis- cussion it was decided to form a club, and in con- nection therewith a debating class, at which any suhject,political, moral or social, could be dismissed, on giving sufficient notice to the chairman.—A com- mittee of management was elected,and the following officers were appointed—President, Mr. T. Bellfield ; vice-president, Mr. T. Houghton; secretary, Mr. T. O'Brien, assistant secretary, Mr. J. Si m cock, treasurer, Mr. Houghton. Several short and inspirit- ing addresses were given by the members present. and it was impressed upon them the necessity of making a honest emdeavour to assist the . Liberal party to the utmost of their ability. Votes of thanks were accorded the chairman and others and the meeting terminated. atAn, CARTS for children.—Garland, Ironmonger, Warring- ton and Earleatown.--ildat.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
PAPERMAKERS AND THE SHIP CANAL.

The following firms connected with the papermaking trade accepted invitations to visit the Ship Canal Works on Wednesday : J. Bracken and Sons, Luddenden, York- sisire ; Bury Papermaking Company, Limited ; Edwin Butterworth and Co., rag merchants, Manchester ; Bent- ley and Jackson, machinists, Bury; W. S. Birch and :Sons, Limited, china clay merchants, Manchester; Burn- side and Cooper, paper stock merchants, Bolton ; Thos. and James Chadwick, Ordsall Hall Paper Mills; William Chadwick and Sons, Broughton Grove and Agecroft Hall; Carlisle, Son and Co., Primrose Paper Mills, Clitheroe ; Deeply Vale Paper. Company, Bury; Drynan and Co., Mawson Chambers, Deansgate ; East Lancashire Paper Companyc Limited, Radcliffe; Samuel Evans and Co., Derby ; Fisher and Co., Kettlabrook Mills, Farnworth ; •Gateback Gunpowder Mills, Kendal; Gillespie and Mason, Newton-le-Willows ; Levenstein, 21 Minshul-et. ; Magee • Paper Stock Company, 55 Great Howard-st., Liverpool ; Henry Newall and Sons, wood pulp importers, Manches- ;ter ; Ockleston and Fitzgerald, 544, Faulkner-3f,, Man- chester ;Robert Ocklestab, Milbank Paper ; Olive and Partingtoa, Glossop ; Olive Brothers, Woolfold Paper Mill, Bury; Mr. Leonard Pace, George-st. ; Peebles and :Son, Rishton Paper Mills, Rishton, near Blackburn; H. D. Pochin and Co., Salford; Rarasbottom Paper Com- pany Limd ; Star Paper Company Limited, Penis- cowles ; Fan Paper Company Limited, Feniscowles ; James Spicer and Sons; J. W. Southern, Store-st. Saw E.fills ; Samlesbury Paper Mill, Oughton, near Preston ; -Thin and Sinclair, Liverpool; Union Paper Works Com- pany Limited, Beltield, Rochdale; John Wild and Sons, Broad DuLners Mills, Radcliffe ; VValford and Co., jute cuttings imorters, Liverpool • Harry B. Wood, Man- chester; Yates, Duxbury, and gptis, Wood Paper Mills, irvand Bolton. The party were accompanied by one of the directors, and Mr. Boddington ; Mr. Marslital Stevens representing the Manchester Ship Canal Com- pany. At Runcorn the party were entertained at luncheon at Bridgewater House, and before making the return journey most of the visitors went to inspect the Weaver sluices, which are amongst the most interesting features of the canal in that neighbourhood. It was stated that the works between Eastham and the mouth of the WAver are being pushed forward with all speed, in order that this section of the canal may be completed by the beginning of next year. The visitors,upon thoir re- turn,were served with tea in the Salford Mission-room, and there opportunity was taken to acknowledge the courtesy of the Directors.—Mr. Lightbown the Sun Paper Com- pany, Limited) moved that the best thanks of those present be given to the Directors of the Ship Canal Com- pany. He made some observations on the importance of the undertaking and of inland navigation generally, and expressed a hope that the Manchester Ship Canal would receive energetic support from the paper trade when it was opened.—The motion was seconded by a gentle- man representing the Star Paper Company, supported by Dr. Peter Loyle, and carried by acclamation.—Mr. Boddington, in responding, said it afforded the Directors pleasure to entertain a party of gentlemen representing such an important industry as the paper trade.—Mr. Marshall Stevens also acknowledged the compliment. He said it was wonderful how little idea people had of the extent of the paper trade. He believed he was cor- rect in saying that, as regarded imports, that trade did not stand second even to the cotton trade of the country. That might seem a strong statemant to make, but an examination of the Board of Trade returns would show that the imports of esparto grass, wood pulp, and other raw material used in the paper manufacture amounted to not less than half a million tons; and, in addition,there was imported annually 100,000 tons of manufactured paper and millboard ; to say nothing of the vast amount of raw material furnished by the country itself. Of course the cotton trade was confined almost entirely to this district. It was not so with the paper trade. He thought probably one-third of the paper trade would be carried on in the district which would ultimately be served by the Ship Canal—a district, that was to say, which included one-fifth of the entire population of the United Kingdom. The canal would thus beable to save the paper trade every year a sum of money which, if it came into their coffers, would suffice 'for all the maintenance and working expenses of the -canal. (Hear, hear.) That again might be a strong 'statement, but it could be borne out by figures. Of coarse the trade could not effect that saving unless it made use of the canal. (Hear, hear.) If such was the effect on the paper trade, what success might they not hope for when all the other trades in the district became equally users of the canal and sources of income 7 He expected when the canal was opened their difficulty would be how to deal with the large amount of traffic that would come to them. That they would have that traffic he did not for a moment doubt, supported as they -were by the sentiment and sympathy of traders through- out the entire district. (Applause.) The company then separated.

div.head: "Slit GLADSTONE " MYTH.
div.p: THE "Slit GLADSTONE " MYTH.

The great Sir Gladstone myth is at lenuth exploded. In an article on our ex-Premier published in a Paris paper, the Revue Diplomatique Frenchmen are expressly informed that there is no such a persQn as Sir Gladstune, but that the correct style of the person thus usually re- ferred to abroad is "Le Right Honourable William Ewart Gladstone." The writer sums up Mr. Gladstone's -character and career in flattering terms. He has not been satisfied, we are reminded, to show the ordinary -qualities of a statesman. He has never ceased to be in the eyes of all Europe the indefatigable apostle of [Liberal ideas ; and in all his writings, in all his speeches, he has consistently raised his authoritative voice in favour of the , oppressed. At the present day the illustrious octog,en- - arian, still full of ardour and enthusiasm, has this conso- , lation, vouchsafed to few politicians, that he has won ,most of the causes he has defended, and that he now sees in course of realization nearly all the projects he has ever advocated.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMIIER 13. 1800
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMIIER 13. 1800
THE PARISH CHURCH.

The annual sermons on behalf of the day schools will be preached in the Parish Church to-morrow (Sunday), the preacher being the Rey. T. M. Wil- son, M.A., headmaster of Clifton College, and archdeacon designate of Manchester.
JUBILEE SINGERS.

A party of coloured people known as the "Jubilee Singers," gave a service of sacred song in the Co- operative Hall, on Saturday night. The entertain- ment was described as a ' Children's service of song," but the majority of those present were adults. The singing was of a fair quality, and some very nice pieces were presented. During the even- ing temperance addresses were given, and on Sun- day evangelistic services were held in the same place. On Tuesday evening, the same company visited the Congregational schoolroom, and a service of song was presented to a mdderate audience.

NEWTON LAKE. As announced a fortnight ago, the beautiful sheet of water known as Newton lake was opened to the public on Monday morning. Mr. W. Darrow, son o the late keeper of Dean dam, has been appointed lake keeper, and a couple of the boats which war e formerly used by the late Mr. J. Lane have been placed on the lake for hire. The fact that it is open has not yet become generally known, and thus the privilege has not been taken advantage of to any appreciable extent. Should the present favourable weather continue, however, it is expected that the inhabitants of Earlestown and Newton will avail themselves of the pleasure of a row. There have been several applications from anglers, and as ahere is a good supply of fish, lovers of the rod and line may be sure of excellent sport.

div.head: ACCIDENT TO A WORKMAN.
div.p: ACCIDENT TO A WORKMAN.

On Wednesday morning, whilst a labourer named John Leigh was following his employment at Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co.'s works, he accidentally fell from some scaffolding to the ground. He was re- moved to the Infirmary, where it was found that his injuries, though not serious, necessitated his deten- tion at the institution.

div.head: NEW WESLEYAN MINISTERS.
div.p: THE NEW WESLEYAN MINISTERS.

On Thursday evening the newly-appointed Wes- leyan ministers—the Rev. A. Freeman and the Rev. T. Ross—were received at a conversazione in Bold- St. schoolroom. There was a large gathering, and the new ministers were accorded a hearty welcome. The room had been decorated for the occasion, and a musical programme was carried out.
PRESENTATION OF A GOLD DIPLOMA TO MR. T. MORRIS.

We understand that the committee of the Liver- pool Industrial Polytechnic Exhibition have written to thank Mr. Thomas Morris, of Warrington, for his exhibition of curios of iron and steel, which have, the committee state, been interesting and instruct- ing to the many thousands who had attended the exhibition. It has also been decided by the execu- tive of the day staff to. present Mr. Morris with a gold diploma.

div.head: _Music IN THE PARK.
div.p: _Music IN THE PARK.

The band of the Ist Vol. Batt. (P. of W. V.) South Lancashire Regiment will play the following programme in the Park on Sunday, Sep. 14th, at 3.15 p.m. March, "heaving Billows," E. Swift; overture, "Caliph de Bagdad," Boieldieu ; selection, "Hear us, Lord" (Stabat Mater), Rossini; selection, " Reminiscenes of Verdi " ; euphonium solo, " True till death," Gatty ; selection, "Great is the Lord," Paxton; selection, " Victory," Round; "God save the Queen." Thomas Armstrong, conductor.

div.head: RE-DISTRIBUTION OF THE WARDS.
div.p: THE RE-DISTRIBUTION OF THE WARDS.

As announced in our advertising columns Mr. C. N. Cresswell, barrister-at-law, who has been appoin- ted by the Secretary of State to be a commissioner under the Warrington Extension and Water Act, will hold a public inquiry on Wednesday next at the Town Hall, to consider the scheme to be proposed for the delimitation of the nine wards into which the extended borough is to be divided, for the apportionment of existing councillors among the wards, &c. All persons are invited to attend the inquiry, and an burgess or owner or other inhabi- tant affected by the scheme may make objections thereto, or submit alternative schemes for the consideration of the Commissioner. Notices of objections to the scheme—which may be inspected at the Town Clerk's office—should be sent in writing to the Town Clerk on or before Tuesday. CRITCHLEY, High Class Tailor. Bold-3t.,Warrington.—Advt. BOWLING AT THE LIBERAL CLUB.

On Saturday afternoon, a main at bowls was opened on the ground at the Liberal Club. There were numerous competitors, and some of the heats will not be finished till this afternoon. There was a large attendance of spectators, and much in- terest in the games was displayed. The ground was in splendid condition. The contest for , the first and second pac. te,l ink lade this afternoon, between Mr. Peter Langley and Mr. John Nevins, and at the conclusion of the main the prizes will be distributed. On Saturday, after play had concluded, the competitors and friends to the number of 54, proceeded to the Patten Arms , Hotel, where an excellent tea was provided by the Host, Mr. Kiernan. An enjoyable and social even- ing was subsequently spent, Mr. T. Morris being in the chair, the vice-chairs being tilled by Councillors Flood and Beaman, TiR BIRTH AND DEATH RATE oP For the week ending Saturday, September 6th, 1890.—The mean temperature was 55.85 Fahrenheit, and therefore 425 degrees higher than the pre- ceding week. The maximum temperature, 71 Fahrenheit, was recorded on the 6th inst, and the minimum temperature, 33 Fahrenheit, lon the Ist inst. The rainfall measured .31 ins. The general direction of the wind was Westerly. During the week, which was the 36th of the current year, 36 births and 18 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 18.72 per thousand, against 21.32, the average of the previous four weeks, and against 28.04 the corresponding week of last year. The deaths included 2 from diarrhcea, 2 from phthisis, 1 from cancer, 1 from old age, 2 from lung disease, 3 from brain disease, 1 from kidney disease. Two cases of scarlatina were reported under the re- quirements of the Act of Parliament.—JoHN H. tioutvim., Medical Officer of Health.

div.head: DRUIDS' DINNER.
div.p: DRUIDS' DINNER.

On Thursday evening the Past District officers of the Warrington District z'ociety of Druids sat down to a good and substantial dinner at the Waggon and Horses Inn, Buttermarket-st., the following Past District Grand Masters, &c., being present, viz., P.D.G.M. William Beswick, P.D.G.M. Samuel Dun- bobbin, P.D.G.M. John Booth, P.D.G.M. Thos. Bate, P.D.G.11. George I Roughley, P.D.G.M. Edward Waimsley, P.D.G.M. Edward Poulton, P.D.G.M. Levi Bradburn, P.D.G.M. James Wilcock, P.D.G.M. Wm. Bibby, P.D.G.M. Peter Langley, P.D.G.M. Henry Kent, P.D.G.M. Thomas Roberts, P D.G.M. Henry Lloyd, D.G.M. Wm. Croskill, and D.D.G.M. Thos. Eden. The dinner being over the P.D. officer's lecture was given by P.D.G.M. John Booth, the rest of the evening being taken up with songs, recita- tions, and short addresses, given by those present. It was announced by the collector, P.D.G.M. Peter Langley, that the childrens' family funeral fund of this district was worth £1,980 and had 1,500 mem- bers on its books; this was corroborated by the Secretary. The total worth of the widow and fl orphan's fund was given by the secretary, P.D.G.M. John Booth, as £753 3s. 7 d. The District Corres- ponding Secretary, P.D.G.M. Thomas Roberts, . gave the present worth of the funeral fund of the district as £1,063 9s. 10d. and the district management fund account as £l9 Is. 3d. He stated that thevarious lodges had during the past year made 120 new mem- bers, the total number of financial members en the books being 1,295. They had during the same period paid £383 in deaths, viz., 33 members, five wives and three widows. A hearty vote of thanks was given to the chairman,vice-chairman,and &etre tary,and the , business of the evening was brought to a close:

div.head: FLOWER _SHOW_ AT HOUGHTON-,
div.p: THE FLOWER _SHOW_ AT HOUGHTON-,

The annual show of the Houghton Horticultural Society, held at Myddleton Hall, was concluded on Saturday. The prizes were distributed by Miss Comber. Before the distribution took place, Canon Penrhyn, rector of Winwick, remarked on the ex- cellent quality of the exhibits, considering the un- favourable weather during the last few months. He said he should be happy to support the society, which appeared to be in a flourishing condition. ' The Rev. J. Carson, curate of VVinwick, proposed a vote of thanks to Miss Comber for distributing the prizes, and also thanked the company present for their attendance and support. In connection with the show the annual sports for juveniles resident in Winwiek parish took place in the afternoon. There was a large attendance. Appended is the list of the events :—Race for girls under ten (handicap), SO yards: 1, Elizabeth Hill; 2, Annie Berry. Race for boys under ten, 80 yards: 1, William Rowles ;2, Harry Rowles. Race for girls under 15 (80 yards): 1, M. E. Upton; 2,. Ilettie Sweetlove. Race for boys under 15 years (120 yards) : 1, Harry Rowles ; 2, Richard Melling. Sack race for boys under 16 years (60 yards) 1, Alex Thompson; ' William Britch. Three-leg race for boys under 16 years (100 yards) : George Britch and William Britch. Running hop, skip and jump for youths : 1, Joseph Johnson; 2, William Britch. Potatoe race for girls under 13 years : 1, 'fettle Sweetlove ;2, Emily Hill. Potatoe race for boys under 16 years: 1, Alex Thompson ; 2, Joseph Hewitt. Smoking race for men (200 yards) : 1, Joseph Colburn. The events were keenly contested and the entries large. The Committee were Messrs. Joshua Ball, Joseph Swinton, W. Carson, Peter Longton, and George Mather; handicapper, Mr. J. Ball ; judges, Messrs. J. Swinton and P. Longton; clerk of the course, Mr. W. Carson. At the con- clusion of the sports' Miss Margaret Comber pre- sented the prizes to the successful competitors, and a vote ot thanks was accorded her. The Golborna Brass Band played a selection of music for dancing. &e., under the conductorship of Mr. Peter Cook, the bandmaster.

div.head: LIMM.
div.p: LIMM.

A NEW BANK FOR LlMM.—Parr's Banking Company, of Warrington, are about to open a branch of their estab- lishment at Lymm, and have taken premises. BALVATION ARMY TEA.—On Saturday afternoon a tea was given by the captain and members of the Salvation Army to 12.5 children, at the barracks in Booth's-lane. After tea an entertainment took place, in which the children joined. The tea was got up by subscription.

ACCIDI;NT AT TH/3 CONSRIZVA2I,7I4 -CLOB.—An ;iccident took place on Monday at the new Conservative Club, to a bricksetter named John Wood, who fell off a scaffold , on the second storey on to the window sill below, a dis- tance of about three feet, considerably injuring his ribs. He is unable to follow his employment yet, but fortun- , acely no bones were broken. CARRIAGE ACCIDENT.—AII accident occurred to a party of visitors on Sunday afternoon. They were being driven , in a landau, and as they were turning in Bridgewater-st., the vehicle, from some unexpected cause, completely overturned. All the occupants were thrown out, but escaped serious injury. The driver's face was, however, badly cut. The lamps of the conveyance were smashed and the seats broken.

LYatm GRAMMAR SCHOOL.—Two pupils of the above school have succeeded in the Oxford Local E,CArnination —Master Jeffery Ouston and Master W. H. Jones. Con- sidering the youth of both these boys (born in 1878), the result is gratifying to the School and teachers. During the year fifteen pupils have been presented for various public examinations, all of whom passed except one,whe failed only in one subject. CHOIR tREAT.—Mr. and Mrs. Ridgway on Saturday Invited the members of the choir of Bt. Peter's, Ought- rington, to an excursion to Chester. About 36 members availed themselves of the invitation, including Mr. 0. G. Smith, the organist. The Rector and Mrs. Knocker, together with Mr. and Mrs. Ridgway, accompanied the excursion. The party left Lymm by the 8.37 train and on arrival at Chester went to the service at the cathedral, alter which they took a row on the Dee as far as Eaton Hall. Dinner was provided at "The Golden Lion." The party returned to Lymm by the 9.20 train. DEATH AND FUNERAL Os' Mn. ALFRED DUTTON.—The death of Mr. Alfred Nickson Dutton, youngest sOll of the late Mr. Richard Dutton' of Stanttiorrie Hall, Middle- wich, and brother of Mr. Richard Dutton, of West View, Lymm, occurred on the 31st ult. The deceased had been in failing health for some time, and a change of air and scene had been sought at Lymm, but the disease had advanced too far for permanent relief. The funeral took place yesterday week, at St. Wilfred's Church, Davenhain. Wreaths were sent by Mrs. Moss, Havens. croft Hall; Miss Birch, Armitage Lodge, Rugeley ; Mr. Cooke, Mrs. R. Boyd, Mr. R. Dutton, Sister Mary, Mr. and Mrs. Yarwood, Miss Knight, Jane Richardson ' • the staff of the District Bank, London; Mrs. Harris, Lon- don; tha Sunday schoo teachers, members of the read- ing room, and a number of old women to whom deceased had been a friend in need.

Davies, Sharp, and Kirkconnell, solicitors to the society, was discussed and accepted, and Mr. 11. J. Longton, of Earlestown and Warrington, was appointed solicitor to the society in their stead.

Mr. Elliott, of St. Helens, the former conductor of this society, having intimated that he will be un- abli; to undertake the leadership of the class for the nflxt session, a special committee meeting has been held, at which Mr. E. div.head: Tug SALVATION ARMY,
div.p: Tug SALVATION ARMY,

Since the establishment of a detachment of the Salvation Army in Earlestown, some good results have been achieved. Services are held each evening in the Market Place, and every Thursday night a special contingent visits the town, when addresses are delivered by those who have been converted to the ranks.

div.head: SKITTLE B.ANDICAP.
div.p: SKITTLE B.ANDICAP.

The prizes which were won in this handicap were distributed on Friday night by Mr. Brunton. The handicap has been in progress for some time past, at the Conservative Club, and Mr. W. Rich, who gained first prize, was presented with a marble time piece. There were five other prizes which con- sisted of pipe, walking stick, hat, pocket knife, Ste.

div.head: NARROW ESCA_PR OF A CHILD.
div.p: NARROW ESCA_PR OF A CHILD.

On Monday afternoon, as Mr. George Owen was driving a horse and shandry up Legh-st., a child named Charles Morden four years a age, was knocked down by the horse and narrowly escaped being killed. As the horse was going along Legh-st. the child ran into the street, and before Mr. Owen could pull up the child was knocked down. Dr. Valentine was called in, but the only injury he could find was a slight scar on the face. COL. MCCORQUODALE AND HIS EMPLOICILS. _ _

On Tuesday, the officers, foremen, and. the old hands employed at Messrs. McCorquodale and Co.'s printing works, at Newton, received an intimation that the grounds and gardens attached to the Wil- lows, the residence of Col. McCorquodale, will in future be open to the employOs named and their wives, at any time when the family is away from home. The grounds are well ke2t, and at the present time a.re in splendid condition, and the kind. con- cession will be received in the spirit in which.is has been mute. VOLUNTEER INTELLIGE NCB.

The 29th annual prize meeting of the F company, Newton-le-Willows detachment of the Liverpool Press Guards,. will take place en Saturday, at the range on Highfield Moss. Several good prizes are offered, amongst others being a challenge cup.pre- sented by Colonel Hamilton, " The company's cup," presented bi; Lieutenant-Colonel Wood, challenge cup by Mrs. G. F. McCorquodale. Drill prizes: time- piece value 1010.iiiieasi by Mr. A. C. McCorquodale, and handicap and recruit prizes. If the weather is propitious, some sensational scoring may be- ex- pected.
AN EARLESTONTS MAN IN TROUBLE AT ST- IIELENS. _ _

At the St. Helens T-ow—n-li-a-U, on Tuesday, Moran Griffin, or Davies,. of unsettled residence, but who had been apprehendedat Earlestown, was charged with stealing &silver watch, value .E61.0a., from a. lodging-houseinTontine-st., the property of Eliza Adelaide Ogle„the landlady. It appeared that the prisoner had formerly Lodged at the house, bat. dis- appeared in Jaws last.. The watch was missed from a bedroom, audit was. subsequently found pledged. at Mrs. Thorpe's pawnshop, Ea' rlestown, where,tha prisoner was apprehended on Monday. In reply. to the charge he admitted. taking the watch. On the application of Chief-Constable Wood the prisoner was remanded. until Wednesday), when he was. again brought up and committed to prisomfor two ' months' with hard labour. WAGON Wanits RXCURSIONS. The annual excursion held in connection with the Wagon Works. of the London and North-Westeria Railway Co., took place on Saturday. Owing to Ale privilege extended to the workmen of travellingat quarter faree„it was feared that the excursion this year would not receive the patronage bestowed upon it in previous years, but the result provathat these fears .were groundless. The preceding. cloudless days decided many to accompany the trip, ankles the day came round all the tickets for Blackpool were cleared. out. London and Blackpool were the places decided upon, and on Friday at midnight a special train. left Earleetown for the Metropolis. The fare was considered to be rather high, and in consequence only about 200 people accompanied it, the malority of them going with the intention of staying four days. The Blackpool excursionists, to the number of about 1,200, left Earlestowni.n.two special traists on Saturday morning, abouz six o'clock. The morning dawned beantif oily fine, with a cloudless sky, and. about five o:clock the echoes were awakened, and slumbering trippeas were aromsed, by the shrill notes of a bugle. accompanied by the rumbling of a drum. Shortly afterwards the wagon works band turned out, and soon the streets were alive with men, women, and children, making their way to the station. The trains were got away in good time and without mishap, Blackpool being reached about eight o'clock, Here the trippers dis- persed to enjoy themselves after their bent, many swarming to the beach to obtain an early inhalation of ozone. Later on the Royal Palace Gardens, Winter Gardens. Aquarium, and Piers were in turn visited, and all appeared. to thoroughly enjoy them- selves. With the exception of thetenallorarY loss of one or two children,. everything passed off without. mishap, and after a very pleasant day the return journey was made soon after eight o'clock. Earte4- . town being reacheda.out half-past ten.

div.head: GOOD TEMPLAR'S'.
div.p: GOOD TEMPLAR'S'.

The usual weekly session of the Hope of Earles- town Lodge of Good Templars was held on Monday evening, in the lodgeroom, Bridge-st. Bro. E. Jenkinson, P.C.T., presided, and there was a fair attendance of members. Two candidates were admitted to membership, and several others were proposed. Bro. Jno. Taylor, L.D., read several cir- culars which had been received from the Grand Lodge, and gave a digest of the business to be tran- sacted by the Convention, on Saturday next. A discussion took place, and the representatives who were appointed to attend were instructed how to vote. It was also decided that the Convention be invited to hold the next sitting at Earlestown. A report of the mission meetings held in the preced- ing week was submitted, and thanks were accorded to those who had assisted in carrying them out. A night of harmouy was then spent, and a good selec- tion of melodies, glees, songs, and readings was submitted by the members, a very pleasant session being brought to a close in the usual way.

div.head: ALEXANDRA THEATRE,_ EARLESTOWN:
div.p: ALEXANDRA THEATRE,_ EARLESTOWN:

The boards of this popular place of entertainment were occupied this week by Mr. Gilbert Vernon's Company in "Not Guilty," There have been fairly numerous audiences, and the piece, which is of a sensational character,was well received. The char- acters are well sustained, Mr. Vernon appears in the title role as " Harry Grafton," lover of Nelly Chaddox. Miss Florence Worth as " Nelly " comes out of many difficult situations in a creditable manner, and her representation of the daughter of a miner is quite homely and to the point. Mr. H. J. Moseley as "Nick Chaddox," a miner, and villian of the piece, was rather forced in his manner at times, and he would do well to study carefully the man- nerisms of some of our Lancashire pit men. Miss Emmeline Montague made a capital "Sarah Saw- yer," and the character of Timothy Sprouts was well represented by Mr. T. Irwin. The staging of the piece was well done, the court scene being quite in keeping with till MTV day transacti9na &ill police courts. Next week the energetic lessee, Mr. Davies, purposes at great expense to himself to place before the Earlestown and Newton people an English Opera Company, whose repertoire will embrace "The Bohemian Girl," " Maritana," "La Somnambula," &c., and seeing that the theatre has been considerably improved in many ways, it is hoped the lovers of good music will patronise his efforts.

div.head: WHAT FOLKS ARE SAYING AT EARLESTOWN. BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.
div.p: WHAT FOLKS ARE SAYING AT EARLESTOWN. BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

That Mr. Evans took a step in the right direction at the Commissioners' meeting last week. That it is high time somebody called attention to the accommodation provided for passengers at Earlestown station.

That Earlestown, with ten times the quantity of traffic, is practically worse off in the matter of waiting-rooms than Collins Green. That perhaps the Railway Company will seriously consider the question now that the people's representatives have taken action in the matter. That Mr. Gillespie said it the mooting of the ' question does no good, it cannot possibly make matters any worse. That the glorious weather has given the farmers a chance of gathering and Awing their corn. That the outlook for the harvest is much more hopeful than it was a fortnight ago. That the offer of Miss Evans, .towards the erection 1 of a Congregational Churcls at liaydock, is a very generous one. That such a church is muc)Y needed in the colliery That the Newton, bowlers did well on Saturday to secure the premier prize in the howling com- petition. That they will, and justly so; feel) proud of the high position they have attained in bowling circles. That Literalism in the Newtore division requires a stimulus. That it is about timet the prospective candidate put in an appearance. That for the sake of the cause they hope he will make up his mind forthwith, to stand, hie chance in the divisiom

Sr. HELENS GENTLEMEN IN A.STEAMIIOA.S,COLLISION., On Friday evening Mr. Walter A. Booths of Green Ewalt, Sutton, cashier at the Sherdley Collieries, and Mr. Prank Gardner, of St. Ann's, who have been spending their holidays in the Channel Islamlwere on board the I,4mx, one of the Great Western steamers, which was steaming at full speed across the Channel. There was also sailing down the Channel the North-Germa2 screw steamer Oevelconnevof Hamburg, which was coming from. New York and was laden with oil!. The steamers haul sighted each other,. but by some means they came into collision, the ferceof the collision scattering the passengers all over the deck of the Lynx. The captain was at the time at dinnerwith some of the passengers, and he at once , rushed on deck. It was.tround that the German steamer ' had struck the Lynx onithe port hew, just before the galley. Fearing that the result of the collision would be disastrous to the smaller !steamer„ about twenty of the passengers, including Messrs. Booth and Gardner, elinabcsa on the German steamer, which got away from, the Lynx, ready to. give assistance_ She was not se, seriously damaged as. Was at first expected, and the pas- ' sengers were taken back to the Lynx in the boats of the German steamer. The Lynx resumed her journey, and the passengers were entrahmi at Weymouth, and letk tir their various cleatination.a.

div.p: A YEAR'S HARVEST DESTROYED BY FIRE.

Flames broke out on Thursday night at Oaks Farm, Earshalton, Surrey, the property of Mr. E. B. James, and resulted in the destruction of eleven corn stacks the product of a year's harvest. The loss is estimated at £3,000.

div.head: PRIZEFIGHT IN SURREY.
div.p: PRIZEFIGHT IN SURREY.

A prizefight took place yesterday morning near Crxted, Surrey, between a man named Williamson, of London, and another man named Goodyear, of Northampton, for £2O aside. They fought twenty-nine rouuds, and the Northampton man proved;the victor.

div.head: AN OVERWORKED PRINCESS.
div.p: AN OVERWORKED PRINCESS.

Princess Louise is suffering from indisposition conse- quent on overwork, and H.R.H. has been forbidden by her medical adviser to undertake any public duties at present. }I.R.A.. has had in consequence to forego a promised 'visit to North Staffordshire this autumn.

div.head: LION'S VAN OVERTURNED.
div.p: A LION'S VAN OVERTURNED.

While the lio—st-oc-i Menagerie' was making procession through Dundee yesterday, a van containing two lions was upset. The animals growled and made determined efforts to get out, causing much excitement in the dis- trict. The van, however, was safely replaced on its wheels after much difficulty.

div.head: SHOCKINC SUICIDE AT WREXHAM.
div.p: SHOCKINC SUICIDE AT WREXHAM.

A shocking suicide was perpetrated a-C.V.Fr-eZam yes- terday, a quartermaster-sergeant, named Lees, of the Ist Volunteer Battalion Royal Welsh Fusiliers, blowing his brains out with his rifle, his head being terribly mutilated. The deceased was highly respected by every- body who knew him, and his self-destruction has caused the utmost surprise, as no motive can be assigned for his action.

div.head: ROMANTIC ELOPEMENT AND RECAP CURE.
div.p: ROMANTIC ELOPEMENT AND RECAP CURE.

A sensation has been caused in County Clare by the elopement of Miss Mary Lynch, under 18, the daughter of Mrs. Lynch, a wealthy widow, at Clare Castle, with John Moriarty, a labourer in their employment. The two fell in love, but measures were taken to separate them, and they resorted to flight, proceeding to Foynes on route for America. The mother obtained a warrant, and the police arrested both. ADVENTURE OF CASTAWAY SAILORS.

SAN FRANCISCO, FRIDAY.—A vessel has arrived here bringing eleven men of the schooner C. G. White, whom she rescued in the Behring Sea. The sailors, who were out in boats, lost all trace of their vessel in the dense fog, and were for five days wandering over the ocean in their- open boats. While trying to find shelter on Copper Island, three of the castaways were shot, one being fatally wounded, by natives, who thought they were seal killers.

BOOKMAKERS FINED AT WOLVERHAMPTON. At the Wolverhampton Stipendiary's Court yesterday, George Duffield, of Curzon-street, Nottingham, am IJ. Bull, of New Windsor, near London, described as book- makers, were fined in their absence £25 and £lO and costs respectively for using stands and making bets with various persons at Dunstall Park races on the 19th and 20th of August last. It was stated as the reason why the defendants did not appear to answer the charge that they were at Doncaster races. John Bull is well known in the sporting world as " Chippy Nort m."
THE ALLEGED DOUBLE MURDER BY AN EX-
SOLDIER.

The trial tock place at Old Bailey, yesterday, of Walter Hargan, aged 27, an ex-soldier, for the murder of William Lambert and Jelin Wheeler at Kingsland. Mr. Horace Avory stated the case for the prosecution, and said the prisoner who had served in the British army, recently returned from America. He was a customer at the Waggon and Horses public-house, Kingsland, which was frequented by the two deceased men. They were in the public-house on the 30th July and created a disturbance. The landlady was protected by the prisoner, who after,. , wards left. The deceased followed him. Someone called the prisoner, who stopped, and, turning round,.shot both men dead. ATTEMPTED MURDER OF A PLATELAYER. A MAN AND WIFE ARRESTED.

During Thursday night, a platelayer named Charles Regan, of Reddish, in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway, was brought to the Stockport Infirmary by Lancashire police officers. Regan presented a pitiable spectacle, and was cowered with blood flowing from lacerated wounds on the head. Began charges three persons with attempting to murder him at Black- brook, a lonely part of the high road to Manchester, between Stockp)rt and Levenshulme. One assailant got away when the police appeared on the scene, but Wm. Hancock and his wife, giving their address at Primrose- st., Manchester, were arrested and taken to Stockport Police Office for the night, being sent on to Manchester yesterday morning. On inquiry at the infirmaryyeeter- day morning, the information was given that Regan was rather better than it was thought possible for him to be when first treated. Still his condition is critical. THE SOUTHAMPTON STRIKE. THE SITUATION YESTERDAY.

Mr. John Burns, who arrived at midnight on Thurs. day,was joined yestesday morning by Mr. Ben Tillet and Mr. J., H. Wilson, of the Seamen and Firemen's Union. They were at ten o'clock in consultation with Mr. M'Carthy. Mr. Sprow was not with them. Four hundred men are at work in the docks, including a few union men. Crews have been obtained for several steam- ships sailing yesterday. The streets are crowded, but the town in quite. 'Subsequently to yesterday morning's conference, Mr. Burns at art outdoor meeting told the dockers to adjourn to the Assembly Hall, where he coulki submit to them definite instructions which he had brought from the- exe- cutive of the DOcker's Union in London,. The men pre- sent then proceeded to the Assembly Hall in a tredy. Prior to the opening of the proceedings,. messengem ar- rived and urgedthosc dockers who, in gursuance tathe previous night'S-resolution, had returned' to work should be again callecll out. Theseamen'and firemen concerned in the dispute number about 700. It was in their inte- rests that Mr. Wilson: came down but the Press Agee- ciation is informed by one of the down, that there is no alteration inthe position of affairs. At 10.0 Mr. Ahn Burns proceeded to dieplatform 'address the strikers,.and was received with enthusiastic -cheering. Commencing his speech with "Now, dotut iwaste my time and yours; we must get to business," hs ,delivered a short address in which he expressed regret not to have been at Southampton sooner to stand shoulder to shoulder with them in the struggle. Hs said he came with definite-instructions from the Execu, tive of the Docker's-Union, Landon, and WAS to consult with the strike coinntitNes, after whicli a decision would be announesd. The conference at the Victoria Assembly Rooms was•strictly private. " Nupress repre— sentatives are admitted," said Mr. Burns." andnone wilt be-admitted without dockers' ticket. Any outsider at— tempting to enter will be chucked out and treated to a lively five minutes. Our decision will be given to you, here at,the platform—pert-raps at noon to-day-,four p.m.,. midnight, or noon temorrow." The Central I,tews repre- sentative was informed unofficially by Mr_ Itl‘Carthy,. that the decision on 'Fliursciay to instruct the men to return to work will be confirmed. There areindications that, if so, the ins:tractions will not be unanimously obeyed-.

div.head: ACCIDENT AT HOWLEY.
div.p: ACCIDENT AT HOWLEY.

A serious accident occurred yesterday. afternoon ta a man named GiLbert Warburtni. about pears of age, who was employed at Howley Mills. 7tlli,rough the breaking of a chain of a hoist he re- ceived a fall that resulted in his receiving injuries rothe back. Ithr• was removed to tha Infirmary, whore he is now.recoiving every attention.

ACCIDENT TO A TRAM DRIVER, On Saturday afternoon a singular,- accident happened ,on the Havdock tram lines, by whinh a, driaer, named ICharles Reeves. sustained a sevene injury to.hie eye. Whilst Qn the journey the water glass tubs•burst, and pieces of glassstruek him in the ey,e. Mr. Janson, the manager,,at once sent the unfortunate mazt to the Eye Hospital,,at LiVerpool, in charge of two. mein. It is stated that the average t' life" acme of these glass tubes is about twelve months in other towns. An examination of Cite explodud tube showed that above the water mark, tho glass was eaten away, and, this cout.d. only be attri- buted to some corrosive element in the St. Helens water. Fearing that a similar effect was bekg made on My, boilers, they were submitted to a eiitieat examination, with the result that whilst the injurious elements did not corrode the boilers or glasa plates, they. were acting as a corrosive on the glass. Although nothing of the kind is necessary in other towzrs, Mr. Johnson (manager) has devised, since the accident, a plan by which drivers, whilst having a full view of the gauge,which is very im- portant, will abbTautely protedtd tO PierT ill the event o,f 4 similar accident,

REUBEN PEARSON, AFTER more than 25 years' experience in the treatment of disease, is pleased to be able to commend to the publie the testimony, voluntarily offered by many of his past patients. In cases of Rheumatism, Gout, Sciatica and Lumbago, his Massage and other treatment has proved marvellously success- ful. For some years past he has made this treatment a spe- cial feature and study, and in the cases he has bad under the sanction and supervision .3f Medical men. he has produced re. suits which even they admit have been singular and excep- tional. " REUBEN'S HYDRO," F ask Cottages, Greenfield, October 6th. DEAR SIR, It is with no small feeling of gratitude to you and for the good of humanity in general that I write to you, and you are at liberty to make such use of this testimonial as you think proper. I was under the treatment of several doctors where I live, foe Sciatica, but to no use. I was then sent to Buxton for a time. I received no relief under their treatment. and I was then told by the doctors that they could do nothing for me and that I should never again be able to walk straight, I felt this to be very poor consolation and bad naturally a great desire to recover, then the doctor advised me to go into the Manchester Infirmary. I was there fifteen weeks and had a good kind doctor, but I got worse every week until I could not walk. I went through the most agonising pain that ever man could go through. I was blistered and burned with hot needles having them put in my leg and the electric battery was played on them whilst they were in. I thought they were trying me for a soldier to see if I could stand steel ; but thanks to providence you came to my relief. You know the situation I was left in, but you did not go by on the other side, but acted the part of the Good Samaritan. fOr which I thank God, for in nine weeks under your treatment I could move about to the no small astonishment of my neighbours, for none ever thought. I believe, to see me walk straight again, and my doctor stated that he could not believe it was me when he saw me. And, Sir, through the blessing of God through your treatment I enjoy a better state of health, than I have done for a long time before, and for your kind treatment to me may Heaven smile upon you and yours. I remain yours, AMBROSE SCHOFIELD. REUBEN'S HYDRO', ALTRINCRAM. EXTRA CHARGE AFTER 8 p.m.

RUNCORN UN lON.—CONTRACTS FOR PROVISIONS AND SUPPLIES, FOR THE HALF-YEAR ENDING 28TH MARCH, 1891. The Guardians of the Poor of the Runcorn Union are desirous of receiving Tenders from parties willing to Contract for the supply of Flour and Oatmeal, Groceries, Peas, Cheese, Salt Butter; Cod Liver and Paraffin Oil; Quinine; Good Beef, to consist of vein and brisket pieces, the price to include about 401bs. per week of the Best Butchers' Meat for the Officers, and Sides of Mutton; Best Brand (Ists) American or English Bacon; Potatoes; Wheat Straw; Drapery and Cloth- ing; Men's, Women's, Boy's, and Girl's Shoes, of various sizes, as per samples to be seen at the Workhouse. Button; House Coal (Colliery to be named) ; Coke; Good Deal Coffins, specifying size, and including plate with name, age and date of death, to be delivered in the Union when and where required; Carting at per mile, and Funeral at per Funeral. Parties Tendering for the supply of the above-mentioned Goods, will be required to deliver the same at the Work- house, free of cost to the Guardians, how and when required. Tenders to be accompanied with samples (except Drapery Goods), as far as practicable. The Guardians do not bind themselves to accept the lowest or any Tender. Persons desirous of Tendering must apply by letter, to my Office, in Frodsliam, for a Printed Form of Tender (and none other can be entertained), where a sehedule of the various articles required and further particulars can be obtained. Sealed Tender, addressed to the Guardians, to be for- warded to the Clerk's Office, Frodsham, on or before Monday the 22nd day of September, 1890, indorsed " Tender for .' The Tenders will be opened and considered at a Meeting of the Guardians to be held in the Board-room, Dutton, on the 23rd September, 1890, at Two p.m. Parties whose Tenders are accepted must enter into a written contract, and be prepared to enter into a bond with two sureties, if required by the Guardians. By order of the Board. H. LINARER, Clerk to the Guardians. Frodsham, let September, 1890.

IVVARRINGTON UNlON.—Persohs wining to CONTRACT for the supply of any of the undermentioned articles from Michaelmas to Lady Day next, to be delivered free of expense at the Warrington Union Workhouse, or at the Indus- trial Schools, Padgate, at such times and in such quantities as the Board of Guardians shall direct, arerequested to send in TENDERS, properly sealed, endorsed, and free of expense, addressed to the Clerk to the Guardians, before four o'clock , p.m. on Tuesday, the 23rd day of September instant. The following are the articles for which tenders are required : Groceries and Provisions Glazing Beef and Mutton Brushes Joints for Officers Coffins Milk Best Oakum Rope for picking Flour and Meal Best Penmaenmawr Stone Loaves of Bread for breaking purposes Beer and Porter Leather Straw and Potatoes Wood for cutting into Fire- Drapery, Ac. wood Cord and Twill • Carbolic Soap Coal and Slack Earthenware Shoes and Clogs Samples of any of the above may be seen on application to the Master of the Workhouse. The work of the Lower Division comprises a regular course of instruction in English, French. the rudiments of Latin, elementary Mathematics and Science, with Reading, Writing, Arithmetic, Drawing, Drill, and Vocal Music, and all other elements of a sound modern education.
